ELA.overview: ELA 7 moves through units on short stories, a novel (The Call of the Wild), informational and argument reading, poetry, A Midsummer Night's Dream, research, Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry, and speeches/debate. Read texts aloud together when they are hard, ask your child to point to the exact words that prove each answer, and require written responses in claim–evidence–explanation form. Keep 20–30 minutes of independent reading daily toward the 25-book goal, and use the rubrics in each assessment key so feedback is specific.

weeks.prep: Print 'Thank You, Ma'am' from CommonLit; sticky notes; a reading-interest survey (make one: favorite genres, last book loved, reading habits). Read the story yourself first (about 10 minutes).
misconceptions: Treating characterization as only what the narrator says directly. Show that Mrs. Jones's actions (dragging Roger home, feeding him) reveal more than any adjective.
Calling any group of words with a noun a clause. A clause has a subject AND a verb; a phrase lacks one of them.

days.guide: Your child completes the survey, sets a 25-book goal and writes a journal entry about a memorable story. Help pick the first independent book and set a daily reading time. Check before moving on: ask "What makes a reading goal realistic?" Look for: It fits your reading speed and time: e.g., 25 books ≈ one book every 1½ weeks with 20–30 minutes a day.

questions.q: What makes a reading goal realistic?
questions.a: It fits your reading speed and time: e.g., 25 books ≈ one book every 1½ weeks with 20–30 minutes a day.

days.guide: Read the story aloud (alternate paragraphs). Model one sticky note: 'Trait: strong/bold — Evidence: she kicks him and drags him home.' Your child adds at least five more. Check before moving on: ask "What does Roger try to do at the start, and what happens?" Look for: He tries to snatch Mrs. Jones's purse; the strap breaks, he falls, and she grabs him and drags him to her home.

questions.q: What does Roger try to do at the start, and what happens?
questions.a: He tries to snatch Mrs. Jones's purse; the strap breaks, he falls, and she grabs him and drags him to her home.

questions.q: Why does Roger say he wanted the money?
questions.a: To buy a pair of blue suede shoes.

days.guide: Explain direct (narrator states the trait) vs indirect (speech, thoughts, actions, effect on others, looks). Your child fills the chart and writes a paragraph on how she changes Roger, citing two quotes. Check before moving on: ask "Give an example of indirect characterization of Mrs. Jones." Look for: She leaves her purse on the daybed where Roger could take it, showing trust and kindness.

questions.q: Give an example of indirect characterization of Mrs. Jones.
questions.a: She leaves her purse on the daybed where Roger could take it, showing trust and kindness.
He stops wanting to run and wants her to trust him; he sits where she can see him and can barely get out 'Thank you, ma'am' at the end.

days.guide: Teach: phrase = no subject-verb pair (prepositional: 'in the dark'; participial: 'carrying a purse'); clause = subject + verb; independent stands alone, dependent begins with words like because, when, although. Your child labels 15 sentences. Check before moving on: ask "Label: 'When she got him home'" Look for: Dependent clause (subject 'she', verb 'got', begins with 'when').

questions.a: Dependent clause (subject 'she', verb 'got', begins with 'when').
Prepositional phrase.

days.guide: Discuss: was Mrs. Jones's choice wise? Model building on a point ('I agree, and also…'). Then give the quiz (see key). Check before moving on: ask "What does Mrs. Jones give Roger at the end?" Look for: Ten dollars to buy the blue suede shoes (after feeding him).

questions.q: What does Mrs. Jones give Roger at the end?
questions.a: Ten dollars to buy the blue suede shoes (after feeding him).

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Direct characterization = narrator states a trait; 2) Indirect = shown through words, actions, thoughts, looks, effects; 3) Example: she makes him wash his face (caring/firm); 4) 'Because he was hungry' = dependent clause; 5) 'with blue suede shoes' = prepositional phrase. Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear claim, two or more accurately quoted and cited pieces of evidence, explanation that connects each quote to the claim; 3 = claim and evidence but thin explanation; 2 = evidence summarized rather than quoted, or weak link to claim; 1 = opinion without evidence. Discussion checklist: listens, builds on others, cites the text, stays respectful.

weeks.prep: Print 'The Most Dangerous Game' (public domain), plot diagram template. Preview: the villain hunts humans; violence is mostly implied but tense.
misconceptions: Confusing setting description with plot events. Setting = time, place, atmosphere (dark, 'Ship-Trap Island').
Thinking foreshadowing is the same as a prediction the reader makes. Foreshadowing is a clue the author plants.

days.guide: Read the first third aloud. Your child lists setting details that create danger (the island's name, sailors' dread, the dark, the rocks, the 'moist black velvet' night). Check before moving on: ask "Why do sailors fear Ship-Trap Island?" Look for: It has a bad reputation; Whitney says sailors have a 'curious dread' of the place.

questions.q: Why do sailors fear Ship-Trap Island?
questions.a: It has a bad reputation; Whitney says sailors have a 'curious dread' of the place.

questions.q: What happens to Rainsford early in the story?
questions.a: He falls off the yacht at night and swims to the island.

days.guide: Read the middle. Your child charts the three tricks on a plot diagram and notes foreshadowing (e.g., Whitney's talk of 'hunters and huntees'). Check before moving on: ask "Name Rainsford's three tricks." Look for: Malay man-catcher (injures Zaroff's shoulder), Burmese tiger pit (kills one of the hounds), Ugandan knife trap (kills Ivan).

questions.a: Malay man-catcher (injures Zaroff's shoulder), Burmese tiger pit (kills one of the hounds), Ugandan knife trap (kills Ivan).

days.guide: Finish the story. Your child writes a paragraph on how the jungle setting drives conflict with three cited details. Check before moving on: ask "How does Rainsford escape the final chase?" Look for: He leaps off a cliff into the sea, then sneaks into Zaroff's bedroom.

questions.q: How does Rainsford escape the final chase?
questions.a: He leaps off a cliff into the sea, then sneaks into Zaroff's bedroom.

questions.q: What does the last line imply?
questions.a: 'He had never slept in a better bed' implies Rainsford killed Zaroff.

days.guide: Teach each root with two examples on the board (mal: malfunction, malicious; bene: benefit, benevolent; vis/vid: vision, evident; dict: predict, dictionary; port: transport, portable). Your child skims the story for words with these roots, then builds a 15-word web with a definition for each. Check by covering the definitions and having your child explain three words using the root.

questions.a: Bad — malicious, malfunction.
Carry — transport, portable.

days.guide: Give the reading quiz with two constructed responses, then the 10-item root quiz, without notes. Grade together using the key, and have your child rewrite one constructed response to add a quotation if it lacked one. Check before moving on: ask "What does Zaroff hunt and why?" Look for: Humans, because animals no longer challenged him; he wants prey that can reason.

questions.q: What does Zaroff hunt and why?
questions.a: Humans, because animals no longer challenged him; he wants prey that can reason.

weeks.assessment_key: Reading quiz: CR1 (setting builds suspense) proficient answers cite the island's name, the dark jungle, the sounds of the hunt. CR2 (Rainsford changes) proficient: he begins saying animals have no feelings and ends understanding the hunted's fear. Root quiz: mal = bad, bene = good, vis/vid = see, dict = say, port = carry (plus five word meanings: benefit = good result, dictate = say aloud to be written, visible = can be seen, malnutrition = bad nourishment, export = carry out).

weeks.prep: Print 'The Tell-Tale Heart' and find the LibriVox audio. Parental preview: a murder and dismemberment, told calmly; suitable for most 7th graders, but read first.
misconceptions: Believing the narrator because he says he is sane. Point to his actions: the obsession with the eye, the murder, hearing a heart.
Putting commas between cumulative adjectives ('three old men'). Use the 'and' test.

days.guide: Play the LibriVox recording while your child follows the printed text, pausing after each paragraph. Your child marks every place the narrator insists he is not mad (e.g., the opening 'why will you say that I am mad?'). Ask: why would a sane person need to keep saying so?

questions.q: Why does the narrator kill the old man?
questions.a: Because of the old man's 'vulture' eye — not for money or anger.

days.guide: Draw a T-chart labeled 'What he claims' and 'What his actions show.' Model one row ('I am calm' vs. he shrieks and confesses), then your child adds at least five rows with quotes. Finish with a 3–4 sentence explanation of why he is unreliable.

questions.a: He insists he is calm and sane while describing an obsessive murder and hearing a dead man's heart.

days.guide: Read the climax aloud twice, once flatly and once with the dashes and repetition emphasized. Model how 'louder! louder! louder!' speeds the pace, then your child finds two more examples (dashes, the repeated heartbeat, sound words) and writes a paragraph explaining how they create a tense, frantic mood.

questions.a: The repetition speeds the pace and shows rising panic, building tension.

days.guide: Teach the rule: if 'and' between the adjectives sounds right and order can switch, use a comma. Your child edits 12 sentences. Check before moving on: ask "'The dark, silent room'—comma correct?" Look for: Yes: 'dark and silent' works.

questions.a: Yes: 'dark and silent' works.
No comma: 'old and wooden' sounds odd; they are cumulative.

days.guide: Review the officers' visit in the story, then your child rewrites the climax in about 300 words from an officer's point of view (third person or first person 'we'), including what the officers notice about the narrator. Then give the point-of-view quiz. Check before moving on: ask "What does the narrator do at the end?" Look for: He confesses, shrieking to tear up the planks to find the heart.

questions.q: What does the narrator do at the end?
questions.a: He confesses, shrieking to tear up the planks to find the heart.

weeks.assessment_key: POV quiz: 1) First person. 2) Unreliable narrator = one whose account can't be trusted. 3) Evidence: insists he is not mad. 4) Officers came because a neighbor heard a shriek. Rewrite rubric: 4 = consistent third-person/officer POV, accurate events, shows officers' growing suspicion, ~300 words; 3 = minor POV slips; 2 = retells same POV; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Writing notebook, colored pens; reread 'Thank You, Ma'am' as a mentor text for dialogue and a quick, vivid opening.
misconceptions: Summarizing the whole day instead of one moment. Have your child zoom in on a 10-minute 'seed' moment rather than a 'watermelon' topic like 'my vacation'.
Rushing the climax in one sentence. Teach 'slow down the hot moment' with sensory details, internal thoughts and short sentences.
Ending with 'and then I went home.' Ending should reflect on what the moment taught or changed.

days.guide: Model your own heart map (people, places, firsts, fears). Your child brainstorms at least 10 moments, circles three with a clear conflict or turning point, and tells you each in 1 minute; pick the one with the most feeling. Check before moving on: ask "Why is 'the day I froze on the high dive' better than 'summer camp'?" Look for: It is one focused moment with a conflict (fear) and a turning point, so it can be told in detail.

questions.q: Why is 'the day I froze on the high dive' better than 'summer camp'?
questions.a: It is one focused moment with a conflict (fear) and a turning point, so it can be told in detail.

days.guide: Draw a story mountain. Your child fills in exposition (who/where), 3+ rising-action events, the climax, falling action and reflection. Check before moving on: ask "Where does the reflection go and what does it do?" Look for: At the end; it explains what the narrator learned or how they changed.

questions.q: Where does the reflection go and what does it do?
questions.a: At the end; it explains what the narrator learned or how they changed.

days.guide: Show how Hughes starts in the action ('She was a large woman with a large purse…' and the snatch happens at once). Your child drafts two openings (dialogue, action, or setting) and chooses the stronger. Check before moving on: ask "Rewrite 'I am going to tell you about my first race' as an action lead." Look for: Example: 'My spikes bit into the track as the starter raised the gun.'

questions.q: Rewrite 'I am going to tell you about my first race' as an action lead.
questions.a: Example: 'My spikes bit into the track as the starter raised the gun.'

days.guide: Your child finishes the draft (600–900 words). Check that the climax is at least a full paragraph with senses and thoughts. Check before moving on: ask "Name three ways to slow down a climax." Look for: Sensory details, internal thoughts/feelings, dialogue, and short sentences or fragments for pace.

questions.q: Name three ways to slow down a climax.
questions.a: Sensory details, internal thoughts/feelings, dialogue, and short sentences or fragments for pace.

days.guide: Your child reads aloud; you give two specific glows ('Your dialogue sounds real') and one grow ('Show what you were thinking at the top'). Your child writes 2–3 revision goals. Check before moving on: ask "What makes feedback useful?" Look for: It is specific and points to a place in the draft, not just 'good job'.

questions.a: It is specific and points to a place in the draft, not just 'good job'.

weeks.assessment_key: Completion check (not graded for polish): 600–900 words; identifiable exposition, conflict, climax and reflection; at least one dialogue or sensory passage; 2–3 written revision goals. Mark 'complete' only if all parts are present.

weeks.prep: Print 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi' (Project Gutenberg); revision checklist; choose an unseen CommonLit short story with its questions for Day 5 (read it yourself first).
misconceptions: Writing a theme as one word ('courage'). A theme is a complete sentence about life: 'True courage means protecting others even when you are afraid.'
Putting opinions ('This awesome story…') into an objective summary. Summaries report only what happens.

days.guide: Your child revises with the checklist: add 3+ transitions, cut or shorten one slow section, expand the climax. Compare before and after aloud. Check before moving on: ask "Which transitions show time passing?" Look for: 'Later that afternoon', 'by the time', 'meanwhile', 'suddenly'.

questions.a: 'Later that afternoon', 'by the time', 'meanwhile', 'suddenly'.

days.guide: Your child edits the narrative for one thing at a time: commas after introductory clauses, run-ons, then spelling. Read it aloud together to catch missing words, then your child types and prints the final copy with a title. Check before moving on: ask "Correct: 'When the whistle blew I ran.'" Look for: 'When the whistle blew, I ran.' — comma after an introductory dependent clause.

questions.q: Correct: 'When the whistle blew I ran.'
questions.a: 'When the whistle blew, I ran.' — comma after an introductory dependent clause.

days.guide: Read the story together, taking turns by section. Your child records each conflict (Karait, Nag, the eggs, Nagaina) in a chart: what happens, what Rikki does, and what it shows about his courage. Ask how Rikki's confidence grows after each fight.

questions.q: How does Rikki come to live with Teddy's family?
questions.a: A flood washes him out of his burrow; the family finds and revives him.

Karait (small snake in the dust), Nag (in the bathroom, with the father's shotgun finishing him), then Nagaina (after he destroys her eggs and she threatens Teddy; he follows her into her hole and kills her).

days.guide: Model one objective-summary sentence. Your child writes a summary and a theme statement with three pieces of evidence. Check before moving on: ask "A strong theme statement with evidence?" Look for: 'Courage grows through action': Rikki is young but kills Karait, then Nag, then faces Nagaina in her burrow.

questions.q: A strong theme statement with evidence?
questions.a: 'Courage grows through action': Rikki is young but kills Karait, then Nag, then faces Nagaina in her burrow.

days.guide: Give the unseen CommonLit story and its questions with a 45-minute limit and no help. Score with the CommonLit key and the constructed-response guidance below; note weak skills (theme, point of view) for review. Check before moving on: ask "What does an objective summary leave out?" Look for: Opinions, judgments and minor details.

questions.q: What does an objective summary leave out?
questions.a: Opinions, judgments and minor details.

weeks.assessment_key: Narrative rubric (4–1 each): Focus/ideas (one clear moment, meaningful reflection); Organization (strong lead, logical sequence, transitions); Development (dialogue, sensory detail, slowed climax); Language/conventions (clause commas, spelling). Proficient = mostly 3s. Unit test: score selected responses with the CommonLit key; constructed responses proficient if they state an answer, quote the story accurately, and explain; theme answers must be complete sentences.

weeks.prep: Get The Call of the Wild (Gutenberg or library); a map showing California, Washington, the Alaska panhandle and the Yukon; a short Klondike Gold Rush article (National Park Service 'Klondike Gold Rush' pages work). Parental preview: the novel includes dog fights, beatings with a club and animal deaths.
misconceptions: Reading Buck's changes only as 'getting worse.' London presents them as adapting to survive — help your child weigh both views with evidence.
Guessing word meanings without evidence. Model hunting for a synonym, contrast or example clue in the same or next sentence.

days.guide: Read the article together. Your child locates Santa Clara, Seattle, Skagway and Dawson on the map, traces the route north and explains why big dogs were valuable. Check before moving on: ask "Why were large, strong dogs stolen and sold in 1897?" Look for: Gold was found in the Klondike; prospectors needed strong, warm-coated dogs to haul sleds over snow.

questions.q: Why were large, strong dogs stolen and sold in 1897?
questions.a: Gold was found in the Klondike; prospectors needed strong, warm-coated dogs to haul sleds over snow.

days.guide: Read Chapter 1, 'Into the Primitive', aloud or with audio. Your child lists three lessons from the man in the red sweater with quotes. Check before moving on: ask "Who sells Buck and why?" Look for: Manuel, the gardener's helper on Judge Miller's place, to pay his gambling debts.

questions.a: Manuel, the gardener's helper on Judge Miller's place, to pay his gambling debts.

questions.q: What does the man in the red sweater teach Buck?
questions.a: That a man with a club is a 'lawgiver' who must be obeyed — Buck is beaten until he stops attacking, though he is not broken in spirit.

days.guide: Model one word with a context clue. Your child defines 10 words from chapters 1–2 (e.g., primitive, imperious, ferocity, latent, discretion), then checks a dictionary and notes which clues worked. Check before moving on: ask "What does 'primitive' mean in the chapter title?" Look for: Early, wild, basic — the uncivilized state Buck is entering.

questions.q: What does 'primitive' mean in the chapter title?
questions.a: Early, wild, basic — the uncivilized state Buck is entering.

days.guide: Read Chapter 2, 'The Law of Club and Fang'. Your child writes a journal entry on Curly's death and what it teaches Buck. Check before moving on: ask "How does Curly die?" Look for: She makes friendly advances to a husky, is slashed, and when she falls the other huskies swarm and kill her.

questions.a: She makes friendly advances to a husky, is slashed, and when she falls the other huskies swarm and kill her.

questions.q: What lesson does Buck take from it?
questions.a: There is no fair play: once a dog is down, it is finished — so he must never go down.

days.guide: Discuss 'becoming worse or adapting?' — each side gives two pieces of evidence. Then give the chapters 1–2 quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Name two survival skills Buck learns in Chapter 2." Look for: Digging a sleeping hole in the snow; eating fast and stealing food (bacon) when hungry; finding water under ice.

questions.q: Name two survival skills Buck learns in Chapter 2.
questions.a: Digging a sleeping hole in the snow; eating fast and stealing food (bacon) when hungry; finding water under ice.

weeks.assessment_key: Chapters 1–2 quiz: 1) Buck is a St. Bernard–Scotch shepherd mix living at Judge Miller's place in the Santa Clara Valley. 2) Manuel sells him to pay gambling debts. 3) The man in the red sweater teaches the law of the club. 4) Curly is killed by huskies after a friendly approach — the law of fang. 5) Perrault and François are the French-Canadian mail couriers who buy him. 6) Spitz is the lead dog Buck comes to hate. Journal rubric: 4 = cites specific events and explains the change in Buck's thinking; 2 = retells only.

weeks.prep: The Call of the Wild; a character tracker (columns: trait gained/lost, evidence, page).
misconceptions: Calling 'Buck pulled hard, and Spitz watched' complex. It's compound — two independent clauses joined by 'and'. Complex needs a dependent clause (because, when, although…).
Seeing the Buck–Spitz rivalry as random violence. London frames it as a struggle for leadership of the team.

days.guide: Read Chapter 3, 'The Dominant Primordial Beast'. Your child charts each clash (Spitz taking Buck's sleeping nest at Lake Le Barge, Buck defending Pike from Spitz, the rabbit chase) leading to the fight. Check before moving on: ask "What triggers the final fight?" Look for: During a rabbit chase Spitz cuts across and kills the rabbit Buck is chasing; Buck attacks him.

questions.a: During a rabbit chase Spitz cuts across and kills the rabbit Buck is chasing; Buck attacks him.
He uses imagination as well as strength — feints high and goes low, breaking Spitz's front legs; then the circle of dogs closes in on Spitz.

days.guide: Model one tracker row: 'Gained: cunning — he sides with Pike to undermine Spitz (p. __).' Your child adds at least four traits gained and two lost, each with a page citation. Ask which change matters most for his survival and why.

questions.q: Give a trait Buck gains and evidence.
questions.a: Cunning — he deliberately undermines Spitz's authority by siding with dogs Spitz punishes.

days.guide: Teach the four sentence types with one example each. Your child labels sentences in a London passage and writes one of each about Buck. Check before moving on: ask "Write a compound-complex sentence about Buck." Look for: Example: 'Because Spitz stole his nest, Buck attacked, and the fight was on.' (one dependent + two independent clauses)

questions.q: Write a compound-complex sentence about Buck.
questions.a: Example: 'Because Spitz stole his nest, Buck attacked, and the fight was on.' (one dependent + two independent clauses)

days.guide: Read Chapter 4 aloud or with audio. Your child lists how Buck takes the lead position and two ways he leads differently than Spitz, with quotes. Discuss whether Buck is a better leader or just a stronger one.

questions.q: How does Buck get the lead position?
questions.a: He refuses to let Sol-leks take it and stays out of reach of François's club until they give him the lead.

questions.q: How is he different as leader?
questions.a: He enforces discipline firmly (on Pike and Joe) so the team works together and makes record time.

days.guide: Give the chapters 3–4 quiz without the book. Then model combining one set of choppy sentences into a compound-complex sentence; your child combines the other four and labels the independent and dependent clauses. Check before moving on: ask "Combine: The trail was hard. Dave was sick. He would not leave the traces." Look for: 'Although Dave was sick and the trail was hard, he would not leave the traces, and he pulled until he collapsed.' (any correct compound-complex)

questions.q: Combine: The trail was hard. Dave was sick. He would not leave the traces.
questions.a: 'Although Dave was sick and the trail was hard, he would not leave the traces, and he pulled until he collapsed.' (any correct compound-complex)

weeks.assessment_key: Chapters 3–4 quiz: 1) Spitz steals Buck's nest at Lake Le Barge. 2) Buck sides with Pike against Spitz to undermine him. 3) The rabbit chase sparks the fight; Spitz dies when the pack closes in. 4) François tries Sol-leks as leader; Buck refuses until he gets the lead. 5) Under Buck the team improves. 6) Dave, sick, insists on pulling until he is shot. Combining exercise: each of 5 rewrites must contain at least one dependent and two independent clauses with correct commas.

weeks.prep: The Call of the Wild; Venn diagram template; connotation word sets on cards.
misconceptions: Treating a foil as an enemy. A foil is a character whose contrast highlights another's traits (Hal's cruelty highlights Thornton's kindness).
Thinking synonyms are interchangeable. 'Thin', 'skinny', 'gaunt' and 'emaciated' differ in feeling and degree.

days.guide: Read Chapter 5 together. Your child lists at least five choices Hal, Charles and Mercedes make that show ignorance, each with a quote, and predicts what will happen to them. Ask what Buck's refusal to get up at the end shows he senses.

questions.a: Overloading the sled, overfeeding then starving the dogs, Mercedes riding on the sled, beating exhausted dogs, ignoring warnings about the melting ice.

days.guide: Define a foil (a character who contrasts with another to highlight traits). Your child fills a Venn diagram comparing how Hal and John Thornton treat the dogs, with at least three differences and one similarity, then writes two sentences explaining how the contrast makes Thornton's kindness stand out. Check before moving on: ask "How are Hal and Thornton foils?" Look for: Hal beats and starves the dogs; Thornton is gentle and saves Buck — the contrast makes Thornton's kindness stand out.

questions.q: How are Hal and Thornton foils?
questions.a: Hal beats and starves the dogs; Thornton is gentle and saves Buck — the contrast makes Thornton's kindness stand out.

days.guide: Model ranking 'thin, skinny, gaunt, emaciated' from mildest to most extreme and discuss the feeling of each. Your child ranks four more word sets, then finds three of London's word choices in Chapter 5 describing the starving dogs and explains the effect. Check before moving on: ask "Rank thin, skinny, gaunt, emaciated from mild to extreme." Look for: Thin, skinny, gaunt, emaciated.

questions.q: Rank thin, skinny, gaunt, emaciated from mild to extreme.
questions.a: Thin, skinny, gaunt, emaciated.

days.guide: Read Chapter 6. Your child lists three things Buck does out of love for Thornton (the rapids, Black Burton, the thousand-pound sled) and writes a paragraph on how this love differs from his earlier obedience to people. Ask: is this the first time Buck has truly loved a human?

questions.q: What does Buck do for Thornton?
questions.a: Saves him from the rapids, attacks Black Burton, and wins Thornton's bet by pulling a sled with a thousand pounds of flour.

days.guide: Hold a 10-minute discussion on loyalty: Buck to Thornton, Dave to his work, and whether Buck owes loyalty to his old life. Each speaker must cite one page. Then give the chapters 5–6 quiz.

questions.a: They fall through the river ice and drown with the dogs.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Hal, Charles, Mercedes are inexperienced. 2) Thornton warns them about the ice. 3) Buck refuses to rise; Thornton cuts him loose. 4) Buck saves Thornton in rapids. 5) Buck wins the $1,600 bet pulling 1,000 lb. Venn diagram: at least 3 contrasts with evidence.

weeks.prep: The Call of the Wild; one film adaptation clip (the 2020 film is widely available; preview it — it changes the plot and uses a CGI Buck); theme tracker.
misconceptions: Including opinions or minor details in the summary. Check every sentence: 'Could someone who hated the book agree this happened?'
Writing a theme as a single word. Coach: 'What does the book say ABOUT survival?'

days.guide: Read Chapter 7 together. Your child notes the two pulls on Buck (Thornton and the wild) and what finally decides between them. Discuss whether the ending is happy, sad or both, citing the final paragraphs.

questions.a: While Buck is away in the forest, the Yeehats attack the camp and kill Thornton, Hans, Pete and the dogs.
Buck kills several Yeehats, joins the wolf pack, becomes the legendary 'Ghost Dog', and returns each summer to mourn at the place Thornton died.

days.guide: Model a two-sentence chunk. Your child writes a 200-word objective summary from Buck's kidnapping to his joining the wolves. Check before moving on: ask "Which sentence is objective: 'Hal was a cruel fool' or 'Hal beat the starving dogs'?" Look for: 'Hal beat the starving dogs' — it reports an event without judgment.

questions.q: Which sentence is objective: 'Hal was a cruel fool' or 'Hal beat the starving dogs'?
questions.a: 'Hal beat the starving dogs' — it reports an event without judgment.

days.guide: Your child chooses one theme and finds six quotations from at least four chapters that develop it, writing one sentence of commentary for each. Check that the final theme statement is a complete sentence, not one word. Check before moving on: ask "Write a complete theme statement about nature vs. civilization." Look for: Example: 'When the comforts of civilization are stripped away, instincts hidden deep inside can take over.'

questions.q: Write a complete theme statement about nature vs. civilization.
questions.a: Example: 'When the comforts of civilization are stripped away, instincts hidden deep inside can take over.'

days.guide: Watch 10–15 minutes of an adaptation covering a scene you've read. Your child lists two changes (plot, characters, tone) and explains a possible reason for each (audience, rating, length, visual effect). Check before moving on: ask "Why might a film soften the violence?" Look for: To reach a family audience and earn a lower rating.

questions.q: Why might a film soften the violence?
questions.a: To reach a family audience and earn a lower rating.

days.guide: Model turning a topic into a thesis about how setting shapes Buck. Your child writes the thesis and outlines three body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence and two quotations with page numbers. Check that every topic sentence supports the thesis.

questions.a: 'The brutal Northland setting transforms Buck from a pampered pet into a leader of the wild by teaching him the law of club and fang, the need for cunning, and the pull of his ancestors.'

weeks.assessment_key: Summary rubric: 4 = 180–220 words, all major stages (Judge Miller's → kidnapping → club/fang lessons → Spitz → leader → Hal's party → Thornton → wolves), no opinions; 3 = one stage missing; 2 = opinions or major gaps; 1 = retells a single part. Outline: arguable thesis about setting; three topic sentences each tied to the thesis; two cited quotes per paragraph.

weeks.prep: Essay outline; Purdue OWL pages on quotations and MLA in-text citations; print 'To Build a Fire' (public domain) excerpt for the test. Parental preview: in 'To Build a Fire' the man freezes to death.
misconceptions: Dropping quotes in without introduction ('plop quotes'). Teach the sandwich: introduce, quote, explain.
Putting the period before the parenthetical citation. MLA: "...the club" (London 12).

days.guide: Show three hook types (question, vivid image, quotation). Your child drafts an introduction with a hook, two to three sentences of context (author, title, situation), and the thesis as the last sentence. Read it aloud and ask: does the thesis say how setting shapes Buck?

questions.q: What three parts should the introduction have?
questions.a: Hook, brief context (author, title, basic plot), and thesis.

days.guide: Model one claim-evidence-commentary paragraph. Your child drafts three body paragraphs with embedded, cited quotes. Check before moving on: ask "Punctuate: London writes the club was a revelation (page 14)." Look for: London writes that the club 'was a revelation' (14).

questions.q: Punctuate: London writes the club was a revelation (page 14).
questions.a: London writes that the club 'was a revelation' (14).

days.guide: Your child drafts a conclusion that restates the thesis in new words and ends with a larger insight. Then they add or improve transitions at the start of each body paragraph ('Beyond physical survival…', 'Most importantly…'). Read the essay aloud together to test flow.

questions.a: Restate the thesis in new words, sum up the reasoning, and leave a final insight — not new evidence.

days.guide: Your child edits in three passes: sentence variety (start some sentences with a phrase or clause), quotation punctuation, then spelling. Check two quotes together for correct MLA format before your child prints the final essay. Check before moving on: ask "Fix: Buck learns 'the law of club and fang.' (London 20)" Look for: Buck learns 'the law of club and fang' (London 20).

questions.q: Fix: Buck learns 'the law of club and fang.' (London 20)
questions.a: Buck learns 'the law of club and fang' (London 20).

days.guide: Give the unit 2 test: Call of the Wild passages plus the 'To Build a Fire' excerpt, 50 minutes, no book. Score with the key and discuss any constructed response below proficient. Check before moving on: ask "In 'To Build a Fire,' why does the man's fire go out?" Look for: He builds it under a snow-laden spruce tree; his movements shake the branches and snow falls and smothers it.

questions.q: In 'To Build a Fire,' why does the man's fire go out?
questions.a: He builds it under a snow-laden spruce tree; his movements shake the branches and snow falls and smothers it.

weeks.assessment_key: Essay rubric (4–1): Thesis is arguable and about setting; each body paragraph has claim, 2 embedded quotes with citations, and commentary; logical transitions; conclusion; correct MLA punctuation. Unit test answers: The Call of the Wild items as in prior quizzes; 'To Build a Fire': the man ignores the old-timer from Sulphur Creek's advice not to travel alone in extreme cold; the dog's instinct is wiser than the man's judgment; the man dies and the dog heads to camp; theme — nature is indifferent and human pride/lack of imagination can be fatal.

weeks.prep: Three ReadWorks articles (free account) on technology and teens, including one on teen screen time; a two-central-ideas graphic organizer.
misconceptions: Confusing topic ('screen time') with central idea ('Too much screen time can hurt sleep').
Choosing structure by one signal word. Look at how the whole article is organized.

days.guide: Preview headings and first lines of three articles. Your child labels each structure and names the signal words. Check before moving on: ask "Which signal words suggest cause-effect?" Look for: Because, as a result, therefore, led to, consequently.

questions.a: Because, as a result, therefore, led to, consequently.
Problem, issue, one solution, to fix this.

days.guide: Read the screen-time article together. Your child uses the organizer to trace two central ideas, noting in each paragraph which idea it develops and the supporting detail. Ask: what does the author want us to understand about screen time?

questions.q: What's the difference between a topic and a central idea?
questions.a: A topic is the subject (screen time); a central idea is the point the author makes about it (e.g., heavy screen use is linked to poorer sleep).

days.guide: Model the first sentence of a summary (title, author, central ideas). Your child writes a 5–7 sentence objective summary including both central ideas and key details. Check for and remove any opinion words.

questions.a: Personal opinions, 'I think', and minor details.

days.guide: Introduce the 10 words with student-friendly definitions and an example. Your child writes a sentence about the article using each word correctly. Quiz orally by giving a definition and asking for the word.

questions.a: 'The article reports a significant drop in sleep among heavy users.'

days.guide: Give an unseen ReadWorks article with its questions, plus two short prompts: name the structure with a signal word, and state two central ideas. Score with the ReadWorks key and the rubric below. Check before moving on: ask "How do you find a central idea?" Look for: Look at the title, introduction, topic sentences and conclusion for the repeated point.

questions.q: How do you find a central idea?
questions.a: Look at the title, introduction, topic sentences and conclusion for the repeated point.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: use ReadWorks key for multiple choice; for structure, correct label + one signal word cited; central ideas stated as full sentences with two supporting details each. Summary rubric: 4 = both central ideas, key details, objective, concise.

weeks.prep: A CommonLit or newspaper op-ed on later school start times; a persuasive ad or speech video (1–3 minutes); rating chart (relevant? sufficient?).
misconceptions: Thinking any statistic is good evidence. It must be relevant to the claim and enough to support it.
Confusing counterclaim with the author's claim.

days.guide: Read the op-ed aloud. Model labeling the claim, then your child labels reasons, evidence and the counterclaim in different colors. Ask your child to state the claim in one sentence.

questions.a: The opposing view the author acknowledges (and usually rebuts).

days.guide: Make a chart with each piece of evidence and columns 'relevant?' and 'sufficient?'. Your child rates each one and explains, e.g., a single anecdote is weak while a study of thousands of students is strong. Ask which piece of evidence is most convincing.

questions.q: Is 'my cousin is always tired' sufficient evidence for later start times?
questions.a: No — it is one anecdote; studies of many students would be stronger.

days.guide: Your child finds phrases where the author introduces and responds to opponents ('Critics claim…', 'Yet…', 'However…') and explains how the author makes her own view sound more reasonable. Ask: did she treat opponents fairly? Check before moving on: ask "Why acknowledge opponents?" Look for: It shows fairness and lets the author rebut them, making the argument stronger.

questions.a: It shows fairness and lets the author rebut them, making the argument stronger.

days.guide: Watch a 1–3 minute ad or speech twice. Your child lists each claim and any bandwagon appeals or loaded words, then rates the reasoning. Discuss how the techniques try to persuade without real evidence.

questions.a: Arguing you should do something because everyone else does.
Emotionally charged words meant to sway feelings rather than prove a point.

days.guide: Give a new argument text with the quiz items in the key. Your child works independently for 30 minutes. Review answers together, focusing on evidence evaluation.

questions.a: Evidence is relevant, sufficient and logically connected to the claim.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (for any argument text): identify claim (one sentence), two reasons, one piece of evidence and whether it is relevant/sufficient, counterclaim and rebuttal, and one rhetorical technique. Proficient = all identified correctly with quoted text. Chart: each piece of evidence rated with a reason.

weeks.prep: Two articles on zoos (one pro, one con — CommonLit, Newsela or Britannica ProCon); highlighters in three colors (statistics, expert, anecdote).
misconceptions: Thinking both authors must disagree on facts. They often use different facts or emphasize different ones.
Writing a position with no counterclaim.

days.guide: Read the pro-zoo article together. Your child highlights statistics in one color, expert quotes in another and anecdotes in a third, then counts each type. Ask which type the author relies on most.

questions.a: A quote from a zoologist or conservation scientist.

days.guide: Read the anti-zoo article and highlight it the same way. Your child compares the counts with Text A and notes which facts appear in only one article. Check before moving on: ask "Example of anecdotal evidence?" Look for: A story about a single animal showing stress behaviors.

questions.a: A story about a single animal showing stress behaviors.

days.guide: Model a contrast sentence ('While A emphasizes…, B focuses on…'). Your child writes a paragraph comparing how the two authors use different evidence and what effect each choice has on the reader. Check before moving on: ask "Model sentence?" Look for: 'While Author A emphasizes breeding programs for endangered species, Author B focuses on animals' stress in captivity.'

questions.a: 'While Author A emphasizes breeding programs for endangered species, Author B focuses on animals' stress in captivity.'

days.guide: Your child chooses a position on 'Should zoos exist?' and fills the organizer with at least five pieces of evidence from both articles, noting the source and type. Check that each piece directly supports the position. Check before moving on: ask "What makes evidence strong?" Look for: Specific, credible source, directly supports the claim.

questions.a: Specific, credible source, directly supports the claim.

days.guide: Your child drafts a one-sentence claim and a counterclaim-with-rebuttal sentence. Give feedback: is the claim arguable, and does the rebuttal answer the opposing reason with evidence? Check before moving on: ask "Example counterclaim sentence?" Look for: 'Some argue that zoos keep animals in unnatural conditions; however, accredited zoos…'

questions.a: 'Some argue that zoos keep animals in unnatural conditions; however, accredited zoos…'

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison paragraph rubric: 4 = names each author's claim, contrasts specific evidence types with examples, explains the effect of each emphasis. Evidence organizer: 5+ items with source and type.

weeks.prep: Evidence organizer from week 13; an argument essay template (intro, 2 body paragraphs, counterclaim/rebuttal, conclusion); 12 wordy practice sentences.
misconceptions: Stating evidence without explaining it. After every quote, require one or two sentences beginning 'This shows…'.
A rebuttal that only repeats the claim. It must answer the opposing reason with evidence.

days.guide: Model an introduction with a hook, two sentences of background on zoos, and the claim. Your child drafts their own and reads it aloud; check that the claim is arguable and appears at the end. Check before moving on: ask "Is 'Zoos are interesting' a claim?" Look for: No — it isn't arguable. A claim: 'Accredited zoos should exist because they protect endangered species.'

questions.a: No — it isn't arguable. A claim: 'Accredited zoos should exist because they protect endangered species.'

days.guide: Your child drafts two body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence (reason), two cited pieces of evidence and explanation after each. Use the question 'So what does this prove?' to push for explanation. Check before moving on: ask "How do you cite a source in-text?" Look for: Name the author or source and add a parenthetical, e.g., (Smith) or (Association of Zoos and Aquariums).

questions.q: How do you cite a source in-text?
questions.a: Name the author or source and add a parenthetical, e.g., (Smith) or (Association of Zoos and Aquariums).

days.guide: Model the 'Some argue… However…' structure. Your child drafts a paragraph that fairly states the opposing view, then rebuts it with evidence. Check that the rebuttal uses evidence, not just repetition.

questions.a: 'Some argue that animals suffer in zoos. However, modern accredited zoos design habitats around natural behaviors and track animal welfare.'

days.guide: Show a wordy sentence and its concise version. Your child fixes 12 practice sentences, then cuts at least five wordy phrases ('in my opinion', 'due to the fact that') from the draft. Check before moving on: ask "Make concise: 'In my personal opinion I think that zoos are basically good.'" Look for: 'Zoos are beneficial.'

questions.q: Make concise: 'In my personal opinion I think that zoos are basically good.'
questions.a: 'Zoos are beneficial.'
'Because'.

days.guide: Your child drafts a conclusion that restates the claim in new words, sums up the reasons, and ends with a call to action. Read the whole draft aloud together. Check before moving on: ask "Example call to action?" Look for: 'Visit and support accredited zoos that fund conservation.'

questions.a: 'Visit and support accredited zoos that fund conservation.'

weeks.assessment_key: Draft completion: introduction with claim; two body paragraphs each with reason + 2 cited evidence + explanation; counterclaim and rebuttal; conclusion with call to action. Check each element present; return with comments.

weeks.prep: Highlighters (3 colors), revision checklist, a timer for the speech; an unseen argument text with questions (CommonLit) for Day 5.
misconceptions: Revising = fixing spelling. Revision is improving ideas and organization; editing is fixing errors.
Reading the speech from paper without eye contact.

days.guide: Your child color-codes the essay: claim (yellow), evidence (green), reasoning (blue). A paragraph with little blue needs more explanation; revise those first. Check that paragraphs are in a logical order with transitions.

questions.q: What does a paragraph with no reasoning color show?
questions.a: Evidence is not explained — add commentary.

days.guide: Your child edits for grammar and adds or fixes in-text citations, then creates a Works Cited page. Check two citations together for format before publishing. Check before moving on: ask "What goes on a Works Cited page?" Look for: Full source information for every source cited.

questions.q: What goes on a Works Cited page?
questions.a: Full source information for every source cited.

days.guide: Your child turns the essay into a 2-minute speech using note cards, not the full essay. Practice once with you timing; give feedback on eye contact and volume, then perform. Check before moving on: ask "Two delivery skills?" Look for: Eye contact and adequate volume.

questions.a: Eye contact and adequate volume.

days.guide: Your child writes a one-paragraph reflection naming the single revision that improved the essay most and explaining why. Ask for a before-and-after example. Check before moving on: ask "Good reflection includes?" Look for: A specific revision, why it mattered, what to do next time.

questions.a: A specific revision, why it mattered, what to do next time.

days.guide: Give an unseen argument text with the unit 3 questions, 45 minutes, no help. Score with the key; review evidence-evaluation answers together. Check before moving on: ask "Author's purpose in an op-ed?" Look for: To persuade.

questions.a: To persuade.

weeks.assessment_key: Argument essay rubric (4–1): Claim (clear, arguable), Evidence (relevant, sufficient, cited), Reasoning (explains), Counterclaim (addressed and rebutted), Organization (transitions), Conventions. Speech: eye contact, volume, pacing, within 2 minutes. Unit test: claim, evidence, purpose, structure correctly identified with quotes.

weeks.prep: Print 'Paul Revere's Ride' (Longfellow), 'Annabel Lee' (Poe), 'Mother to Son' (Hughes); colored pencils; 10 word analogies.
misconceptions: Thinking every poem must rhyme.
Confusing alliteration (repeated initial consonant sounds) with any repetition.

days.guide: Read the first stanzas of 'Paul Revere's Ride' aloud while your child taps the galloping rhythm. Model labeling a rhyme scheme with letters; your child labels two stanzas. Ask how the rhythm matches the story.

questions.q: Rhyme scheme of 'Listen, my children, and you shall hear / Of the midnight ride of Paul Revere, / On the eighteenth of April, in Seventy-five; / Hardly a man is now alive / Who remembers that famous day and year.'
questions.a: AABBA.
'One if by land, and two if by sea' — lanterns in the Old North Church tower.

days.guide: Read 'Annabel Lee' aloud slowly. Your child annotates repetition ('kingdom by the sea', 'Annabel Lee'), internal rhyme and alliteration, then writes how these sounds create a haunting, mournful tone. Check before moving on: ask "Internal rhyme example?" Look for: 'For the moon never beams, without bringing me dreams'.

questions.a: 'For the moon never beams, without bringing me dreams'.

questions.q: What does the speaker claim killed Annabel Lee?
questions.a: A wind from a cloud, sent because the angels envied their love.

days.guide: Read 'Mother to Son' aloud. Your child lists each part of the staircase (tacks, splinters, boards torn up, no carpet) and what hardship it could represent, then writes what the poem says about facing life's struggles. Check before moving on: ask "What does 'Life for me ain't been no crystal stair' mean?" Look for: Her life has not been easy or elegant; it has been hard.

questions.q: What does 'Life for me ain't been no crystal stair' mean?
questions.a: Her life has not been easy or elegant; it has been hard.

questions.q: What does she urge her son?
questions.a: Not to turn back or give up — keep climbing.

days.guide: Tell the stories behind Achilles' heel, Pandora's box and the Good Samaritan. Your child explains each allusion's modern meaning, then completes 10 analogies, saying the relationship aloud ('A is to B as…'). Check before moving on: ask "Achilles' heel?" Look for: A weak spot.

questions.a: A weak spot.
Something that unleashes many troubles.

days.guide: Give the poetry-terms quiz, then an unseen short poem; your child identifies two devices and explains their effect on tone. Review together. Check before moving on: ask "What is meter?" Look for: The rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables.

questions.a: The rhythmic pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables.

weeks.assessment_key: Poetry quiz: alliteration, internal rhyme, meter, rhyme scheme, extended metaphor, allusion, tone — each defined with an example from the week. Unseen poem proficient answer identifies two devices and explains their effect on tone.

weeks.prep: Sonnet 18, 'The Road Not Taken', 'Nothing Gold Can Stay', 'O Captain! My Captain!', a free-verse poem (e.g., Whitman 'When I Heard the Learn'd Astronomer'); audio recording of a poem reading.
misconceptions: Reading 'The Road Not Taken' as simply 'take the road less traveled.' The speaker says the roads were 'really about the same'; the poem is about how we tell our choices later.
Thinking free verse has no craft. It uses line breaks, repetition and imagery.

days.guide: Read Sonnet 18 aloud. Your child brackets the three quatrains and the couplet and writes one sentence summarizing each. Ask where the poem turns and how the couplet answers the opening question.

questions.a: 'So long as men can breathe or eyes can see, / So long lives this, and this gives life to thee' — the poem keeps the beloved alive forever.
Line 9, 'But thy eternal summer shall not fade'.

days.guide: Read both Frost poems aloud twice. Your child writes a theme statement for each with two supporting lines. Discuss the common misreading of 'The Road Not Taken' using the line about the roads being 'really about the same.' Check before moving on: ask "Theme of 'Nothing Gold Can Stay'?" Look for: Beauty and innocence are fleeting.

questions.a: Beauty and innocence are fleeting.
People shape the meaning of their choices when they look back.

days.guide: Read 'O Captain! My Captain!' and a free-verse poem aloud. Your child compares rhyme and rhythm and explains how the steady rhyme of 'O Captain!' creates a formal, mournful mood while free verse feels more conversational.

questions.q: What is 'O Captain! My Captain!' about?
questions.a: An elegy for Abraham Lincoln, the 'captain' who died after the 'ship' (the nation) survived the Civil War.

days.guide: Listen to a recorded reading of one poem twice. Your child notes where the reader pauses, speeds up or emphasizes words and how this changes meaning compared with reading silently. Check before moving on: ask "How can pace change meaning?" Look for: Slow reading can stress grief or seriousness; fast reading can stress excitement.

questions.a: Slow reading can stress grief or seriousness; fast reading can stress excitement.

days.guide: Your child chooses one poem and writes a one-page analysis with a claim about how its form shapes meaning, citing at least two specific lines. Check the claim before they draft. Check before moving on: ask "Example claim?" Look for: The sonnet's final couplet resolves the argument by claiming poetry makes beauty eternal.

questions.a: The sonnet's final couplet resolves the argument by claiming poetry makes beauty eternal.

weeks.assessment_key: Analysis rubric: 4 = names the form accurately, cites at least two specific lines, explains how form (rhyme, structure, line breaks) shapes meaning; 3 = form and meaning linked loosely; 2 = summary only; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Poetry notebook; mentor poems from weeks 16–17; semester checkpoint (choose a passage with questions + 10 grammar items).
misconceptions: Writing imagery of sight only.
Memorizing lines without pauses for meaning.

days.guide: Brainstorm a place with your child for each sense. Your child writes a free-verse poem of 12+ lines with at least one image for each of the five senses. Read it aloud and identify each sense together.

questions.a: 'The screen door slaps against its frame.'

days.guide: Your child chooses a form (sonnet, haiku sequence or ballad stanza) and studies the mentor poem's pattern. They write a poem that follows the form; check syllables, rhyme or meter together. Check before moving on: ask "Haiku pattern?" Look for: Three lines of 5, 7, 5 syllables.

questions.a: Three lines of 5, 7, 5 syllables.

days.guide: Reread 'Mother to Son.' Your child chooses an object for life or a challenge (a road, a river, a game) and writes a poem that extends that one metaphor across the whole poem. Check before moving on: ask "What is an extended metaphor?" Look for: A comparison carried through several lines or the whole poem.

questions.a: A comparison carried through several lines or the whole poem.

days.guide: Your child chooses a studied poem and memorizes at least 14 lines, a stanza at a time. Rehearse with you, focusing on pauses at punctuation (not at line ends) and emphasis on key words. Check before moving on: ask "Tip for memorizing?" Look for: Learn a stanza at a time; practice daily.

questions.a: Learn a stanza at a time; practice daily.

days.guide: Host a poetry café: your child performs the memorized poem and one original poem. Then give the semester checkpoint independently and note weak areas for review. Check before moving on: ask "Clause or phrase: 'after the storm'?" Look for: Prepositional phrase.

questions.a: Prepositional phrase.

weeks.assessment_key: Portfolio (3 poems): imagery with 5 senses; form poem follows its form; extended metaphor sustained. Recitation rubric: accuracy, volume, pacing, expression. Checkpoint: score by key; note clause, comma and theme errors for review.

weeks.prep: Folger edition of A Midsummer Night's Dream (free at folger.edu); short Globe Theatre video; character map.
misconceptions: Thinking 'wherefore' means 'where' (it means 'why'). For MND, note 'anon' = soon.
Mixing up Hermia and Helena. Hermia loves Lysander; Helena loves Demetrius.

days.guide: Watch a short video on the Globe Theatre. Your child takes notes on staging (open-air, thrust stage, groundlings, all-male casts, few props). Ask how staging would affect the way the audience imagines the forest.

questions.q: Name two features of the Globe.
questions.a: Open-air roof, thrust stage, groundlings standing in the yard, few sets, male actors played female roles.

days.guide: Read Act 1.1 aloud in parts, pausing for Folger notes. Your child builds a character map of Theseus, Egeus, Hermia, Lysander, Demetrius and Helena with arrows for who loves whom. Check before moving on: ask "What does Egeus demand?" Look for: Hermia must marry Demetrius or face death or life as a nun, under Athenian law.

questions.a: Hermia must marry Demetrius or face death or life as a nun, under Athenian law.

questions.q: What do Hermia and Lysander plan?
questions.a: To run away through the woods to his aunt's house.

days.guide: Model translating one line with the Folger notes. Your child translates 10 lines into modern English and explains any archaic words. Compare two translations for accuracy.

questions.q: Translate 'The course of true love never did run smooth.'
questions.a: Real love never goes easily.

days.guide: Read Act 1.2 with the mechanicals. Your child describes Bottom's personality with three quotes and explains how it creates humor. Check before moving on: ask "Why is Bottom funny?" Look for: He wants to play every role, including the lion and Thisbe, and is overconfident.

questions.a: He wants to play every role, including the lion and Thisbe, and is overconfident.

days.guide: Give the Act 1 quiz without notes. Your child then writes a short summary of the three plotlines introduced so far. Check before moving on: ask "Three plotlines?" Look for: Lovers; Theseus and Hippolyta's wedding; the mechanicals' play (fairies come in Act 2).

questions.a: Lovers; Theseus and Hippolyta's wedding; the mechanicals' play (fairies come in Act 2).

weeks.assessment_key: Act 1 quiz: 1) Theseus is Duke of Athens, marrying Hippolyta. 2) Egeus wants Hermia to marry Demetrius. 3) Hermia loves Lysander. 4) Helena loves Demetrius and tells him of the elopement. 5) The mechanicals plan 'Pyramus and Thisbe' for the wedding. 6) Bottom will play Pyramus. Translation: meaning accurate in modern English.

weeks.prep: A Midsummer Night's Dream; love chart (arrows for who loves whom).
misconceptions: Thinking dramatic irony means sarcasm. It is when the audience knows something characters don't.
Thinking Puck enchants the wrong man on purpose. He mistakes Lysander for Demetrius because of the Athenian clothes.

days.guide: Read Act 2 in parts. Your child explains the Oberon–Titania quarrel and Puck's role in carrying out Oberon's plan. Ask what goes wrong with Puck's mission. Check before moving on: ask "Why do Oberon and Titania quarrel?" Look for: Over a changeling Indian boy Titania refuses to give Oberon.

questions.q: Why do Oberon and Titania quarrel?
questions.a: Over a changeling Indian boy Titania refuses to give Oberon.

questions.q: What does Oberon send Puck to get?
questions.a: The flower 'love-in-idleness', whose juice makes a sleeper love the first creature seen.

days.guide: Define dramatic irony with an example. Your child lists at least three moments when the audience knows more than the lovers and explains how each creates comedy. Check before moving on: ask "Example?" Look for: The audience knows Lysander loves Helena only because of the potion; Hermia does not.

questions.a: The audience knows Lysander loves Helena only because of the potion; Hermia does not.

days.guide: Read Act 3 in parts. Your child makes two love charts with arrows: before the potion and after Act 3.2. Discuss why the lovers' quarrel becomes so heated. Check before moving on: ask "After the potion in 3.2, whom do Lysander and Demetrius love?" Look for: Both love Helena.

questions.q: After the potion in 3.2, whom do Lysander and Demetrius love?
questions.a: Both love Helena.
Bottom, who has a donkey's head.

days.guide: Reread Helena's soliloquy at the end of 1.1. Your child explains what a soliloquy is and what Helena reveals that she wouldn't say in dialogue, citing two lines. Check before moving on: ask "What does she reveal?" Look for: She is jealous and plans to tell Demetrius of the elopement to win his favor; 'Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind.'

questions.a: She is jealous and plans to tell Demetrius of the elopement to win his favor; 'Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind.'

days.guide: Give the Acts 2–3 quiz with the constructed response on dramatic irony. Review together. Check before moving on: ask "Famous Puck line in 3.2?" Look for: 'Lord, what fools these mortals be!'

questions.a: 'Lord, what fools these mortals be!'

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Changeling boy. 2) Love-in-idleness. 3) Puck anoints Lysander by mistake. 4) Puck gives Bottom a donkey head. 5) Titania loves Bottom. CR (dramatic irony): proficient names one instance, explains what the audience knows that characters don't, and how it creates comedy.

weeks.prep: A Midsummer Night's Dream; summary of Ovid's Pyramus and Thisbe.
misconceptions: Thinking all spells are removed. Demetrius stays enchanted, loving Helena.
Missing that Act 5 comedy comes from the bad acting.

days.guide: Read Act 4 in parts. Your child explains how each conflict (lovers, fairy king and queen, Egeus's demand) is resolved and by whom. Check before moving on: ask "How is the lovers' conflict resolved?" Look for: At Oberon’s command Puck removes the spell from Lysander at the end of Act 3 (Demetrius stays enchanted), so Lysander loves Hermia and Demetrius loves Helena; Theseus overrules Egeus.

questions.q: How is the lovers' conflict resolved?
questions.a: At Oberon’s command Puck removes the spell from Lysander at the end of Act 3 (Demetrius stays enchanted), so Lysander loves Hermia and Demetrius loves Helena; Theseus overrules Egeus.

questions.q: How is the fairy conflict resolved?
questions.a: Titania gives up the boy; Oberon releases her.

days.guide: Read a summary of Ovid's Pyramus and Thisbe. Your child compares the myth with the lovers' story and explains how the mechanicals' play parodies it. Check before moving on: ask "How are Pyramus and Thisbe like the lovers?" Look for: Forbidden young lovers who meet secretly — but their story ends in tragedy while the Athenians' ends happily.

questions.q: How are Pyramus and Thisbe like the lovers?
questions.a: Forbidden young lovers who meet secretly — but their story ends in tragedy while the Athenians' ends happily.

days.guide: Read Act 5 in parts. Your child records three audience comments by the nobles and explains what they show about the play and the nobles. Check before moving on: ask "What do the nobles' comments show?" Look for: They mock the actors, adding comedy and showing class differences.

questions.q: What do the nobles' comments show?
questions.a: They mock the actors, adding comedy and showing class differences.

days.guide: Your child writes a theme statement about love or imagination supported by three quotes from different acts. Check that the theme is a complete sentence. Check before moving on: ask "Theme example?" Look for: Love is irrational and can change suddenly.

questions.a: Love is irrational and can change suddenly.

days.guide: Give the full-play quiz on plot, structure and theme. Review together. Check before moving on: ask "How does the play end?" Look for: Puck's epilogue: if the play offended, think it was a dream.

questions.a: Puck's epilogue: if the play offended, think it was a dream.

weeks.assessment_key: Full-play quiz: plot (sequence of acts), structure (three plotlines merge in Act 5), theme (love irrational, imagination). Theme paragraph rubric: 4 = clear claim, two or more accurately quoted and cited pieces of evidence, explanation that connects each quote to the claim; 3 = claim and evidence but thin explanation; 2 = evidence summarized rather than quoted, or weak link to claim; 1 = opinion without evidence.

weeks.prep: A filmed production (1999 film or recorded stage version); scene script for rehearsal; Shakespeare excerpt with questions for the test.
misconceptions: Treating a film as 'wrong' when it changes the script. Analyze why the change was made.
Rushing lines in performance.

days.guide: Watch key scenes from a filmed production. Your child notes how costumes, setting and acting change their understanding of the characters. Check before moving on: ask "How can setting change meaning?" Look for: A modern setting can make the conflicts feel familiar.

questions.a: A modern setting can make the conflicts feel familiar.

days.guide: Your child writes a 5-paragraph comparison essay on how the script and film portray Bottom or Puck. Each body paragraph cites both the script and the film. Check before moving on: ask "What must each body paragraph include?" Look for: Evidence from both script and film.

questions.q: What must each body paragraph include?
questions.a: Evidence from both script and film.

days.guide: Your child chooses a 30-line scene, marks blocking (movement and positions) on the script, and rehearses with family members. Check before moving on: ask "What is blocking?" Look for: Planned movement and positions of actors on stage.

questions.a: Planned movement and positions of actors on stage.

days.guide: Your child performs the scene using voice and gesture. Afterward, discuss interpretation choices and how they changed meaning. Check before moving on: ask "Interpretation choice example?" Look for: Playing Bottom as kind rather than foolish.

questions.a: Playing Bottom as kind rather than foolish.

days.guide: Give the unit test on a Shakespeare excerpt independently. Score with the key. Check before moving on: ask "What does 'thou' mean?" Look for: You (informal).

questions.a: You (informal).

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison essay rubric: thesis, evidence from both, analysis. Performance rubric: memorization/preparation, voice, gesture, blocking. Unit test: answers on language (translation), structure, character with line evidence.

weeks.prep: Library card for public library databases (e.g., Britannica School, Gale); CRAAP test checklist; Purdue OWL MLA citation page.
misconceptions: Choosing a topic too broad ('climate change'). Narrow to a question: 'How do sea walls protect California's coast?'
Trusting a site because it looks professional. Check author, date and purpose.

days.guide: Your child brainstorms topics on an invention, scientist or environmental issue and narrows to one focused research question. Check that it is open-ended and researchable in about four weeks. Check before moving on: ask "Narrow 'Thomas Edison'." Look for: 'How did Edison's research lab change the way inventions were made?'

questions.a: 'How did Edison's research lab change the way inventions were made?'

days.guide: Explain each CRAAP letter with an example. Your child scores five websites on a checklist and explains which are trustworthy. Check before moving on: ask "What does each letter mean?" Look for: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.

questions.a: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.

days.guide: Search the library's student databases together. Your child finds three credible sources and notes why each is credible. Check before moving on: ask "Why are databases more reliable than random sites?" Look for: Their articles are edited/reviewed and from known publishers.

questions.q: Why are databases more reliable than random sites?
questions.a: Their articles are edited/reviewed and from known publishers.

days.guide: Model one MLA citation using Purdue OWL. Your child creates at least four citations in alphabetical order with a hanging indent. Check before moving on: ask "MLA order for a website?" Look for: Author. 'Title.' Site Name, Publisher (if different), Date, URL.

questions.a: Author. 'Title.' Site Name, Publisher (if different), Date, URL.

days.guide: Your child submits the research question, source evaluations and bibliography. Give feedback on focus and source quality. Check before moving on: ask "Good research question test?" Look for: Open-ended, researchable, focused enough for 1,000 words.

questions.a: Open-ended, researchable, focused enough for 1,000 words.

weeks.assessment_key: Proposal: focused question; CRAAP scores for 5 sites with reasons; 3 credible sources. Bibliography: 4 MLA citations, alphabetized, hanging indent, all required elements.

weeks.prep: Index cards or a digital notes doc; five paragraph passages from sources; a documentary clip on the topic.
misconceptions: Thinking changing a few words is paraphrasing. Paraphrase = read, cover the source, write in your own words and structure, then cite.
Dangling modifiers: 'Walking to school, the rain started.'

days.guide: Model a note card with subtopic heading, note in your own words, source and page. Your child takes 15 note cards organized by subtopic. Check before moving on: ask "Why record the source on every card?" Look for: So citations are accurate and plagiarism is avoided.

questions.q: Why record the source on every card?
questions.a: So citations are accurate and plagiarism is avoided.

days.guide: Model paraphrasing: read, cover the source, write from memory, then check. Your child paraphrases five passages and compares each with the original to make sure wording and structure are new. Check before moving on: ask "Is a paraphrase still cited?" Look for: Yes — ideas from a source always need a citation.

questions.a: Yes — ideas from a source always need a citation.

days.guide: Teach misplaced and dangling modifiers with examples. Your child fixes 12 sentences, then checks note cards for the same errors. Check before moving on: ask "Fix: 'Walking to school, the rain started.'" Look for: 'As I was walking to school, the rain started.'

questions.q: Fix: 'Walking to school, the rain started.'
questions.a: 'As I was walking to school, the rain started.'

questions.q: Fix: 'She almost ate the whole pizza' (she ate nearly all of it).
questions.a: 'She ate almost the whole pizza.'

days.guide: Watch a documentary clip on the topic. Your child compares what it emphasizes versus a print source and explains why each medium highlights different things. Check before moving on: ask "What can video emphasize that print can't?" Look for: Visuals, sound, emotion; print can give more detail and data.

questions.q: What can video emphasize that print can't?
questions.a: Visuals, sound, emotion; print can give more detail and data.

days.guide: Model a formal outline format. Your child organizes notes into an outline with a thesis and three subtopics, each with supporting points. Check before moving on: ask "Formal outline format?" Look for: Roman numerals for main sections, capital letters for subpoints.

questions.a: Roman numerals for main sections, capital letters for subpoints.

weeks.assessment_key: Note cards: 15 with source and page. Paraphrase set: five paraphrases in own words and structure with citations. Outline: thesis and three subtopics with supporting points.

weeks.prep: Outline and note cards; word processor; a chart, image or diagram from a credible source for one section.
misconceptions: Stringing quotes together ('quote dumping'). Each body paragraph should be mostly your child's words, with quotes as support.
Adding an image without a caption or credit. Every visual needs a caption explaining what it shows and its source.

days.guide: Model a hook for an informational report (a surprising fact). Your child drafts an introduction ending with a focus statement. Check before moving on: ask "How is a report's focus statement different from an argument's claim?" Look for: It states what the report will explain ('This report explains how…'), not a position to defend.

questions.q: How is a report's focus statement different from an argument's claim?
questions.a: It states what the report will explain ('This report explains how…'), not a position to defend.

days.guide: Model integrating a source: introduce, quote or paraphrase, cite, explain. Your child drafts body section 1 using at least two sources. Check before moving on: ask "Integrate this fact correctly: NASA says sea level rose about 4 inches since 1993." Look for: According to NASA, global sea level has risen about four inches since 1993 (NASA). — introduced, paraphrased, cited.

questions.q: Integrate this fact correctly: NASA says sea level rose about 4 inches since 1993.
questions.a: According to NASA, global sea level has risen about four inches since 1993 (NASA). — introduced, paraphrased, cited.

days.guide: Your child drafts sections 2–3 and inserts one visual with a caption ('Figure 1: … Source: …'). Check before moving on: ask "Why include a visual?" Look for: It shows data or a process more clearly than words alone and supports the reader's understanding.

questions.a: It shows data or a process more clearly than words alone and supports the reader's understanding.

days.guide: Your child drafts a conclusion (restate focus, key takeaways, why it matters) and formats Works Cited (alphabetical, hanging indent, double-spaced). Check before moving on: ask "How is Works Cited ordered?" Look for: Alphabetically by the first word of each entry (usually the author's last name).

questions.a: Alphabetically by the first word of each entry (usually the author's last name).

days.guide: Your child highlights each in-text citation and checks it against a Works Cited entry; fix any mismatches. Check before moving on: ask "An in-text citation says (Lopez) but Works Cited has no Lopez. What's wrong?" Look for: The source is missing from Works Cited (or the citation is wrong); add or correct the entry.

questions.q: An in-text citation says (Lopez) but Works Cited has no Lopez. What's wrong?
questions.a: The source is missing from Works Cited (or the citation is wrong); add or correct the entry.

weeks.assessment_key: Draft checklist: introduction with focus statement; three body sections each citing at least two sources with explanation; one captioned, credited visual; conclusion; Works Cited in MLA format; every in-text citation matches an entry. Return with 2–3 specific revision comments.

weeks.prep: Google Slides or poster board; a TED-Ed talk (5 min) on any topic; presentation rubric printed.
misconceptions: Overloaded slides that the speaker reads aloud. Keep slides to images and a few key words; the speaker explains.
Thinking revision is just spelling. Revising means improving clarity, word choice and flow.

days.guide: Your child revises for clarity, precise vocabulary and smooth quote integration; read one paragraph aloud together to catch awkward spots. Check before moving on: ask "Replace 'a lot of people' with something precise." Look for: 'More than 40,000 Californians' or 'most coastal residents' — a specific, sourced amount.

questions.q: Replace 'a lot of people' with something precise.
questions.a: 'More than 40,000 Californians' or 'most coastal residents' — a specific, sourced amount.

days.guide: Your child does a final edit (spelling, citations, formatting) and publishes 1,000–1,200 words. Check before moving on: ask "Name three things to check in a final edit." Look for: Spelling/grammar, citation punctuation, and Works Cited formatting.

questions.q: Name three things to check in a final edit.
questions.a: Spelling/grammar, citation punctuation, and Works Cited formatting.

days.guide: Your child builds 6–8 slides: title, 4–6 key findings with images, sources slide. Check before moving on: ask "What makes a slide effective?" Look for: One idea per slide, a clear visual, few words, readable font.

questions.a: One idea per slide, a clear visual, few words, readable font.

days.guide: Your child presents for 5 minutes and answers two audience questions. Check before moving on: ask "How should you answer a question you can't answer?" Look for: Say you don't know yet and how you would find out.

questions.q: How should you answer a question you can't answer?
questions.a: Say you don't know yet and how you would find out.

days.guide: Your child writes a reflection, then watches a TED-Ed talk and summarizes its main idea with three supporting details. Check before moving on: ask "What is the difference between a main idea and a supporting detail?" Look for: The main idea is the speaker's central point; details are facts, examples or explanations that support it.

questions.q: What is the difference between a main idea and a supporting detail?
questions.a: The main idea is the speaker's central point; details are facts, examples or explanations that support it.

weeks.assessment_key: Report rubric (4–1): focus; research (3+ credible sources, accurately represented); organization; integration and citation; conventions. Presentation rubric: content accuracy, slide design, delivery (eye contact, volume, pace, 5 min), answers to questions. TED-Ed summary: main idea + 3 accurate details.

weeks.prep: Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry (library); Library of Congress FSA photos of 1930s Mississippi (search 'sharecroppers Mississippi 1936'). Parental preview: the novel depicts racism, a racial slur (in the textbook scene and elsewhere), night riders, burning of Black men, and later a lynch mob; discuss the history before reading.
misconceptions: Thinking racism in the novel is only individual meanness. Help your child see the system: segregated schools, sharecropping debt, unequal law.
Forgetting that Cassie is nine and her view is limited — readers often understand more than she does.

days.guide: Look at 4–6 FSA photographs together. Your child lists observations (housing, clothing, work, children) and questions, then you briefly explain sharecropping and segregation in 1930s Mississippi. Check before moving on: ask "What was sharecropping?" Look for: Farmers worked land owned by someone else and paid with a share of the crop, often staying in debt.

questions.a: Farmers worked land owned by someone else and paid with a share of the crop, often staying in debt.

days.guide: Read Chapter 1 together. Your child explains what Little Man and Cassie do about the textbooks and what this reveals about their characters, citing two quotes. Check before moving on: ask "Why does Little Man refuse the book?" Look for: The inside chart shows it was a worn book passed down from white students, with the condition column listing the Black students' race in an insulting word; he stomps on it.

questions.q: Why does Little Man refuse the book?
questions.a: The inside chart shows it was a worn book passed down from white students, with the condition column listing the Black students' race in an insulting word; he stomps on it.

questions.q: What does this show about Little Man and Cassie?
questions.a: They are proud and refuse to accept humiliation, even when they are punished.

days.guide: Read Chapters 2–3. Your child explains how the bus incident and the night men create tension, citing specific moments. Discuss why the children are so afraid that night.

questions.q: What do the children do to the bus?
questions.a: They dig a ditch in the road that fills with rain; the bus breaks an axle in it.

questions.q: Why are they afraid that night?
questions.a: The night men ride; the children fear they are coming because of the bus.
