days.guide: Discuss first-person point of view. Your child finds two moments where Cassie doesn't fully understand what adults know, and explains how her narration shapes what readers learn. Check before moving on: ask "How does Cassie's narration affect what readers learn?" Look for: We see events through a nine-year-old's eyes: her anger and confusion; adults' reasons are revealed slowly.

questions.q: How does Cassie's narration affect what readers learn?
questions.a: We see events through a nine-year-old's eyes: her anger and confusion; adults' reasons are revealed slowly.

days.guide: Discuss why land matters to the Logans, citing Papa's and Big Ma's words. Then give the chapters 1–3 quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Why is land important to the Logans?" Look for: Owning land gives them independence; they don't have to sharecrop for Harlan Granger.

questions.q: Why is land important to the Logans?
questions.a: Owning land gives them independence; they don't have to sharecrop for Harlan Granger.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Cassie Logan narrates; setting 1933 Mississippi. 2) Siblings Stacey, Christopher-John, Little Man. 3) Textbook incident: books from white school. 4) Mama is a teacher and pastes paper over the chart. 5) Bus splashing and ditch. 6) Mr. Morrison comes with Papa as protection. Discussion notes: two ideas with evidence.

weeks.prep: Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry; perspective chart (character, response to injustice, evidence).
misconceptions: Thinking Big Ma makes Cassie apologize because she agrees with Mr. Simms. She does it to protect Cassie from danger.
Reading T.J. as only a villain; he's also lonely and manipulated.

days.guide: Read Chapter 4 together. Your child explains T.J.'s choices and how Stacey and others react, citing evidence. Check before moving on: ask "What does T.J. do about the test?" Look for: He brings cheat notes; when Mama catches Stacey with them, Stacey takes the blame.

questions.q: What does T.J. do about the test?
questions.a: He brings cheat notes; when Mama catches Stacey with them, Stacey takes the blame.
Stacey goes after T.J. at the Wallace store; Papa's family disapproves of the store.

days.guide: Read Chapter 5. Your child writes a journal entry from Cassie's perspective about what happened at the Barnett Mercantile and how she felt. Check before moving on: ask "What happens at the Mercantile?" Look for: Mr. Barnett keeps serving white customers ahead of T.J.'s order; when Cassie protests, he orders her out.

questions.a: Mr. Barnett keeps serving white customers ahead of T.J.'s order; when Cassie protests, he orders her out.

days.guide: Read Chapter 6. Your child completes a chart comparing how Big Ma, Mama and Uncle Hammer each respond to injustice, citing evidence for each. Check before moving on: ask "How does Uncle Hammer respond to what happened to Cassie?" Look for: He wants to confront Mr. Simms; Mr. Morrison stops him.

questions.q: How does Uncle Hammer respond to what happened to Cassie?
questions.a: He wants to confront Mr. Simms; Mr. Morrison stops him.
She explains the history and danger of racism to Cassie calmly.

days.guide: Your child analyzes five passages for word connotations that show characters' attitudes, explaining the effect of each word. Check before moving on: ask "What does Mr. Simms forcing Cassie to say 'Miss Lillian Jean' show?" Look for: That he expects Black people to show deference to white people.

questions.q: What does Mr. Simms forcing Cassie to say 'Miss Lillian Jean' show?
questions.a: That he expects Black people to show deference to white people.

days.guide: Give the chapters 4–6 quiz with a constructed response on contrasting perspectives. Review together. Check before moving on: ask "What does Cassie learn in Strawberry?" Look for: How deeply unfair the system is.

questions.q: What does Cassie learn in Strawberry?
questions.a: How deeply unfair the system is.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) T.J.'s cheat notes. 2) Mercantile incident. 3) Lillian Jean, Mr. Simms. 4) Big Ma makes Cassie apologize to protect her. 5) Uncle Hammer wants to confront Simms. CR rubric: compares two perspectives with evidence.

weeks.prep: Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry; theme tracker.
misconceptions: Missing the symbol: the fig tree survives among bigger trees.
Thinking Cassie's revenge is just mean.

days.guide: Read Chapter 7. Your child explains Papa's fig tree story and what the tree symbolizes for the Logans. Check before moving on: ask "What does the fig tree symbolize?" Look for: The Logans: small among big trees, but deep roots keep it alive and bearing fruit.

questions.q: What does the fig tree symbolize?
questions.a: The Logans: small among big trees, but deep roots keep it alive and bearing fruit.

days.guide: Read Chapter 8. Your child explains Cassie's plan against Lillian Jean and what it reveals about her. Check before moving on: ask "What is Cassie's plan?" Look for: She pretends to be Lillian Jean's friend, learns her secrets, then fights her in the woods; Lillian Jean won't tell because Cassie knows her secrets.

questions.a: She pretends to be Lillian Jean's friend, learns her secrets, then fights her in the woods; Lillian Jean won't tell because Cassie knows her secrets.

days.guide: Read Chapter 9. Your child tracks the boycott and its consequences in a cause-effect chart. Check before moving on: ask "What happens to Papa?" Look for: His wagon is attacked; his leg is broken.

questions.a: His wagon is attacked; his leg is broken.

days.guide: Your child adds evidence to a theme tracker for 'family strength' and 'standing up to injustice'. Check before moving on: ask "Evidence for 'family strength'?" Look for: The family works together to protect the land.

questions.a: The family works together to protect the land.

days.guide: Discuss the fig tree symbol, then give the chapters 7–9 quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Why does Mama lose her job?" Look for: She teaches about slavery and covered the textbook chart; school board fires her.

questions.q: Why does Mama lose her job?
questions.a: She teaches about slavery and covered the textbook chart; school board fires her.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Fig tree symbol. 2) Cassie's plan. 3) Mama fired. 4) Boycott of Wallace store. 5) Papa's broken leg. Theme tracker: 3+ entries per theme.

weeks.prep: Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry; whole-novel test (prepare items from the key). Parental preview: Chapter 11 includes a mob attack on T.J. and the threat of lynching; Chapter 12 ends with T.J. facing a likely death sentence. Plan time to talk afterward.
misconceptions: Thinking Papa sets the fire by accident or that it was lightning only. The text leads readers (and finally Cassie) to understand Papa set it to stop the mob.
Seeing the ending as 'happy because the land is saved.' It is bittersweet: the land is saved at the cost of crops, and T.J.'s fate is grim.

days.guide: Read Chapter 10. Your child explains how the Logans try to keep their land. Check before moving on: ask "How does Harlan Granger pressure the Logans?" Look for: He has the bank call in the mortgage note early.

questions.q: How does Harlan Granger pressure the Logans?
questions.a: He has the bank call in the mortgage note early.
Uncle Hammer sells his car to pay the note.

days.guide: Read Chapter 11. Your child analyzes the night T.J. is attacked and Papa's decision. Check before moving on: ask "What happened at the Barnett Mercantile?" Look for: T.J. went with R.W. and Melvin Simms to steal a pistol; the Simms brothers attacked Mr. Barnett and blamed T.J.

questions.q: What happened at the Barnett Mercantile?
questions.a: T.J. went with R.W. and Melvin Simms to steal a pistol; the Simms brothers attacked Mr. Barnett and blamed T.J.

questions.q: What does Papa do to stop the mob?
questions.a: He sets fire to his own cotton field so everyone, white and Black, must fight the fire, which stops the lynching.

days.guide: Read Chapter 12. Your child explains what Cassie understands at the end that she did not before. Check before moving on: ask "What does Cassie realize?" Look for: That Papa set the fire, that T.J. will likely die, and she cries for T.J. and for the land.

questions.a: That Papa set the fire, that T.J. will likely die, and she cries for T.J. and for the land.

days.guide: Your child writes an objective summary of the novel and a theme statement. Check before moving on: ask "Theme example?" Look for: Family strength and owning land give people dignity and the power to resist injustice, though at great cost.

questions.a: Family strength and owning land give people dignity and the power to resist injustice, though at great cost.

days.guide: Give the whole-novel test with multiple choice and two constructed responses. Check before moving on: ask "What does the title refer to?" Look for: A spiritual/song the family sings, 'Roll of thunder, hear my cry,' expressing defiance and endurance.

questions.q: What does the title refer to?
questions.a: A spiritual/song the family sings, 'Roll of thunder, hear my cry,' expressing defiance and endurance.

weeks.assessment_key: Novel test multiple choice: Cassie narrator; 1933 Mississippi; textbook; bus ditch; Barnett Mercantile; fig tree; Mama fired; Papa's leg; Hammer sells car; Papa's fire. CR1: theme with 3 pieces of evidence. CR2: how Cassie changes (from not understanding to recognizing the danger and cost of injustice).

weeks.prep: Library of Congress primary sources: photographs of 1930s segregated Black schools and sharecropper families; a short historical article on sharecropping/segregated schools (e.g., Library of Congress 'Jim Crow' or Smithsonian). Roll of Thunder for evidence.
misconceptions: Thinking historical fiction is 'made up' and therefore not useful. Authors invent characters but often use real conditions to show truth about the period.
Using evidence from only the novel. The essay must balance both.

days.guide: Read the historical article and two primary sources together. Your child notes key facts about segregated schooling and sharecropping. Check before moving on: ask "What did the sources show about schools?" Look for: Segregated Black schools received less funding, older books and shorter terms because children were needed in the fields.

questions.q: What did the sources show about schools?
questions.a: Segregated Black schools received less funding, older books and shorter terms because children were needed in the fields.

days.guide: Your child fills a comparison chart of what the novel and historical sources each show about the period. Check before moving on: ask "Something the novel shows that matches history?" Look for: Hand-me-down books, the bus only for white students, sharecroppers' debt to stores.

questions.q: Something the novel shows that matches history?
questions.a: Hand-me-down books, the bus only for white students, sharecroppers' debt to stores.

days.guide: Your child drafts a 5-paragraph essay explaining how Taylor uses or alters history and why. Check before moving on: ask "Why might Taylor alter history?" Look for: To create characters readers care about and focus events through one family.

questions.a: To create characters readers care about and focus events through one family.

days.guide: Your child revises with a checklist focused on balanced evidence from both sources, then edits. Check before moving on: ask "How to check balance?" Look for: Each body paragraph cites both the novel and a historical source.

questions.a: Each body paragraph cites both the novel and a historical source.

days.guide: Your child publishes the essay. Discuss with your child how fiction helps us understand history. Check before moving on: ask "Example answer?" Look for: Fiction lets us feel what it was like to live through history.

questions.a: Fiction lets us feel what it was like to live through history.

weeks.assessment_key: Essay rubric: 4 = thesis on how Taylor uses/alters history and why; each body paragraph cites both the novel and a historical source; explanation; conventions. 3 = imbalanced; 2 = summary; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Five printed ads; Gettysburg Address text and recording; Susan B. Anthony's 'On Women's Right to Vote' (1873); Chief Joseph's 1877 surrender speech.
misconceptions: Thinking pathos is the strongest appeal. A strong argument balances all three.
Thinking parallelism is just repetition. It is repeated grammatical structure.

days.guide: Teach ethos, pathos and logos with examples. Your child finds examples in five advertisements. Check before moving on: ask "A dentist recommends a toothpaste." Look for: Ethos (credibility).

questions.a: Ethos (credibility).
Logos (logic/statistics).

days.guide: Read and listen to the Gettysburg Address. Your child annotates parallelism and purpose. Check before moving on: ask "Example of parallelism?" Look for: 'We can not dedicate—we can not consecrate—we can not hallow—this ground'; 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'.

questions.a: 'We can not dedicate—we can not consecrate—we can not hallow—this ground'; 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'.
To honor the fallen soldiers and rededicate the nation to equality and democracy.

days.guide: Read 'On Women's Right to Vote'. Your child traces Anthony's claims and evidence. Check before moving on: ask "What is her main claim?" Look for: Women are citizens, so denying them the vote violates the Constitution.

questions.a: Women are citizens, so denying them the vote violates the Constitution.
The Preamble: 'We, the people' — not 'We, the white male citizens'.

days.guide: Read Chief Joseph's surrender speech. Your child analyzes how word choice conveys his point of view. Check before moving on: ask "What words show his point of view?" Look for: 'I am tired; my heart is sick and sad'; 'the little children are freezing to death'; 'I will fight no more forever' — grief and exhaustion.

questions.q: What words show his point of view?
questions.a: 'I am tired; my heart is sick and sad'; 'the little children are freezing to death'; 'I will fight no more forever' — grief and exhaustion.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph comparing how two speakers use appeals, then takes the rhetoric quiz. Check before moving on: ask "Which appeal does Chief Joseph mainly use?" Look for: Pathos.

questions.q: Which appeal does Chief Joseph mainly use?
questions.a: Pathos.

weeks.assessment_key: Rhetoric quiz: ethos = credibility, pathos = emotion, logos = logic; parallelism example from Gettysburg; Anthony's claim and evidence; Chief Joseph's tone (sorrowful, weary). Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear claim, two or more accurately quoted and cited pieces of evidence, explanation that connects each quote to the claim; 3 = claim and evidence but thin explanation; 2 = evidence summarized rather than quoted, or weak link to claim; 1 = opinion without evidence.

weeks.prep: Two articles on lowering the voting age to 16 (pro/con — e.g., Newsela, ProCon); index cards for evidence.
misconceptions: Treating a debate as a fight. Model respectful disagreement.
Preparing only your side.

days.guide: Read both articles on lowering the voting age. Your child identifies each author's claim and key evidence. Check before moving on: ask "A common pro reason?" Look for: 16-year-olds work, pay taxes and are affected by laws.

questions.a: 16-year-olds work, pay taxes and are affected by laws.
Concerns about maturity and that most states set adult rights at 18.

days.guide: Your child analyzes how each author emphasizes different evidence and writes a comparison paragraph. Check before moving on: ask "How might authors emphasize different evidence?" Look for: One cites studies on teen civic knowledge; the other cites brain development research.

questions.q: How might authors emphasize different evidence?
questions.a: One cites studies on teen civic knowledge; the other cites brain development research.

days.guide: Assign a side. Your child builds a case with three reasons and evidence cards. Check before moving on: ask "What goes on an evidence card?" Look for: Quote or fact, source, and how it supports the reason.

questions.q: What goes on an evidence card?
questions.a: Quote or fact, source, and how it supports the reason.

days.guide: Your child lists likely opposing arguments and drafts rebuttals for each. Check before moving on: ask "Why anticipate rebuttals?" Look for: To prepare responses and strengthen your case.

questions.a: To prepare responses and strengthen your case.

days.guide: Your child writes and rehearses a 2-minute opening statement. Check before moving on: ask "What should an opening include?" Look for: Claim, roadmap of reasons, a hook.

questions.a: Claim, roadmap of reasons, a hook.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison paragraph rubric: names both claims, contrasts evidence, explains effect. Debate case: three reasons with cited evidence, rebuttals for 2+ opposing arguments.

weeks.prep: Timer; evidence cards; recording device (phone); debate and speech rubrics.
misconceptions: Interrupting during cross-examination.
Using only emotion in a persuasive speech.

days.guide: Your child rehearses the opening statement and cross-examination questions with you. Check before moving on: ask "Good cross-examination question?" Look for: One that reveals a weakness: 'What evidence shows 16-year-olds are less informed than 18-year-olds?'

questions.a: One that reveals a weakness: 'What evidence shows 16-year-olds are less informed than 18-year-olds?'

days.guide: Hold a structured debate with family: opening, rebuttal, cross-examination, closing. Check before moving on: ask "Debate order?" Look for: Opening, cross-examination, rebuttal, closing for each side.

questions.a: Opening, cross-examination, rebuttal, closing for each side.

days.guide: Watch a recording of the debate. Your child evaluates both sides' reasoning with a rubric. Check before moving on: ask "What makes reasoning strong?" Look for: Relevant, sufficient evidence linked to claims.

questions.a: Relevant, sufficient evidence linked to claims.

days.guide: Your child writes a 3-minute persuasive speech on a community issue using ethos, pathos and logos. Check before moving on: ask "Example ethos?" Look for: 'As someone who rides this bike lane every day…'

questions.a: 'As someone who rides this bike lane every day…'

days.guide: Your child delivers the persuasive speech. Give rubric feedback. Check before moving on: ask "What's a call to action?" Look for: A request for audience to do something specific.

questions.a: A request for audience to do something specific.

weeks.assessment_key: Debate rubric: argument, evidence, rebuttal, delivery, respect. Speech rubric: claim, ethos/pathos/logos each used, organization, delivery (eye contact, volume, 3 minutes).

weeks.prep: Timed-writing prompt with two short sources; grammar review sheet; roots/figurative language review game; final exam.
misconceptions: Skipping planning in timed writing. Spend 5 minutes outlining.
Forgetting to cite both sources.

days.guide: Your child writes a 45-minute argument essay responding to a prompt with two short sources. Check before moving on: ask "How to budget 45 minutes?" Look for: 5 plan, 35 write, 5 proofread.

questions.a: 5 plan, 35 write, 5 proofread.

days.guide: Your child scores the timed essay with the rubric and revises one paragraph. Check before moving on: ask "What to revise first?" Look for: Weakest rubric area.

questions.a: Weakest rubric area.

days.guide: Your child completes a mixed review of phrases, clauses, sentence types, modifiers and commas. Check before moving on: ask "Add commas if needed: 'It was a cold dark stormy night.'" Look for: 'It was a cold, dark, stormy night.' — coordinate adjectives pass the 'and' test (cold and dark and stormy).

questions.q: Add commas if needed: 'It was a cold dark stormy night.'
questions.a: 'It was a cold, dark, stormy night.' — coordinate adjectives pass the 'and' test (cold and dark and stormy).

questions.q: Fix the dangling modifier: 'Running for the bus, my backpack fell.'
questions.a: 'Running for the bus, I dropped my backpack.'

days.guide: Review Greek/Latin roots and figurative language with a 40-item review game. Check before moving on: ask "'bene' means?" Look for: Good.

questions.a: Good.

days.guide: Give the year-end ELA exam: reading passages, grammar and a short written response. Check before moving on: ask "Theme vs topic?" Look for: Topic = subject; theme = message about it.

questions.a: Topic = subject; theme = message about it.

weeks.assessment_key: Timed essay rubric: claim, evidence from both sources, reasoning, organization, conventions. Final exam: reading passages scored by key; grammar items; short written response proficient with claim and two pieces of evidence.

weeks.prep: Writing folder; reading log.
misconceptions: Choosing pieces only by grade instead of growth.
Reflection letters without specifics.

days.guide: Your child chooses the best narrative, analysis, argument, research and poem pieces for the portfolio. Check before moving on: ask "Why include a piece that shows growth?" Look for: Shows learning over time.

questions.q: Why include a piece that shows growth?
questions.a: Shows learning over time.

days.guide: Your child revises one earlier piece using everything learned this year. Check before moving on: ask "What to revise?" Look for: Apply a skill learned later, e.g., embedding quotes.

questions.a: Apply a skill learned later, e.g., embedding quotes.

days.guide: Your child writes a reflection letter describing growth, challenges and goals for grade 8. Check before moving on: ask "What makes it strong?" Look for: Specific examples of growth and goals.

questions.a: Specific examples of growth and goals.

days.guide: Total the reading log. Your child gives a 3-minute book talk on the favorite book of the year. Check before moving on: ask "Book talk elements?" Look for: Title, author, hook, no spoilers, recommendation.

questions.a: Title, author, hook, no spoilers, recommendation.

days.guide: Your child presents the portfolio to family, explaining one piece in depth, and creates a summer reading list. Check before moving on: ask "Summer reading list should include?" Look for: Variety of genres, some challenge.

questions.a: Variety of genres, some challenge.

weeks.assessment_key: Portfolio rubric: five pieces present, one revised with visible changes, reflection letter with specific examples and goals. Presentation: explains one piece in depth.

HEALTH.overview: Health 7 is a 25-minute, skills-based course: each week pairs one health concept with a skill (analyzing influences, finding valid information, communicating, deciding, setting goals, practicing behaviors, advocating). Keep lessons conversational, let your child do the talking in role-plays, and connect every topic to real family routines. Preview the mental-health (weeks 9, 11), drug (weeks 18–24) and growth-and-development (weeks 25–28) materials first and teach them in line with your family's values; keep the 988 Lifeline and a trusted-adult list visible all year.

weeks.prep: Gather a health journal, 5–6 packaged foods with Nutrition Facts labels and a measuring cup. Draw a simple wellness wheel (circle cut into physical, mental/emotional, social sections) or print one.
misconceptions: Thinking 'fat' is always bad. Explain that fat is an essential nutrient (energy, cell membranes, absorbing vitamins A, D, E, K); the goal is mostly unsaturated fats and less saturated/trans fat.
Forgetting water is a nutrient. List all six: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.

days.guide: Explain wellness as balance across physical, mental/emotional and social health. Your child rates each area 1–10 on the wheel, shades it, and writes one goal for the lowest area. Ask them to give a reason for each rating.

questions.q: What are three dimensions of wellness?
questions.a: Physical, mental/emotional and social health (some models add spiritual, environmental or intellectual).

questions.q: Why can a problem in one area affect another?
questions.a: They are connected: e.g., poor sleep (physical) makes you irritable (emotional), which can cause arguments with friends (social).

days.guide: Introduce the six nutrients, then your child builds a chart with function and two food sources each. Check the chart against the key in the assessment section.

questions.a: Carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water.

questions.q: Which nutrient is the body's main source of quick energy?
questions.a: Carbohydrates.

questions.q: Which nutrient builds and repairs muscle and other tissues?
questions.a: Protein.

days.guide: Your child logs every drink for one day in cups. Explain that most 12–13-year-olds need roughly 7–8 cups of fluids a day (more for larger or very active teens and in heat). Compare their total and list ways to drink more.

questions.q: Give two jobs of water in the body.
questions.a: Regulating body temperature (sweat), carrying nutrients and oxygen, removing wastes, cushioning joints, aiding digestion — any two.

questions.q: Name an early sign of dehydration.
questions.a: Thirst, dark yellow urine, headache, tiredness or dizziness.

days.guide: Model reading one label: find calories, total fat, carbohydrates, fiber, sugars, protein, and the vitamins/minerals at the bottom. Your child records the main nutrients in five pantry foods and names the food richest in each.

questions.q: On a Nutrition Facts label, where do you find vitamins and minerals?
questions.a: At the bottom: vitamin D, calcium, iron and potassium are required, listed with % Daily Value.

questions.q: A label says 5 g protein per serving and there are 2 servings in the package. How much protein in the whole package?

days.guide: Give a short oral or written quiz (see key). Then your child journals one specific change to try, such as adding a fruit at breakfast.

questions.a: A, D, E and K.

questions.q: Which mineral is most important for strong bones and teeth?
questions.a: Calcium (with vitamin D helping absorb it).

weeks.assessment_key: Nutrient chart: six rows — carbohydrates (main energy; bread, rice, fruit), proteins (build/repair tissue; beans, eggs, meat), fats (stored energy, absorb vitamins A, D, E, K; nuts, olive oil), vitamins (regulate body processes; citrus = vitamin C, carrots = vitamin A), minerals (bones, blood; milk = calcium, spinach/beans = iron), water (temperature, transport, digestion; water, fruits). Quiz key (suggested): 1) carbohydrates 2) protein 3) water 4) calcium 5) vitamins A, D, E, K 6) fats and carbohydrates/protein give energy; vitamins and minerals do not provide calories. Score 5–6 proficient.

weeks.prep: Bookmark MyPlate.gov (MyPlate Plan tool needs age, sex, height, weight, activity). Gather two cereal boxes, five drink containers with labels, a teaspoon and a clear cup and sugar to measure. Body measurements are private — enter them yourself if preferred.
misconceptions: Thinking % Daily Value is the percent of the food that is that nutrient. It is the percent of a whole day's recommended amount in ONE serving; 5% DV or less is low, 20% or more is high.
Comparing labels without checking serving size. Two cereals with different serving sizes must be compared per equal amount (e.g., per cup or per 100 g).

days.guide: Explore MyPlate.gov together and run the MyPlate Plan for your child's age and activity level. Your child copies the daily targets for each food group into the journal.

questions.q: What are the five MyPlate food groups?
questions.a: Fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods and dairy (or fortified soy alternatives).

questions.q: What fraction of the plate should be fruits and vegetables?
questions.a: About half.

days.guide: Model comparing two cereal labels side by side: serving size, added sugars and dietary fiber. Your child decides which is the healthier everyday choice and explains using numbers.

questions.q: Cereal A has 12 g added sugar (24% DV) per serving; cereal B has 3 g (6% DV). Which is high and which is low in added sugar?
questions.a: A is high (20% DV or more); B is close to low (5% DV or less is low, so 6% is moderate-low). B is the better everyday choice.
Fiber helps digestion and keeps you full; higher fiber (3 g+ per serving) usually means more whole grain.

days.guide: Teach: 4 grams of sugar ≈ 1 teaspoon. Your child divides grams of sugar by 4 for five drinks, then measures that many teaspoons into a cup to see it.

questions.q: A 20-oz soda has 65 g sugar. About how many teaspoons is that?
questions.a: 65 ÷ 4 ≈ 16 teaspoons.

questions.q: A sports drink has 34 g sugar. How many teaspoons?
questions.a: 34 ÷ 4 = 8.5 teaspoons.

days.guide: Your child plans breakfast, lunch, dinner and two snacks using their MyPlate targets, listing amounts (cups/ounce-equivalents). Check that every food group appears.

questions.q: Give an example of one ounce-equivalent of grains.
questions.a: One slice of bread, 1 cup of dry cereal, or ½ cup cooked rice or pasta.

questions.q: Name a snack that includes two food groups.
questions.a: Apple slices with peanut butter (fruit + protein), yogurt with berries (dairy + fruit), or whole-grain crackers with cheese (grain + dairy).

days.guide: Your child presents the plan and scores it against MyPlate using the rubric, noting one change. Ask follow-up questions about drinks and added sugar.

questions.q: Why should at least half your grains be whole grains?
questions.a: Whole grains keep the bran and germ, giving more fiber, B vitamins and minerals than refined grains.

questions.q: What is the daily limit for added sugars in the Dietary Guidelines?
questions.a: Less than 10% of daily calories (about 50 g on a 2,000-calorie diet).

weeks.assessment_key: Day meal-plan rubric (4 levels): 4 = all five food groups (fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy/fortified soy) in amounts close to the personal MyPlate Plan, half the plate fruits/veg at meals, at least half grains whole, water or milk as main drinks, limited added sugar, two snacks with two food groups each; 3 = all groups present with minor amount gaps; 2 = missing one food group or heavy on sugary drinks/snacks; 1 = incomplete. Child's evaluation should name at least one strength and one fix.

weeks.prep: Collect 3 food ads aimed at teens (cereal boxes, snack/drink commercials, social media posts), poster paper and markers. Ask a grandparent or relative ahead to be interviewed about a traditional family food.
misconceptions: Believing ads don't affect them. Point out repeated logos, jingles and influencers; ask why companies spend billions if ads didn't work.
Thinking cultural or traditional foods are automatically unhealthy. Most cuisines include vegetables, beans and whole grains; focus on balance and portion, not dropping family foods.

days.guide: Explain internal influences (hunger, emotions, taste, habits) vs external (family, friends, culture, media, cost, availability). Your child draws a web of their own influences and stars the strongest two.

questions.q: Is boredom an internal or external influence on eating?
questions.a: Internal — it is a feeling inside you.

questions.q: Give two external influences on food choice.
questions.a: Family meals, culture, friends, advertising, cost, what's available at home or school — any two.

days.guide: Look at the three ads together. Your child fills a chart: product, target audience, techniques used, missing information.

questions.a: A famous person or influencer promoting a product so fans want to copy them.

questions.q: Why do cereal boxes for kids put cartoon characters at kids' eye level?
questions.a: To catch children's attention so they ask parents to buy it — marketing to a target audience.

days.guide: Your child interviews a family member about a traditional food: what it is, when it is eaten, who taught them, what it means. Write a short summary.

questions.q: How can culture influence what a family eats?
questions.a: Through traditional recipes, holiday foods, spices and ingredients, and rules about food passed down through generations.

days.guide: Your child designs a counter-ad for a healthy food (e.g., carrots, water) using at least two of the same techniques. Check the claim is accurate.

questions.q: Name two persuasive techniques you used and how.
questions.a: Example: bandwagon ('Everyone's grabbing water'), bright colors, a famous athlete, catchy slogan — answer should name and explain two.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph naming the strongest influence on their eating, with an example and a plan to manage it. Check for a clear topic sentence and specific example.

questions.q: How can you reduce the effect of ads on your choices?
questions.a: Notice the technique, ask what is missing, read the label, decide based on your needs rather than the ad.

weeks.assessment_key: Ad analysis (per ad): names the target audience, at least two techniques (celebrity/influencer endorsement, bandwagon, bright packaging/cartoon characters, free prizes, 'fun' or 'cool' appeal, health halo words like 'natural'), and what the ad leaves out (sugar, sodium, cost). Counter-ad rubric: 4 = promotes a healthy food with two clearly named persuasive techniques, accurate claim, clear audience, eye-catching design; 3 = one technique, accurate; 2 = vague message; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find 4 nutrition sources: e.g., a .gov site (MyPlate), a hospital site (KidsHealth), a supplement-selling blog, and a diet influencer post. Parent preview: Day 3–4 discuss body image and eating disorders — keep tone supportive and nonjudgmental, and avoid weight/calorie talk about your child's body.
misconceptions: Believing a source is valid because it looks professional or has many followers. Check the author's credentials, evidence and whether they are selling something.
Thinking eating disorders only affect girls or underweight people. They affect all genders and body sizes; they are serious illnesses that need professional help.

days.guide: Teach the checklist: Who wrote it? What evidence? Why was it written (sell or inform)? When updated? Your child evaluates the four sources and ranks them.

questions.q: Which ending usually means a government source: .com, .gov or .org?
questions.a: .gov (.org can be anyone; .com is commercial).

questions.q: A post says 'Doctors hate this one trick!' and links to a product. Valid?
questions.a: No — no evidence, sensational claim, and the purpose is to sell.

days.guide: Read two fad diet claims (e.g., 'no carbs ever', 'juice cleanse'). Your child compares each to MyPlate and lists risks.

questions.q: Why is cutting out all carbohydrates risky for a growing teen?
questions.a: Carbs are the main energy source for the brain and muscles; cutting them causes fatigue and poor focus and removes fiber, vitamins and minerals.

questions.q: What is the healthiest way to maintain weight?
questions.a: Balanced meals following MyPlate, regular physical activity, adequate sleep — not extreme restriction.

days.guide: Discuss how edited and filtered images create unrealistic standards. Your child rewrites three negative self-talk statements as healthy ones.

questions.q: Rewrite: 'I look terrible compared to everyone online.'
questions.a: Example: 'Online photos are edited. My body is strong and lets me do things I enjoy.'
How you see, think and feel about your own body.

days.guide: Teach warning signs calmly and practice what to say to a friend: 'I'm worried about you. Can we talk to an adult?' Emphasize these are medical illnesses with treatment.

questions.q: Name two warning signs of an eating disorder.
questions.a: Skipping meals, extreme dieting or calorie counting, hiding food, excessive exercise, frequent comments about being fat, rapid weight change.

questions.q: What is the most helpful thing to do if you are worried about a friend?
questions.a: Tell a trusted adult (parent, school counselor, doctor) — don't keep it secret.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key orally or written. Review any missed items.

questions.q: List two questions to ask to decide if health information is valid.
questions.a: Who is the author and are they an expert? Is there evidence? Are they trying to sell something? Is it current?

weeks.assessment_key: Source evaluation: for each source child lists author/credentials, evidence (studies, experts), purpose (inform vs sell), date, and gives a valid/not valid verdict with reason — e.g., MyPlate = valid (USDA, evidence-based, no sales); influencer selling detox tea = not valid (no credentials, selling product). Quiz (suggested): 1) Name 3 signs of a fad diet — promises fast weight loss, cuts out whole food groups, sells products/pills, sounds too good to be true. 2) Why are fad diets risky? — missing nutrients, fatigue, weight regain, can lead to disordered eating. 3) Healthy weight is maintained by balanced eating and regular activity. 4) Name 2 warning signs of an eating disorder — skipping meals, obsessive calorie counting, secret eating, excessive exercise, big weight changes. 5) What to do if worried about a friend — tell a trusted adult.

weeks.prep: Gather a food thermometer (or plan to read the fridge thermometer), ingredients for a simple healthy snack, and an activity/screen-time log sheet for 7 days.
misconceptions: Thinking 60 minutes of activity must be done all at once. Activity can add up across the day in shorter bouts.
Believing you can tell food is safe by smell or look. Bacteria that cause illness often can't be seen or smelled; use a thermometer and the fridge rules.

days.guide: Teach the guideline: ages 6–17 need 60+ minutes of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily, with vigorous, muscle- and bone-strengthening activity at least 3 days each. Your child starts a 7-day log of activity and screen time.

questions.q: How can you tell if activity is moderate vs vigorous?
questions.a: Moderate: you can talk but not sing. Vigorous: you can only say a few words before needing a breath.
Jumping rope, running, basketball, hopscotch — anything with impact.

days.guide: Your child lists 5 benefits of activity and 3 personal barriers, each with a solution.

questions.q: Name three benefits of regular activity.
questions.a: Stronger heart and lungs, stronger muscles and bones, better sleep, less stress, better mood and focus, healthy weight.
Break activity into 10-minute bouts, walk/bike for errands, active family time, move during screen breaks.

days.guide: Teach the four steps: clean, separate, cook, chill. Your child checks the fridge temperature and finds where raw meat should be stored (bottom shelf).

questions.q: What temperature should a refrigerator be?
questions.a: 40°F (4°C) or below.

questions.q: Why store raw meat on the bottom shelf?
questions.a: So its juices can't drip onto ready-to-eat foods (prevents cross-contamination).

days.guide: Your child washes hands 20 seconds, cleans the counter, uses separate boards if needed, and prepares a snack (e.g., veggie wrap). Ask them to narrate each safety step.

questions.q: How long should you scrub hands with soap?
questions.a: At least 20 seconds.

questions.q: To what temperature must chicken be cooked?
questions.a: 165°F internal temperature.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key and total the activity log.

questions.a: Perishable food should not sit at room temperature more than 2 hours (1 hour if above 90°F).

questions.q: Name two symptoms of foodborne illness.
questions.a: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach cramps, fever.

weeks.assessment_key: Activity log: 7 days of activity minutes and screen time, with total MVPA and a note whether the 60-minute daily goal was met. Quiz key (suggested): 1) 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily 2) vigorous activity, muscle-strengthening and bone-strengthening each at least 3 days a week 3) clean, separate, cook, chill 4) fridge at 40°F (4°C) or below, freezer 0°F 5) cook poultry to 165°F, ground beef to 160°F 6) refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours (1 hour if over 90°F) 7) cross-contamination = spreading germs from raw meat to ready-to-eat food.

weeks.prep: Have your child keep a 3-day food log (Thursday–Saturday before, or use recent days). Choose a balanced dinner recipe and buy ingredients. Prepare a unit test (see key) and a 3-week goal tracker.
misconceptions: Writing vague goals like 'eat healthier.' A SMART goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
Comparing a single day to MyPlate and judging harshly. Look at patterns across several days.

days.guide: Your child totals each food group from the 3-day log and compares with MyPlate targets, circling groups that are low or high.

questions.q: If your target is 2.5 cups of vegetables and you averaged 1 cup, how much more do you need daily?
questions.a: 1.5 cups more per day.

questions.q: Which food groups do most teens under-eat?
questions.a: Vegetables, fruits, whole grains and dairy.

days.guide: Teach SMART with an example. Your child writes a nutrition goal and checks each letter.

questions.q: Is 'I will eat more fruit' a SMART goal? Fix it.
questions.a: No — not specific/measurable/time-bound. Fixed: 'I will eat one piece of fruit at breakfast 5 days a week for the next 3 weeks.'

questions.q: What does the 'T' in SMART stand for?
questions.a: Time-bound (has a deadline or time frame).

days.guide: Your child plans and cooks a balanced family dinner with your help, using food safety steps and filling half the plate with vegetables/fruit.

questions.q: Which food groups are in your dinner?
questions.a: Answer should list at least four groups, e.g., chicken (protein), brown rice (grain), broccoli (vegetable), milk (dairy).

days.guide: Play a quick review game with the unit vocabulary (nutrient, % DV, added sugars, fad diet, cross-contamination, SMART goal).

questions.a: Transfer of harmful germs from one food or surface to another, such as raw chicken juices onto salad.
A trustworthy source with expert authors, evidence and no sales motive, such as a government or medical site.

days.guide: Give the unit 1 test (key in assessment section). Then set up the 3-week goal tracker.

questions.q: What is one way you'll track your SMART goal?
questions.a: A daily checkbox chart or app log reviewed each week.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test (suggested 10 items): 1) six nutrients: carbs, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water 2) main energy nutrient: carbohydrates 3) 4 g sugar = 1 tsp 4) 20% DV or more is high, 5% or less low 5) MyPlate groups: fruits, vegetables, grains, protein, dairy 6) half your plate fruits and vegetables 7) two signs of a fad diet (quick results, cuts food groups, sells products) 8) 60 minutes of activity daily 9) clean, separate, cook, chill 10) example of an external influence (ads, family, friends, culture). 9–10 = advanced, 7–8 proficient. Goal tracker: SMART goal written correctly with a daily checkbox chart for 3 weeks.

weeks.prep: Print or display an emotion wheel (free online, e.g., Plutchik or 'feelings wheel'). Choose a short true story of resilience (e.g., a biography article about an athlete or person who overcame hardship).
misconceptions: Believing mental health means always being happy. Healthy people feel the full range of emotions and manage them.
Thinking self-esteem comes only from others' praise. It grows from your own effort, values and strengths.

days.guide: Define mental health: how we think, feel and act, cope with stress, relate to others and make choices. Your child lists 5 traits of emotionally healthy people.

questions.q: List three traits of good mental health.
questions.a: Handles stress, expresses emotions in healthy ways, has positive relationships, asks for help when needed, accepts mistakes, feels good about self.

days.guide: Show how the wheel moves from basic feelings (mad, sad, scared, happy) to precise ones. Your child names precise feelings for three recent events.

questions.q: Why is it helpful to name a precise emotion like 'embarrassed' instead of 'bad'?
questions.a: Naming feelings precisely calms the brain and helps you choose the right coping strategy and explain it to others.

days.guide: Your child lists 10 strengths (skills, character traits); family members add three. Discuss which surprised them.

questions.a: How much you value and respect yourself.

days.guide: Read the resilience story together. Your child lists the setbacks and the skills used to bounce back.

questions.a: The ability to recover or adapt after difficulty or setbacks.
Positive self-talk, asking for support, problem-solving, setting small goals, persistence, learning from mistakes.

days.guide: Your child journals about a personal setback and how they recovered. Score with the rubric.

questions.q: What could you say to yourself after failing a test?
questions.a: Example: 'This was hard, but I can study differently and ask for help. One test doesn't define me.'

weeks.assessment_key: Journal rubric (score each entry 1–4): 4 = names specific emotions precisely, explains the situation and thoughts, identifies at least one coping or resilience skill used (asking for help, positive self-talk, problem-solving, persistence), and reflects on what they learned; 3 = clear but less reflective; 2 = brief, emotion vague ('bad'); 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Have a timer or breathing app ready. Print a blank weekly schedule. Write 12 coping strategies on cards (e.g., exercise, talk to a friend, journal, deep breathing, music, sleep; vs. yelling, skipping meals, isolating, all-night gaming, ignoring homework, using substances).
misconceptions: Thinking all stress is bad. Short-term stress (eustress) can motivate you; chronic, unmanaged stress harms health.
Believing avoiding a problem is coping. Avoidance gives short relief but the stressor grows; healthy coping deals with it or the feelings.

days.guide: Explain fight-or-flight: adrenaline raises heart rate, breathing and muscle tension. Your child lists personal stressors and how their body reacts.

questions.q: Name three physical signs of the stress response.
questions.a: Faster heart rate, rapid breathing, tense muscles, sweating, stomachache, headache.
Anything that causes stress, such as a test, conflict or change.

days.guide: Practice box breathing (in 4 counts, hold 4, out 4, hold 4) for 2 minutes and progressive muscle relaxation (tense each muscle group 5 seconds, release). Ask which felt better.

questions.a: Breathe in for 4 counts, hold 4, breathe out 4, hold 4, and repeat.

questions.q: Why does slow breathing reduce stress?
questions.a: It activates the body's relaxation response, slowing heart rate and calming the fight-or-flight response.

days.guide: Your child fills in a weekly schedule with school, activities, sleep and free time, and breaks one big assignment into steps.

questions.q: How does a schedule reduce stress?
questions.a: It shows what to do when, prevents last-minute cramming and makes big tasks feel manageable.

days.guide: Your child sorts the 12 cards and explains why each unhealthy one makes things worse later.

questions.q: Why is staying up all night gaming an unhealthy way to cope?
questions.a: It avoids the problem and causes sleep loss, which increases stress and irritability.

days.guide: Your child writes a personal stress plan using the rubric checklist.

questions.q: What should you do if stress feels overwhelming for weeks?
questions.a: Talk to a trusted adult or a counselor/doctor; long-lasting stress may need professional help.

weeks.assessment_key: Stress plan rubric: 4 = lists 3+ personal stressors, body signs they notice, at least 3 healthy coping strategies (one physical, one thinking, one social), a time-management step, and a trusted adult to talk to; 3 = most parts, less specific; 2 = only 1–2 strategies; 1 = incomplete. Sort key: healthy = exercise, deep breathing, talking to someone, journaling, music, getting enough sleep, breaking tasks into steps; unhealthy = yelling/hitting, isolating, skipping meals/overeating, procrastinating, excessive screen time, using substances.

weeks.prep: Read KidsHealth teen articles on depression and anxiety first. Parent preview: Day 2 covers suicide warning signs — keep it calm and factual, say you always want to know if your child or a friend is struggling. Save 988 (call or text) in phones. Index card for help card.
misconceptions: Believing talking about suicide puts the idea in someone's head. Research shows asking directly and caringly does not increase risk and can help.
Thinking depression is just being sad or weak. It is a medical condition lasting two weeks or more that affects mood, sleep, appetite and energy, and it is treatable.
Promising to keep a friend's dangerous secret. Safety comes before secrets — tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: Read the articles together and make a two-column symptom list. Emphasize both are common and treatable.

questions.a: Persistent sadness or irritability, loss of interest in activities, changes in sleep or appetite, tiredness, trouble concentrating, feelings of worthlessness.
Excessive worry, restlessness, racing heart, stomachaches, avoiding situations, trouble sleeping.

days.guide: Calmly teach warning signs (talking about wanting to die or being a burden, giving away possessions, withdrawing, sudden mood changes) and the 988 Lifeline. Save 988 together.

questions.q: What number do you call or text in a mental health crisis?
questions.a: 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call 911 if someone is in immediate danger).
Talking about death or wanting to die, saying they are a burden, giving away belongings, withdrawing from friends, extreme mood swings.

days.guide: Your child lists five trusted adults with how to reach each (in person, phone).

questions.a: They listen, keep you safe, take you seriously and would help you get support.

days.guide: Role-play: you play a friend who seems down; your child encourages talking to an adult. Switch roles.

questions.q: Your friend says 'Promise you won't tell anyone.' What do you say?
questions.a: 'I care about you too much to keep this secret. Let's talk to an adult together.'

days.guide: Your child makes a wallet/phone help card and you check it against the key.

questions.a: Crisis Text Line (text HOME to 741741), a school counselor, a doctor, or 911 in an emergency.

weeks.assessment_key: Help card: includes 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988), Crisis Text Line (text HOME to 741741), 911 for emergencies, names and numbers of at least 3 trusted adults, and one coping strategy. Role-play rubric: 4 = notices signs, expresses care using 'I' statements, listens without judging, urges talking to an adult and offers to go with them, does not promise secrecy; 3 = most elements; 2 = advice only; 1 = does not involve an adult.

weeks.prep: Write scenario cards: 9 relationship behaviors (e.g., listening, respecting 'no', checking your phone constantly, name-calling, hitting, threatening, supporting goals, jealousy, pressuring) and 3 peer-pressure situations.
misconceptions: Confusing assertive with aggressive. Assertive = clear, respectful, firm; aggressive = hostile or blaming; passive = giving in.
Thinking an I-message is any sentence that starts with 'I'. It must state your feeling, the specific behavior and why/what you need, not blame.

days.guide: Your child sorts the cards into healthy, unhealthy, abusive and explains each.

questions.q: Is a friend checking your phone without asking healthy?
questions.a: No — unhealthy, it shows lack of trust and respect for privacy (controlling).

questions.q: Name three signs of a healthy relationship.
questions.a: Respect, trust, honesty, good communication, support, accepting boundaries.

days.guide: Teach the formula: 'I feel ___ when ___ because ___. I would like ___.' Your child rewrites five 'you' statements.

questions.a: 'I feel upset when my things get broken because they matter to me. I'd like you to ask before borrowing them.'

days.guide: Your child listens to a family member talk for 3 minutes, then summarizes what they heard. The speaker rates accuracy.

questions.a: Eye contact, not interrupting, nodding, paraphrasing ('So you're saying…'), asking questions.

days.guide: Role-play peer-pressure situations; coach your child to use an assertive voice and body language.

questions.q: A friend says 'Just skip practice with us, everyone is.' Give an assertive response.
questions.a: 'No thanks, I'm going to practice. Want to hang out after?'

questions.q: What is the difference between passive, aggressive and assertive?
questions.a: Passive gives in; aggressive attacks or blames; assertive states your view clearly and respectfully.

days.guide: Give the quiz in the assessment key and score one final role-play with the rubric.

questions.q: Why are I-messages better than you-messages in a conflict?
questions.a: They express feelings without blaming, so the other person is less defensive and more likely to listen.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (suggested): 1) healthy relationship traits: respect, trust, honesty, good communication, support 2) I-message formula: 'I feel ___ when ___ because ___; I'd like ___' 3) active listening: eye contact, don't interrupt, nod, paraphrase, ask questions 4) assertive = stating needs respectfully and firmly 5) example of unhealthy: jealousy/controlling, put-downs; abusive: hitting, threats. Role-play rubric: 4 = firm 'no', assertive body language (eye contact, steady voice), gives reason or alternative, leaves if needed; 3 = says no but hesitates; 2 = gives in partly; 1 = gives in.

weeks.prep: Preview a Common Sense Education cyberbullying lesson. Write three upstander scenarios (in person, group chat, online game). Think of a recent sibling conflict to use.
misconceptions: Thinking teasing that 'everyone does' isn't bullying. Bullying is repeated, intentional and involves a power imbalance; it hurts regardless of intent claims.
Responding to cyberbullies or deleting the evidence. Don't reply; screenshot/save, block, report and tell an adult.

days.guide: Define bullying (repeated, intentional, power imbalance) and the four types. Your child gives an example of each.

questions.q: Give an example of social bullying.
questions.a: Excluding someone on purpose, spreading rumors, or getting others to ignore someone.

questions.q: What three features make something bullying rather than a single conflict?
questions.a: It is intentional, repeated and involves a power imbalance.

days.guide: Teach upstander strategies: don't laugh, speak up if safe, support the target privately, get an adult, report. Your child writes responses to three scenarios.

questions.q: Someone posts a mean meme about a classmate in your group chat. What can an upstander do?
questions.a: Don't like or share it, say 'Not cool,' reach out to the classmate, screenshot and report it to an adult.

days.guide: Teach: 1) cool off 2) each tells their side with I-messages 3) listen and restate 4) brainstorm solutions 5) choose a fair solution 6) follow up. Apply to a real sibling conflict.

questions.q: Why is cooling off the first step?
questions.a: Strong emotions make it hard to think and listen; calming down prevents saying hurtful things.

days.guide: Teach DECIDE: Define the problem, Explore options, Consider consequences, Identify values, Decide and act, Evaluate. Your child walks through a social dilemma.

questions.q: What do the letters in DECIDE stand for?
questions.a: Define the problem, Explore alternatives, Consider consequences, Identify values, Decide and act, Evaluate the result.

days.guide: Your child writes a step-by-step cyberbullying action plan; score with the rubric.

questions.q: Should you reply to a cyberbully?
questions.a: No — don't respond; save evidence, block, report and tell an adult.

weeks.assessment_key: Cyberbullying action plan rubric: 4 = includes don't respond/retaliate, save evidence (screenshots), block the person, report on the platform, tell a trusted adult (and school if a classmate), and support the target; 3 = most steps; 2 = only 1–2 steps; 1 = incomplete or suggests retaliating.

weeks.prep: Poster paper or a phone for a short video; stationery for gratitude letters. Write a unit 2 test (see key).
misconceptions: Confusing empathy with sympathy. Sympathy feels sorry for someone; empathy tries to understand how they feel from their point of view.
Thinking advocacy means just telling people what to do. Effective advocacy uses facts, a clear message and a positive call to action.

days.guide: Read three short scenarios (new kid, friend who lost a game, sibling who is left out). Your child describes what each person might feel and what they need.

questions.a: Understanding and sharing another person's feelings by imagining their point of view.

days.guide: Your child designs a kindness or anti-bullying poster/video for a specific audience with a call to action.

questions.q: What is a call to action? Give one.
questions.a: A specific thing you want people to do, e.g., 'Invite someone new to sit with you this week.'

days.guide: Explain research linking gratitude to better mood. Your child writes three thank-you letters and starts a daily 'three good things' list.

questions.q: How can practicing gratitude affect mental health?
questions.a: It increases positive emotions, reduces stress and improves relationships.

days.guide: Review unit 2 with a quick quiz game using vocabulary cards.

questions.q: What is the difference between an upstander and a bystander?
questions.a: A bystander watches and does nothing; an upstander takes safe action to help.

days.guide: Give the unit 2 test (see key).

questions.q: Name one way to promote inclusion in your community.
questions.a: Invite someone new, start a club open to all, speak up against exclusion, learn about others' cultures.

weeks.assessment_key: Campaign rubric: 4 = clear positive message, a specific call to action (e.g., 'Sit with someone new'), accurate facts, aimed at a specific audience, creative design; 3 = clear message, weak call to action; 2 = unclear; 1 = incomplete. Unit 2 test (suggested): 1) resilience = bouncing back 2) three body signs of stress 3) two healthy coping strategies 4) 988 Lifeline 5) two signs of depression 6) I-message formula 7) four types of bullying (physical, verbal, social, cyber) 8) upstander actions 9) DECIDE steps 10) empathy definition. 9–10 advanced, 7–8 proficient.

weeks.prep: Look up CDC WISQARS or a CDC fact sheet on teen injuries (leading causes for ages 10–14: motor-vehicle crashes, suffocation, drowning, falls; for 15–19 motor-vehicle crashes lead). Print a home safety checklist; have a bike helmet ready.
misconceptions: Calling injuries 'accidents' that can't be prevented. Most unintentional injuries are predictable and preventable.
Thinking you must lose consciousness to have a concussion. Most concussions do not involve passing out.

days.guide: Look at CDC data together. Your child identifies the top causes of injury death for teens and one prevention for each.

questions.q: What is the leading cause of injury death for U.S. teens?
questions.a: Motor-vehicle crashes.

questions.q: Name one way to prevent motor-vehicle injuries as a passenger.
questions.a: Always wear a seat belt; ride in the back seat until age 13; don't distract the driver.

days.guide: Your child walks the house with the checklist, testing a smoke alarm and noting hazards.

questions.q: How often should smoke alarms be tested?
questions.a: Monthly (replace batteries at least yearly or as directed).

questions.q: Where should medicines and cleaners be stored?
questions.a: Locked or high, out of children's reach, in original containers.

days.guide: Fit a helmet: level on head, about two finger-widths above the eyebrows, side straps forming a V under the ears, chin strap snug (one finger fits). Teach concussion signs.

questions.a: Headache, dizziness, confusion, nausea/vomiting, blurred vision, sensitivity to light, memory problems.

questions.q: What should an athlete do if a concussion is suspected?
questions.a: Stop playing immediately ('when in doubt, sit it out') and see a doctor before returning.

days.guide: Teach water safety (swim with a buddy, lifeguarded areas, life jackets, never dive into unknown water) and bike rules (ride with traffic, obey signals, be visible).

questions.q: Which direction should you ride a bike on the road?
questions.a: With traffic, on the right side.

questions.q: Why never dive into shallow or unknown water?
questions.a: Risk of hitting the bottom and causing head or spinal cord injury.

days.guide: Your child writes a family injury-prevention plan using the audit results.

questions.q: Give one fix for a fall hazard.
questions.a: Secure loose rugs with backing, add lighting/handrails on stairs, clean up clutter.

weeks.assessment_key: Home audit: checks smoke detectors (test monthly), fire extinguisher, escape routes, medicines and cleaners locked/high, rugs and stairs for fall hazards, carbon monoxide detector; lists 3 hazards found with fixes. Family plan rubric: 4 = addresses falls, fire, poisoning, vehicle/bike/water safety with specific actions and who is responsible; 3 = three areas; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Do a test search of your child's name first. Pick one app/device to review privacy settings on together. Collect or write 6 sample messages (3 phishing, 3 legitimate). Preview Common Sense lesson on online predators.
misconceptions: Thinking deleted posts are gone. Screenshots, archives and servers can keep them; assume anything posted is permanent.
Believing online predators are easy to spot. Groomers often pretend to be peers, give compliments and gifts, and ask for secrecy.

days.guide: Search your child's name together. Discuss what a digital footprint is and how colleges and employers may see it.

questions.a: The trail of information you leave online — posts, photos, comments, searches — that can be permanent.

questions.q: Name two things to never share publicly.
questions.a: Home address, phone number, school name, passwords, real-time location, birth date.

days.guide: Sit together and review privacy settings on one app: private account, location off, who can message you.

questions.q: Why turn off location sharing in apps?
questions.a: It can reveal where you live or are, which strangers could use.

days.guide: Teach grooming warning signs: flattery, gifts, asking for secrecy, moving to private chat, asking for photos or to meet. Teach: stop, block, screenshot, tell an adult; report to CyberTipline.

questions.a: Asking to keep the relationship secret, giving gifts or excessive compliments, asking for personal photos, wanting to meet in person, isolating you from family.

questions.q: An online 'friend' asks you to keep your chats secret. What do you do?
questions.a: Stop chatting, don't send anything, save the messages and tell a trusted adult.

days.guide: Your child examines 6 messages and marks phishing ones, citing clues.

questions.q: List three clues of a phishing message.
questions.a: Urgent threats, requests for passwords or personal info, misspellings, odd sender address, links that don't match the real site, prizes that are too good to be true.

days.guide: Write the family media agreement together and sign it.

questions.q: What should you do if you see something online that makes you uncomfortable?
questions.a: Don't respond, take a screenshot, close it, and tell a trusted adult.

weeks.assessment_key: Family media agreement rubric: 4 = includes screen-time limits and device-free times/places, privacy rules (no sharing address, school, location, passwords), who you can chat with, what to do with uncomfortable messages (don't reply, screenshot, tell an adult), consequences and signatures; 3 = most items; 2 = only time limits; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Write scenario cards (a heated argument at a game, a friend talking about bringing a knife to school, an older teen inviting your child to 'join the crew'). Parent preview: discuss serious topics calmly.
misconceptions: Thinking telling an adult about a weapon is 'snitching.' Reporting prevents someone from getting hurt; safety outweighs loyalty.
Believing fighting back is the best way to earn respect. De-escalating or walking away is the strongest and safest choice.

days.guide: Explain risk factors increase the chance of violence and protective factors decrease it. Your child sorts examples.

questions.q: Give two protective factors against violence.
questions.a: Caring family, positive friends, involvement in sports/clubs, connection to school, trusted mentors.

days.guide: Model calming phrases: 'I don't want to fight,' 'Let's take a break,' calm voice, open hands, leave. Role-play two scenarios.

questions.a: Stay calm and lower your voice, give the person space, listen, avoid insults, walk away and get help.

days.guide: Discuss why reporting weapons saves lives, and how gangs recruit (belonging, money, protection) and the real costs (violence, prison, family harm).

questions.q: A classmate shows you a weapon in his backpack. What do you do?
questions.a: Get away from the situation and tell a trusted adult or school official immediately.

questions.q: Why might a gang appeal to a teen?
questions.a: They promise belonging, protection, respect or money — needs that can be met safely through family, teams and mentors.

days.guide: Your child applies DECIDE to two risky scenarios and writes a choice for each.

questions.q: Why is 'Consider consequences' important in risky situations?
questions.a: It makes you think about short- and long-term results for you and others before acting.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key.

questions.q: What is the safest response if someone tries to start a fight with you?
questions.a: Stay calm, don't respond to insults, walk away and tell an adult.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (suggested): 1) risk factors: exposure to violence, substance use, gang contact, access to weapons 2) protective factors: supportive family, school connection, positive activities, good friends 3) de-escalation: stay calm, lower voice, give space, listen, walk away 4) if you know about a weapon: tell a trusted adult immediately/use anonymous tip line 5) gangs recruit by offering belonging, protection, money. Scenario rubric: response uses a decision model, chooses a safe option, involves an adult.

weeks.prep: Visit Ready.gov/kids. Gather kit supplies: water (1 gallon per person per day for 3 days), nonperishable food, flashlight, batteries, first aid kit, medicines, radio, phone charger, copies of documents, masks (N95 for smoke). Check your county's alert system (e.g., sign up for local emergency alerts).
misconceptions: Running outside or standing in a doorway during an earthquake. Drop, Cover and Hold On under sturdy furniture; doorways aren't safer in modern homes.
Thinking a cloth mask protects from wildfire smoke. Only well-fitted N95/KN95 respirators filter fine smoke particles; staying indoors with filtered air is best.

days.guide: Practice Drop, Cover, Hold On; your child identifies safe spots (under sturdy tables) and dangers (windows, tall furniture).

questions.q: What are the three steps during an earthquake?
questions.a: Drop to your hands and knees, Cover your head and neck (under a sturdy table), Hold On until shaking stops.

questions.q: If you're in bed during an earthquake, what should you do?
questions.a: Stay in bed, cover your head and neck with a pillow.

days.guide: Learn evacuation terms (warning = go now; watch = be ready) and check the AirNow AQI scale.

questions.q: At what AQI level is air 'unhealthy for sensitive groups'?
Name two ways to protect yourself from wildfire smoke.
questions.a: Stay indoors with windows closed, use air filters/HEPA, wear an N95, limit outdoor exercise.

days.guide: Fill out a family communication plan with contacts and meeting places.

questions.a: Long-distance calls/texts often go through when local lines are overloaded, and that person can relay messages.

days.guide: Build or update the 72-hour kit using the checklist.

questions.q: How much water should a 4-person family store for 3 days?
questions.a: 4 people × 1 gallon × 3 days = 12 gallons.

days.guide: Run an evacuation drill: alarm, grab kit, meet outside. Time it and discuss improvements.

questions.q: What should you do if your exit is blocked by smoke?
questions.a: Use your second exit; stay low under smoke; feel doors for heat before opening.

weeks.assessment_key: Emergency plan: lists out-of-area contact, two meeting places (near home and outside neighborhood), evacuation routes, how to get alerts, pets and medical needs. Kit checklist: at least 3 days' water (1 gal/person/day), food, flashlight, batteries, radio, first aid kit, medications, phone charger, important document copies, cash, whistle, N95 masks. Drill completed in a set time with everyone at the meeting spot.

weeks.prep: First aid kit, bandages, gloves, a pillow for choking practice. Consider a Red Cross or AHA course for hands-on certification. Write the unit 3 test.
misconceptions: Putting butter or ice on burns. Cool a minor burn under cool running water for about 10–20 minutes, then cover loosely.
Hanging up when calling 911. Stay on the line until the dispatcher says to hang up.

days.guide: Practice a mock call: location, what happened, how many hurt, your name/number, stay on the line.

questions.q: What is the most important information to give a 911 dispatcher first?
questions.a: Your exact location (address or landmarks).

questions.q: What does a Good Samaritan law do?
questions.a: It protects people who give reasonable emergency help in good faith from being sued.

days.guide: Practice with gloves: press a clean cloth on a 'cut', clean and bandage; cool a 'burn' under running water.

questions.q: How do you stop bleeding from a cut?
questions.a: Apply firm, direct pressure with a clean cloth or gauze; raise it if possible; get help if bleeding doesn't stop.

questions.q: How should you treat a minor burn?
questions.a: Cool under cool running water about 10–20 minutes, don't pop blisters, cover loosely with sterile gauze; no ice or butter.

days.guide: Teach the universal sign (hands at throat). Practice abdominal thrusts on a pillow — never on a person.

questions.q: What is the universal choking sign?
questions.a: Hands clutched at the throat.

questions.q: Where do you place your fist for abdominal thrusts?
questions.a: Just above the navel, thumb side in, below the ribcage, then quick inward-and-upward thrusts.

days.guide: Review unit 3 with flash cards and a mock 911 call.

questions.q: If a choking person can cough forcefully, what should you do?
questions.a: Encourage them to keep coughing; be ready to help if they can't breathe, speak or cough.

days.guide: Give the unit 3 test (see key).

questions.q: Name one emergency where you call 911.
questions.a: Someone is unconscious, not breathing, severely bleeding, choking and unable to breathe, a fire, a serious crash.

weeks.assessment_key: Skills check: 911 call states location first, what happened, number of people hurt, stays on line; cut care: gloves, pressure with clean cloth, wash small cuts, bandage; burn: cool water 10–20 min, no ice/butter, cover; choking: recognizes universal sign, asks 'Are you choking?', gives abdominal thrusts (fist above navel, quick inward-upward thrusts) and calls 911. Unit 3 test (suggested): 1) leading cause of teen injury death — motor vehicle crashes 2) helmet fit 3) concussion signs 4) digital footprint 5) phishing clues 6) grooming signs 7) Drop, Cover, Hold On 8) 1 gallon water/person/day 9) burn care 10) universal choking sign.

weeks.prep: Explore NIDA for Teens 'Brain and Addiction' pages. Prepare 10 myth/fact cards. Parent preview: units 18–24 cover drugs — make clear your family expectations.
misconceptions: Thinking addiction only happens to 'weak' people. Addiction is a brain disease; teens are more vulnerable because the brain is still developing.
Believing natural or prescription means safe. Cannabis, tobacco and prescription opioids can all be harmful or addictive.

days.guide: Explain the prefrontal cortex (planning, judgment, impulse control) matures into the mid-20s while the reward system develops earlier.

questions.q: What does the prefrontal cortex do?
questions.a: Controls decision-making, planning, judgment and impulse control.

questions.q: At about what age is the brain fully developed?
questions.a: Around the mid-20s (about age 25).

days.guide: Your child diagrams the reward pathway (VTA → nucleus accumbens → prefrontal cortex) and labels dopamine.

questions.q: How do drugs 'hijack' the reward pathway?
questions.a: They cause a much larger dopamine surge than natural rewards, teaching the brain to crave the drug and making everyday pleasures feel less rewarding.

days.guide: Define tolerance, dependence, withdrawal, addiction with a nicotine example.

questions.a: Needing more of a drug to get the same effect.
Uncomfortable physical and mental symptoms (irritability, cravings, headache) when a person stops using a drug they depend on.

days.guide: Your child sorts 10 cards into myths and facts and explains each.

questions.q: Myth or fact: 'Prescription drugs are safe to share because a doctor prescribed them.'
questions.a: Myth — they're prescribed for one person's body and condition; misuse can cause overdose or addiction.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key.

questions.q: Why are teens more likely than adults to become addicted?
questions.a: Their brains are still developing; the reward system is mature but impulse control isn't, and early use changes brain wiring.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (suggested): 1) prefrontal cortex controls judgment, planning, impulse control; develops into mid-20s 2) dopamine = brain chemical linked to pleasure/reward and motivation 3) drugs flood the reward pathway with dopamine, so natural rewards feel less satisfying 4) tolerance = needing more for the same effect 5) dependence = body needs the drug to feel normal 6) withdrawal = unpleasant symptoms when stopping 7) addiction = compulsive use despite harm 8) why teens are at higher risk — developing brain. Myth/fact examples: 'You can't get addicted to vaping' — myth; 'Most teens don't use drugs' — fact.

weeks.prep: Print CDC e-cigarette fact sheets ('Quick Facts on the Risks of E-cigarettes'). Find 2–3 vape ad images (from news articles or Truth Initiative). Find California Healthy Kids Survey or CA Youth Tobacco Survey data online.
misconceptions: Thinking vapes are just water vapor. The aerosol contains nicotine, ultrafine particles, flavoring chemicals and heavy metals.
Thinking one vape pod has little nicotine. Some pods contain as much nicotine as a pack of 20 cigarettes or more.

days.guide: Your child lists short-term (bad breath, yellow teeth, coughing, reduced stamina, higher heart rate) and long-term effects (lung cancer, heart disease, stroke, COPD/emphysema).

questions.q: Name two long-term effects of smoking.
questions.a: Lung and other cancers, heart disease, stroke, COPD/emphysema, gum disease.
Smoke breathed in by nonsmokers from someone else's cigarette; it also causes disease.

days.guide: Read CDC facts together and highlight nicotine content and health effects.

questions.q: Why is nicotine especially harmful to teens?
questions.a: It is highly addictive and can harm the parts of the developing brain that control attention, learning, mood and impulse control.

questions.q: What's in vape aerosol besides nicotine?
questions.a: Ultrafine particles, flavoring chemicals like diacetyl, volatile organic compounds and heavy metals such as nickel, tin and lead.

days.guide: Your child analyzes vape ads: flavors, bright colors, sleek tech look, influencers.

questions.q: Why are candy and fruit flavors a marketing technique?
questions.a: They appeal to young people, hide harshness of nicotine and make vaping seem harmless.

days.guide: Read survey data and calculate or describe trends (e.g., percent of 7th graders who have ever vaped).

questions.q: What is the legal age to buy tobacco products, including vapes, in California?
If most 7th graders have never vaped, what does that tell you about 'everyone is doing it'?
questions.a: It's a false norm — most teens do not vape.

days.guide: Your child creates the fact sheet and you score it with the rubric.

questions.q: Name a resource for teens who want to quit vaping.
questions.a: Truth Initiative's 'This is Quitting' (text DITCHVAPE to 88709), Kick It California, a doctor or counselor.

weeks.assessment_key: Vaping fact sheet rubric: 4 = at least 4 accurate facts (most vapes contain nicotine; nicotine is highly addictive and harms the developing brain's attention/learning; aerosol has harmful chemicals and metals; one pod can equal a pack of cigarettes; flavors target youth; age 21 to buy in CA), cites CDC or similar source, peer-friendly design, includes refusal tip or quitting resource (e.g., text 'DITCHVAPE' to 88709, or Kick It California); 3 = 3 facts with source; 2 = 1–2 facts; 1 = inaccurate.

weeks.prep: NIDA for Teens alcohol pages, 2–3 alcohol ads from magazines/online. Write a short quiz.
misconceptions: Believing coffee, cold showers or sleep 'sober someone up' quickly. Only time lowers BAC — the liver processes alcohol at about one standard drink per hour.
Thinking someone passed out from drinking should 'sleep it off.' They may have alcohol poisoning; call 911 and keep them on their side.

days.guide: Explain alcohol is a depressant that slows the brain. Your child labels effects on brain, liver, heart, stomach.

questions.q: Is alcohol a stimulant or a depressant?
questions.a: A depressant — it slows down the central nervous system.

questions.q: Which organ breaks down most alcohol?
questions.a: The liver.

days.guide: Define BAC and list factors; discuss why teens are affected more.

questions.a: Blood alcohol concentration — the percent of alcohol in a person's blood.

questions.q: Name three factors that affect BAC.
questions.a: Amount drunk, how fast, body weight/size, sex, whether there's food in the stomach.

days.guide: Teach the signs of alcohol poisoning and the response: call 911, stay with the person, keep them on their side, don't let them 'sleep it off.'

questions.q: Name three signs of alcohol poisoning.
questions.a: Confusion, vomiting, seizures, slow or irregular breathing, blue or pale skin, low body temperature, can't be awakened.

questions.q: Why place a vomiting, drowsy person on their side?
questions.a: To prevent choking on vomit.

days.guide: Your child analyzes ads and lists what's left out (health risks, accidents, addiction, cost).

questions.q: What do alcohol ads usually show, and what do they leave out?
questions.a: They show fun, friends, success and attractive people; they leave out hangovers, injuries, crashes, addiction and health problems.

days.guide: Give the quiz from the assessment key.

questions.q: What is the legal drinking age in the U.S.?
