Removing from only one side of a hanger. Whatever you remove from one side, remove from the other to stay balanced.

days.guide: Show tape diagrams: 3 equal parts of x plus a piece 5 = total 20 (3x + 5 = 20) vs 3 equal parts each (x + 5) = 20. Your child matches 6 stories. Check before moving on: ask "Diagram: 4 boxes each 'x + 2', total 28. Equation?" Look for: 4(x + 2) = 28.

Model the snack problem. Your child writes equations for several situations. Check before moving on: ask "4 friends each buy a $2.50 snack and share a $6 pizza. Total cost?" Look for: 4(2.50) + 6 = $16.

questions.q: 4 friends each buy a $2.50 snack and share a $6 pizza. Total cost?
If the total is t and snack cost is s: equation?

days.guide: Draw a hanger: 3 triangles and 2 circles (each circle = 1) on the left, 11 circles on the right. Your child removes 2 from each side, then splits into 3. Check before moving on: ask "Solve 3x + 2 = 11." Look for: x = 3.
Model 'same to both sides' with written steps. Your child solves 10 and checks each. Check before moving on: ask "5x − 4 = 21?" Look for: x = 5.
Give the quiz (see key). Check before moving on: ask "Equation for 'twice a number plus 7 is 19'?" Look for: 2n + 7 = 19; n = 6.

questions.q: Equation for 'twice a number plus 7 is 19'?

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Diagram 5 parts of x and 3 = 23 → 5x + 3 = 23, x = 4. 2) 2(x + 6) = 20, x = 4. 3) Story: 3 tickets plus $4 parking is $31 → 3t + 4 = 31, t = 9. 4) 6x + 1 = 25, x = 4. 5) Match diagram to 3(x − 2) = 12, x = 6.

weeks.prep: Paper algebra tiles (cut rectangles for x and small squares for 1; use two colors for negative).
misconceptions: Distributing to only the first term: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 3 is wrong; it is 2x + 6.
Multiplying by a fraction's reciprocal but forgetting the sign: dividing by −2/3 = multiplying by −3/2.

days.guide: Solve 2(x + 3) = 14 both ways: divide by 2 (x + 3 = 7) and distribute (2x + 6 = 14). Your child solves 4 more both ways. Check before moving on: ask "2(x + 3) = 14?" Look for: x = 4 by either method.

questions.a: x = 4 by either method.

days.guide: Model −2/3 x + 5 = −7. Your child solves several with negative and fractional coefficients. Check before moving on: ask "−2/3 x + 5 = −7?" Look for: −2/3 x = −12, x = 18.
Your child solves 8 word problems: define a variable, write, solve, check. Check before moving on: ask "Gym: $25 sign-up + $15/month, total $130. Months?" Look for: 25 + 15m = 130, m = 7.

Solve one problem by working backward and by equation. Your child writes which made more sense. Check before moving on: ask "A number is doubled, then 9 is subtracted to get 21. Number?" Look for: Backward: 21 + 9 = 30, ÷ 2 = 15. Equation: 2n − 9 = 21, n = 15.

questions.q: A number is doubled, then 9 is subtracted to get 21. Number?
questions.a: Backward: 21 + 9 = 30, ÷ 2 = 15. Equation: 2n − 9 = 21, n = 15.

days.guide: Give the quiz (see key). Check before moving on: ask "3(x − 4) = −6?" Look for: x = 2.

weeks.prep: Number line, colored pencils.
misconceptions: Not reversing the inequality when multiplying or dividing by a negative. Test a value to check.
Open vs closed circles: ≤, ≥ use closed; <, > use open.

days.guide: Model 'at least 13' as h ≥ 13 with a closed circle. Your child writes and graphs several. Check before moving on: ask "'No more than 8 people'?" Look for: p ≤ 8, closed circle at 8, shade left (whole numbers only in context).

questions.a: p ≤ 8, closed circle at 8, shade left (whole numbers only in context).

days.guide: Test values in −2x > 6. Your child discovers solutions are x < −3 and states the reversal rule. Check before moving on: ask "Is x = −5 a solution to −2x > 6?" Look for: Yes: 10 > 6.

questions.a: No: 0 > 6 is false.

days.guide: Model 5x − 3 ≥ 22. Your child solves 10 and graphs. Check before moving on: ask "5x − 3 ≥ 22?" Look for: x ≥ 5.

Solve the budget problem together, discussing the meaning of a decimal answer. Check before moving on: ask "$8/hour with $40 saved, more than $150?" Look for: 40 + 8h > 150 → h > 13.75; she must work at least 14 whole hours.

questions.a: 40 + 8h > 150 → h > 13.75; she must work at least 14 whole hours.

days.guide: Give the quiz (see key). Check before moving on: ask "−x ≤ 4?" Look for: x ≥ −4.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) 'At least 18' → a ≥ 18, closed circle. 2) 3x + 2 < 14 → x < 4. 3) −4x ≥ 20 → x ≤ −5. 4) x/2 − 1 > 3 → x > 8. 5) Graph x > −2: open circle, shade right. 6) $5 per hour with $12, at least $60 → h ≥ 9.6 → 10 hours.

weeks.prep: Area model templates (rectangles split into parts).
misconceptions: Combining unlike terms (3x + 2 = 5x).
Dropping a negative sign when distributing: −2(x − 4) = −2x + 8, not −2x − 8.

days.guide: Rewrite 5 − 3x as 5 + (−3x). Your child tests equivalence by substituting x = 2 in both forms. Check before moving on: ask "Is 8 − 2x equivalent to −2x + 8?" Look for: Yes — commutative after writing as 8 + (−2x).

questions.a: Yes — commutative after writing as 8 + (−2x).

days.guide: Model 6(2x − 5) with an area model. Your child expands and factors. Check before moving on: ask "Expand 6(2x − 5)." Look for: 12x − 30.

Model 3x − 4 − 7x + 2.5. Your child simplifies and checks with x = 1. Check before moving on: ask "Simplify." Look for: −4x − 1.5. Check x = 1: original 3 − 4 − 7 + 2.5 = −5.5; simplified −4 − 1.5 = −5.5.

questions.a: −4x − 1.5. Check x = 1: original 3 − 4 − 7 + 2.5 = −5.5; simplified −4 − 1.5 = −5.5.

days.guide: Model a + 0.05a = 1.05a. Your child solves 4 similar problems. Check before moving on: ask "Write a 20% decrease of p two ways." Look for: p − 0.20p and 0.80p.

questions.q: Write a 20% decrease of p two ways.

days.guide: Give the quiz (see key). Check before moving on: ask "Simplify −2(x − 4) + 3x." Look for: x + 8.

weeks.prep: visualpatterns.org (pick two patterns), calculator, graph paper.
misconceptions: Writing an expression that only fits step 1. Test the expression on at least three steps.
Treating break-even as revenue alone. Break-even is where revenue = cost.

days.guide: Show a visual pattern; describe how it grows. Your child writes two different-looking expressions and shows they are equivalent. Check before moving on: ask "Pattern: 5, 8, 11, 14 tiles. Expression for step n?" Look for: 3n + 2 (check n = 1: 5).

questions.q: Pattern: 5, 8, 11, 14 tiles. Expression for step n?
questions.a: 3n + 2 (check n = 1: 5).

days.guide: Model: supplies cost $30 plus $0.50 per cookie; cookies sell for $1.25. Your child finds break-even. Check before moving on: ask "Break-even?" Look for: 1.25c = 30 + 0.50c → 0.75c = 30 → c = 40 cookies.
Plan A: $30 + $5 per GB; Plan B: $50 flat. Your child writes equations and an inequality for when A is cheaper. Check before moving on: ask "When is A cheaper?" Look for: 30 + 5g < 50 → g < 4 GB.
Your child finds and corrects errors in 6 worked solutions, writing the error in words. Check before moving on: ask "Error: −3x < 12 → x < −4." Look for: Dividing by −3 must reverse: x > −4.

questions.a: Dividing by −3 must reverse: x > −4.

days.guide: Give the quiz (see key) and collect the fundraiser write-up. Check before moving on: ask "Simplify 2(3n + 1) − n." Look for: 5n + 2.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Pattern 4, 7, 10 → 3n + 1. 2) 2(x − 3) = 3x − 4 → x = −2. 3) 4x − 5 > 11 → x > 4. 4) Break-even: $20 costs + $2/item, sells $6 → 5 items. Write-up rubric: correct cost/revenue expressions, correct break-even, interpretation.

weeks.prep: Index cards for the equation sort; Illustrative Mathematics unit 6 practice problems.
misconceptions: Forgetting to check solutions — require substitution.
Writing an inequality where an equation is meant (look for 'at least', 'more than').

days.guide: Your child sorts 15 cards by solution and strategy and explains groupings. Check before moving on: ask "Which have the same solution: 2x + 4 = 10, 3(x − 1) = 6, x/3 = 1?" Look for: All have x = 3.

questions.q: Which have the same solution: 2x + 4 = 10, 3(x − 1) = 6, x/3 = 1?
questions.a: All have x = 3.

days.guide: Your child writes one equation and one inequality word problem with full solutions. Check before moving on: ask "What makes a good word problem?" Look for: Clear quantities, a question, and a unique answer that fits the context.

questions.q: What makes a good word problem?
questions.a: Clear quantities, a question, and a unique answer that fits the context.

days.guide: Swap problems with a parent or sibling; each solves and checks. Check before moving on: ask "How do you check an inequality answer?" Look for: Substitute a value from the solution set and one outside it.

questions.q: How do you check an inequality answer?
questions.a: Substitute a value from the solution set and one outside it.

days.guide: Mixed review from IM practice set. Check before moving on: ask "−3(x + 2) = 12?" Look for: x = −6.
Give the unit 6 test (see key). Check before moving on: ask "6 − 2x ≥ 0?" Look for: x ≤ 3.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 6 test sample answers: 1) 4x − 9 = 15 → 6. 2) −2(x − 5) = 4 → 3. 3) 2/3 x + 1 = 9 → 12. 4) 7 − x < 2 → x > 5. 5) Expand −3(2x − 1) = −6x + 3. 6) Simplify 5x − 2 − 3x + 8 = 2x + 6. 7) $15 per hour plus $20 tips, at least $110 → h ≥ 6. 8) Equation from tape diagram correct.

weeks.prep: Protractor, paper strips, brads (paper fasteners).
misconceptions: Mixing up complementary (90°) and supplementary (180°). Mnemonic: C comes before S, 90 before 180.
Thinking vertical angles are angles that look vertical. They are opposite each other at an intersection.

days.guide: Draw two intersecting lines. Your child measures all four angles and records sums and equal pairs. Check before moving on: ask "One angle is 65°. The adjacent angle on the line?" Look for: 115°.

questions.q: One angle is 65°. The adjacent angle on the line?

days.guide: Model x + 47 = 90. Your child finds complements and supplements. Check before moving on: ask "Complement of 47°?" Look for: 43°.
Build an X with strips and a brad and rotate. Your child records vertical-angle pairs. Check before moving on: ask "One angle is 130°. Its vertical angle?" Look for: 130°.

questions.q: One angle is 130°. Its vertical angle?

days.guide: Model (2x + 10) + 3x = 180. Your child solves 10. Check before moving on: ask "Solve." Look for: 5x + 10 = 180, x = 34; angles 78° and 102°.
Give the quiz (see key). Check before moving on: ask "Complementary angles x and 2x?" Look for: x = 30°, 60°.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Complement of 28° = 62°. 2) Supplement of 95° = 85°. 3) Vertical angle of 54° = 54°. 4) x + 3x = 180 → x = 45. 5) (x + 20) + 2x = 90 → x = 70/3 ≈ 23.3. 6) Three angles on a line: 40, x, 75 → x = 65.

weeks.prep: Straws, scissors, ruler, protractor, compass.
misconceptions: Thinking any three lengths form a triangle. The two shorter sides must add to more than the longest.
Thinking three angles determine one triangle. They fix the shape, not the size.

days.guide: Cut straw sets (e.g., 3-4-5, 3-4-8, 4-4-8, 5-5-5). Your child tests each and states the triangle inequality. Check before moving on: ask "3, 4, 8 cm?" Look for: No: 3 + 4 = 7 < 8.

questions.a: No: 4 + 4 = 8 collapses flat.

days.guide: Your child draws triangles with angles 50°, 60°, 70° of different sizes. Check before moving on: ask "Are they the same?" Look for: Same shape (scaled copies), different sizes — not unique.

questions.a: Same shape (scaled copies), different sizes — not unique.

days.guide: Model SAS with ruler and protractor. Your child constructs and compares with someone else's. Check before moving on: ask "Sides 5 and 7 cm with 40° between: unique?" Look for: Yes — SAS gives one triangle.

questions.q: Sides 5 and 7 cm with 40° between: unique?
questions.a: Yes — SAS gives one triangle.

days.guide: Your child classifies 8 condition sets. Check before moving on: ask "Angles 90°, 60°, 40°?" Look for: No triangle — sum is 190°.

questions.a: No triangle — sum is 190°.
Exactly one triangle.

days.guide: Give the quiz (see key). Check before moving on: ask "Third side of a triangle with sides 5 and 9 must be between…?" Look for: 4 and 14.

questions.q: Third side of a triangle with sides 5 and 9 must be between…?
questions.a: 4 and 14.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) 2, 3, 6: no triangle. 2) 5, 6, 7: one. 3) Angles 30, 60, 90: many (any size). 4) Two sides + included angle: one. 5) Angles 100, 100, x: none. Straw table: correct yes/no for every set.

weeks.prep: Clay or play dough, dental floss, cereal box, Toblerone-style triangular box, ruler.
misconceptions: Using the side face instead of the base for a triangular prism. The base is the triangle; height is the distance between triangles.
Forgetting ½ in triangle area.

days.guide: Your child slices clay shapes parallel and perpendicular to the base and sketches cross sections. Check before moving on: ask "Cube sliced parallel to a face?" Look for: A square.

questions.q: Cube sliced parallel to a face?
questions.a: A square.

questions.q: Cylinder sliced perpendicular to its base (vertically through the middle)?
questions.a: A rectangle.

days.guide: Model V = Bh. Your child finds volumes. Check before moving on: ask "Rectangular prism 3 × 4 × 5?" Look for: 60 units³.

questions.a: 60 units³.

questions.q: Triangular prism, triangle base 6 and height 4, length 10?

days.guide: Your child decomposes L-shaped prisms into two rectangular prisms. Check before moving on: ask "L-shaped base area 22 cm², height 5 cm?" Look for: 110 cm³.

questions.q: L-shaped base area 22 cm², height 5 cm?
questions.a: 110 cm³.

days.guide: Measure the boxes. Your child computes volumes with units. Check before moving on: ask "Cereal box 30 × 20 × 7 cm?" Look for: 4,200 cm³.
Give the quiz (see key). Check before moving on: ask "Cross section of a square pyramid parallel to the base?" Look for: A smaller square.

questions.q: Cross section of a square pyramid parallel to the base?
questions.a: A smaller square.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Cylinder cut parallel to base: circle. 2) Prism 2 × 5 × 8: 80. 3) Triangular prism base area 15, height 9: 135. 4) Triangle base 10, h 3, prism length 12: 180. 5) Cube side 4: 64. Sketches: correct shape for each slice.

weeks.prep: Cardstock, tape, ruler, scissors.
misconceptions: Counting only 3 faces of a rectangular prism. There are 6 (3 pairs).
Using cubic units for surface area. Surface area is square units.

days.guide: Your child draws, cuts and folds nets of triangular and rectangular prisms. Check before moving on: ask "How many faces in a triangular prism net?" Look for: 5 (2 triangles, 3 rectangles).

questions.q: How many faces in a triangular prism net?
questions.a: 5 (2 triangles, 3 rectangles).

days.guide: Model SA as the sum of face areas. Your child finds SA including a prism with a hole. Check before moving on: ask "2 × 3 × 4 prism SA?" Look for: 2(6 + 8 + 12) = 52 units².

questions.a: 150 units².

days.guide: Your child classifies 8 situations then solves. Check before moving on: ask "Wrapping a gift?" Look for: Surface area.

questions.a: Surface area.
Volume.

days.guide: Mixed review; one of each topic. Check before moving on: ask "Supplement of 72°?" Look for: 108°.
Give the unit 7 test (see key). Check before moving on: ask "Cube with volume 27. Surface area?" Look for: Side 3; SA = 54.

questions.a: Side 3; SA = 54.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 7 test sample answers: 1) Complement of 35 = 55. 2) x + 2x + 30 = 180 → 50. 3) 4, 5, 10: no triangle. 4) Prism 4 × 5 × 6 volume 120, SA 148. 5) Triangular prism (3-4-5 right triangle, length 10): V = 60, SA = 12 + 120 = 132. 6) Cross section of cylinder parallel to base: circle.

weeks.prep: Coins, dice, paper bag with colored tiles (e.g., 5 red, 3 blue, 2 green).
misconceptions: Thinking past results affect future independent events (gambler's fallacy).
Expecting experimental results to exactly match theory in few trials.

days.guide: Your child places 10 events on a 0–1 line and justifies. Check before moving on: ask "Rolling a 7 on one die?" Look for: 0, impossible.

questions.a: 0, impossible.

days.guide: Your child lists sample spaces. Check before moving on: ask "Two coins?" Look for: HH, HT, TH, TT (4).

questions.a: HH, HT, TH, TT (4).

days.guide: Your child draws 50 times with replacement and records relative frequencies. Check before moving on: ask "Red drawn 22 of 50 times. Relative frequency?" Look for: 0.44.

questions.q: Red drawn 22 of 50 times. Relative frequency?

days.guide: Your child compares to theory (red = 5/10 = 0.5) and explains. Check before moving on: ask "Why do more trials help?" Look for: Experimental probability tends to get closer to theoretical (law of large numbers).

questions.a: Experimental probability tends to get closer to theoretical (law of large numbers).

days.guide: Give the quiz (see key). Check before moving on: ask "P(even on a die)?" Look for: 3/6 = 1/2.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) P(5 on a die) = 1/6. 2) P(blue) from 5R 3B 2G = 3/10. 3) Sample space of a 4-color spinner: 4 outcomes. 4) 'Likely' is between 0.5 and 1. 5) 30 heads in 50 flips: 0.6 experimental vs 0.5 theoretical.

weeks.prep: Two dice, coins, random number generator (random.org or a calculator).
misconceptions: Counting a sum like 7 as one outcome instead of 6 ordered pairs.
Too few simulation trials. Emphasize more trials give better estimates.

days.guide: Model a tree for 3 shirts × 2 pants. Your child draws trees for outfits and coin-die combos. Check before moving on: ask "Coin and die outcomes?" Look for: 12.

questions.a: 12 outfits.

days.guide: Your child completes the 6 × 6 sum table. Check before moving on: ask "P(sum = 7)?" Look for: 6/36 = 1/6.
Design: H = girl, flip 3 coins per trial. Your child runs 30 trials. Check before moving on: ask "Theoretical P(at least 2 girls)?" Look for: 4/8 = 1/2.
Model: digits 1–3 = make, 4–10 = miss. Your child simulates 5 shots many times. Check before moving on: ask "Theoretical answer?" Look for: About 0.47.

questions.a: About 0.47.

days.guide: Give the quiz (see key). Check before moving on: ask "P(two heads in two flips)?" Look for: 1/4.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Outfits from 4 shirts, 3 pants = 12. 2) P(sum 8) = 5/36. 3) P(HH) = 1/4. 4) P(at least one head in 2 flips) = 3/4. 5) Simulation design must state model, trial, success, number of trials.

weeks.prep: A long novel, random number generator, graph paper.
misconceptions: Thinking a large sample is unbiased. A large biased sample is still biased.
Expecting every sample to give the same mean.

days.guide: Your child identifies population and sample in 8 scenarios and judges bias. Check before moving on: ask "Surveying soccer fans about the favorite sport — biased?" Look for: Yes, not representative.

questions.q: Surveying soccer fans about the favorite sport — biased?
questions.a: Yes, not representative.

days.guide: Your child samples random pages and computes mean word length. Check before moving on: ask "Why random pages?" Look for: Every page has an equal chance, giving a representative sample.

questions.a: Every page has an equal chance, giving a representative sample.

days.guide: Your child takes 5 samples of 10 words and compares means. Check before moving on: ask "What do differing means show?" Look for: Sampling variability.

questions.a: Sampling variability.

days.guide: Model MAD. Your child compares two plant groups. Check before moving on: ask "Means 12 and 18, MADs about 2. Meaningful?" Look for: Yes — difference is 3 MADs, more than 2, so it is meaningful.

questions.a: Yes — difference is 3 MADs, more than 2, so it is meaningful.

days.guide: Give the quiz (see key). Check before moving on: ask "Population for a survey of 50 of 1,000 students?" Look for: All 1,000 students.

questions.q: Population for a survey of 50 of 1,000 students?
questions.a: All 1,000 students.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz: 1) Survey of 7th graders: population = all 7th graders at the school. 2) Random sample best. 3) Mean of 2, 4, 6, 8 = 5; MAD = 2. 4) Means differ by 3 MADs: meaningful. Report: proficient includes method, mean, variability.

weeks.prep: Survey form, ruler (for drop test), graph paper, calculator; cumulative review set; final exam (IM end-of-year or Khan course challenge).
misconceptions: Comparing groups by single values instead of measures of center and spread.
Using a sample of convenience for 'random'.

days.guide: Your child writes a statistical question and sampling plan. Check before moving on: ask "Is 'How fast is my reaction?' statistical?" Look for: No — it has one answer; compare groups for variability.

questions.q: Is 'How fast is my reaction?' statistical?
questions.a: No — it has one answer; compare groups for variability.

days.guide: Your child collects 10+ per group with the ruler-drop test and creates dot plots. Check before moving on: ask "Why the same procedure for everyone?" Look for: Fair comparison.

questions.q: Why the same procedure for everyone?
questions.a: Fair comparison.

days.guide: Your child computes mean and MAD, writes conclusions, presents. Check before moving on: ask "Mean 18 cm vs 14 cm, MAD 3. Meaningful?" Look for: Difference 4 is about 1.3 MADs — not strongly meaningful.

questions.q: Mean 18 cm vs 14 cm, MAD 3. Meaningful?
questions.a: Difference 4 is about 1.3 MADs — not strongly meaningful.

days.guide: Cumulative review; target weak units from earlier checks. Check before moving on: ask "Area of circle with r = 3?" Look for: 9π ≈ 28.26.
Give the final exam; set goals for Math 8. Check before moving on: ask "Solve −2x + 7 = 15." Look for: x = −4.

weeks.assessment_key: Final exam sample answers: 1) Scale factor 6→15: 2.5. 2) y = 4x through (3,12). 3) C for d = 10: 31.4. 4) $80 with 15% off: $68. 5) −7 − (−3) = −4. 6) 3x − 5 = 16 → 7. 7) Complement of 38: 52. 8) Prism 3 × 4 × 5: 60. 9) P(sum 7) = 1/6. Investigation rubric: 4 = statistical question, random sample, correct mean/MAD, valid conclusion; 3 = minor errors; 2 = missing parts; 1 = incomplete.

PE.overview: PE 7 follows a FITNESSGRAM pre-test/post-test year: fitness concepts (FITT, heart rate, strength, flexibility), invasion, net and striking games, dance, track and field and outdoor skills. Each lesson should be about 80% moving: warm up dynamically, teach one or two cues, practice, then play, and finish with a brief written reflection. Coach with short cues and quick feedback ('plant foot beside the ball'), use a phone video for self-analysis, and keep a fitness portfolio of every score. Always check the space for hazards, keep water handy, and stop for pain, dizziness or chest discomfort.

weeks.prep: Mark two lines 20 meters apart with cones on a flat, non-slip surface. Download the free FITNESSGRAM PACER audio (or plan a measured mile on a track). Stopwatch, fitness journal, and a printout of the FITNESSGRAM Healthy Fitness Zone (HFZ) chart for your child's age and sex.
misconceptions: Starting the PACER too fast. The early levels are slow on purpose; the goal is to reach the line just as the beep sounds.
Doing static stretches before vigorous exercise as the warm-up. Warm up with dynamic movement; save holding stretches for the cool-down.

days.guide: Teach a 10-move dynamic warm-up (jog, high knees, butt kicks, carioca, leg swings, arm circles, walking lunges, skips, side shuffles, inchworms) and a 5-stretch static cool-down held 20–30 seconds. Your child leads it back to you.

questions.q: Why warm up dynamically before exercise?
questions.a: It raises heart rate, body temperature and blood flow to muscles and moves joints through their range, preparing the body and reducing injury risk.

questions.q: When should static stretches be done?
questions.a: During the cool-down after activity, holding each 15–30 seconds without bouncing.

days.guide: Explain the PACER: run 20 m before each beep; the pace gets faster each level (about each minute). Practice 5 minutes, turning at the line with one foot over it.

questions.q: What happens if you reach the line before the beep?
questions.a: Wait at the line for the beep, then run back.
The second time you don't reach the line before the beep.

days.guide: Warm up, then run the PACER (or timed mile). Record laps or time immediately. Walk to cool down.

questions.a: Aerobic capacity — how well the heart and lungs deliver oxygen to working muscles.

days.guide: Your child takes a 30-minute brisk walk or bike ride and logs date, activity, minutes and effort.

questions.q: Why include an easy day after a hard test?
questions.a: Active recovery promotes blood flow and lets muscles recover while still building the habit.

days.guide: Compare the score to the HFZ chart and write one observation and one goal idea.

questions.q: What is the Healthy Fitness Zone?
questions.a: The FITNESSGRAM score range linked to good health for your age and sex; scores below it are 'Needs Improvement.'

weeks.assessment_key: Baseline record is complete when it shows the date, test (PACER laps or mile time), the score and the HFZ category (Needs Improvement / Healthy Fitness Zone). For the PACER, the score is the number of laps completed (the test ends the second time the runner fails to reach the line before the beep). Proficient: test done with honest effort and correct pacing, result recorded with one written observation.

weeks.prep: Mat, measuring strip for curl-ups (3 inches/7.6 cm wide for ages 10+), yardstick or sit-and-reach box, 12-inch ruler for trunk lift, FITNESSGRAM cadence audio (one rep every 3 seconds). Weigh/measure privately; body composition is optional.
misconceptions: Pulling on the neck or lifting the whole back off the mat during curl-ups. Keep arms straight, palms sliding along the strip, head returns to mat each rep.
Lifting the trunk as high as possible in the trunk lift. The test stops at 12 inches; arching higher strains the back.

days.guide: Teach curl-up form: knees bent ~140°, feet flat, arms straight with fingers on the strip, curl up until fingertips slide across, back down until head touches. Practice at cadence, then test.

questions.q: What is the difference between muscular strength and muscular endurance?
questions.a: Strength is the most force a muscle can produce once; endurance is how many times or how long it can keep working.

questions.q: What does the curl-up test measure?
questions.a: Abdominal muscular strength and endurance.

days.guide: Teach 90° push-up: body straight like a plank, lower until elbows reach 90°, push up to straight arms, at the 3-second cadence. Test to max.

questions.q: What are two common push-up form errors?
questions.a: Sagging hips or piking, not lowering to 90° at the elbow, not fully extending arms, not keeping cadence.

days.guide: Trunk lift: lie face down, lift upper body slowly up to 12 inches max, hold to measure, two tries. Sit-and-reach: one leg straight, the other bent, reach forward four times and hold the fourth; test each side.

questions.a: Only one leg is straight at a time, reducing strain on the lower back.

questions.q: What does the trunk lift measure?
questions.a: Back extensor strength and flexibility.

days.guide: Optional: record height and weight privately; explain BMI is a screening estimate of body composition and doesn't measure muscle vs fat directly.

questions.a: The proportion of fat mass to lean mass (muscle, bone, organs) in the body.

days.guide: Your child enters all scores in the portfolio and highlights strengths and one area to improve.

questions.q: Name the five health-related fitness components.
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition.

weeks.assessment_key: FITNESSGRAM baseline record: PACER/mile, curl-ups (count to max 75, stops at second form error or when cadence is missed), 90° push-ups (max 75, stops at second form error), trunk lift (inches, max 12), back-saver sit-and-reach (inches each side, max 12), optional BMI/body composition kept private; each with HFZ status. Proficient = all tests completed with correct form and recorded with dates.

weeks.prep: Jump rope, cones, 8 task cards (jumping jacks, squats, plank, mountain climbers, jump rope, wall sit, lunges, push-ups), interval timer app set to 40 s on / 20 s off, calendar. Print a 6–20 Borg RPE scale or 1–10 scale.
misconceptions: Goals like 'get fitter.' SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound — e.g., 'add 8 PACER laps by January 15.'
Racing through reps with poor form to boost count. Quality reps first; count only good-form reps.

days.guide: Model writing a SMART goal from a baseline score. Your child writes two (one cardio, one strength/flexibility).

questions.q: Is 'I will do more push-ups' SMART? Fix it.
questions.a: No. Fixed: 'I will increase from 10 to 16 push-ups by the January re-test by doing push-ups 3 days a week.'

days.guide: Demonstrate each station, then run 40 s on / 20 s rest, 2 rounds. Your child records reps.

questions.a: A series of exercise stations done one after another with short rests, working different muscle groups.

questions.q: Name the main muscles used in mountain climbers.
questions.a: Core (abdominals), shoulders, hip flexors and legs.

days.guide: Your child plans weekly activities that support each goal and posts them on a calendar.

questions.q: How often should you train push-ups to improve muscular endurance?
questions.a: About 2–3 non-consecutive days per week.

days.guide: Repeat the circuit; challenge to beat day-2 reps with good form.

questions.q: Why might reps improve after only a few days?
questions.a: Better technique, pacing and familiarity (nervous system learning) more than big muscle changes.

days.guide: Your child journals and rates perceived exertion (RPE).

questions.a: Rating of Perceived Exertion — a self-rating of how hard exercise feels (e.g., 6–20 Borg scale or 1–10).

weeks.assessment_key: SMART goals (2): each names a fitness test, a measurable target based on baseline, a realistic increase and a date, plus 2 action steps. Circuit log: reps at each of 8 stations for 2 rounds on both days and RPE. Proficient: both goals meet all SMART criteria and day-4 log shows attempt to increase reps.

weeks.prep: Hula hoops, a blindfold or scarf, soft obstacles (pillows, cones), 3–5 soft balls, a rope circle for 'toxic waste', and at least 3 people. Clear the area of sharp edges for the blind walk.
misconceptions: Shouting over each other to solve challenges. Teams improve when one person speaks at a time and the group listens and tries ideas.
Blaming a teammate after a failed attempt. Focus on the plan, not the person: 'What can we change next try?'

days.guide: Group holds hands in a circle and passes a hoop around without letting go. Time 5 tries and discuss strategies between tries.

questions.q: What strategy helped improve your time?
questions.a: Example: bending low, coordinating movements, verbally guiding the next person.

days.guide: Guide a blindfolded partner through obstacles with only voice cues; switch roles. Coach specific cues: 'stop', 'two small steps right'.

questions.q: What makes a verbal cue effective?
questions.a: It's specific, short and calm — direction plus distance (e.g., 'three steps forward').

days.guide: Establish a throwing pattern (say name, toss underhand); add balls each round.

questions.q: Why say the person's name before throwing?
questions.a: It gets their attention and prepares them to catch, avoiding drops.

days.guide: Untangle a human knot or move 'toxic waste' with ropes without touching it.

questions.q: What role does a leader play in group challenges?
questions.a: Organizes ideas, keeps everyone involved, keeps the group calm and focused.

days.guide: Discuss and write a reflection using the rubric.

questions.q: Name one communication strategy that worked this week.
questions.a: Open answer — e.g., one person speaks at a time, using names, specific directional cues.

weeks.assessment_key: Teamwork rubric (score 1–4 in each): communication (clear, specific cues), listening (lets others speak, builds on ideas), encouragement (positive words), problem-solving (suggests and tests strategies). Reflection: proficient answer names 2 strategies that worked (e.g., counting out loud, assigning roles, giving step-by-step cues like 'two steps left') and one personal goal.

weeks.prep: Cones, a frisbee/flag, pinnies or colored shirts for two teams, a few friends or family members. Print a sportsmanship checklist (shakes hands, follows rules, accepts calls, encourages, includes everyone).
misconceptions: Thinking leaders are the loudest or best players. Leaders organize, include others and model fair play.
Arguing every close call. In friendly games, call it fairly, offer a redo if unsure, and move on.

days.guide: Your child plans and leads a 5-minute warm-up (moves, counts, demonstrations).

questions.q: Name two qualities of a good warm-up leader.
questions.a: Clear loud instructions, demonstrates moves, watches participants, keeps it moving, encourages.

days.guide: Play capture the flag (each team guards a flag; tagged players go to 'jail' until freed). Players call their own tags honestly.

questions.a: Playing fair, following rules, respecting opponents and officials, and being gracious whether winning or losing.

days.guide: Role-play four conflicts (disputed call, ball hog, sore loser, rule-bender) and solve them with I-messages or rock-paper-scissors redo.

questions.q: Two players disagree on whether a tag happened. What is a fair solution?
questions.a: Discuss calmly, and if still unclear, replay the point (do-over) or use rock-paper-scissors.

days.guide: Design a new tag game with an inclusion rule; teach and play it, then revise.

questions.q: Give an example of an inclusive rule.
questions.a: Players who are tagged can rejoin after 10 jumping jacks, so no one sits out long.

days.guide: Your child self-assesses with the checklist.

questions.q: How should you act after losing a game?
questions.a: Shake hands, congratulate the winners, think about what to improve, no excuses or blaming.

weeks.assessment_key: Game design rubric: 4 = clear objective, boundaries, safety rule, rules that include all players (e.g., everyone must touch the ball/tag rotates), tested and revised after play; 3 = playable with minor gaps; 2 = unclear rules; 1 = incomplete. Sportsmanship checklist self-assessment with honest examples.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball (size 4 or 5), cones, a sturdy wall, a partner. Set up a cone goal 1 m wide at 10 m for the test.
misconceptions: Passing with the toe. The inside of the foot gives a bigger, flatter surface for accuracy.
Stopping the ball dead under the feet. A good first touch cushions the ball a step away in the direction you want to go.

days.guide: Teach: plant non-kicking foot beside the ball pointing to the target, turn kicking foot out, lock ankle, strike the middle of the ball, follow through. 50 wall passes each foot.

questions.q: Where should the plant foot point when passing?
questions.a: At the target, beside the ball.
A firm foot gives a cleaner, more accurate pass.

days.guide: Toss or pass balls to your child to receive with sole, inside foot and thigh, cushioning into one controlled touch.

questions.q: How do you 'cushion' the ball when receiving?
questions.a: Relax and pull the receiving surface back slightly as the ball arrives to absorb its speed.

days.guide: Pass back and forth while jogging through cones; lead the partner by passing into their path.

questions.q: Why pass ahead of a moving teammate?
questions.a: So they can run onto the ball without stopping.

days.guide: Play 3-v-1 rondo: three passers in a square keep the ball from one defender; switch when the defender wins it.

questions.q: What helps the passers keep possession?
questions.a: Quick passes, moving to open angles, using two touches or fewer, communicating.

days.guide: Run the accuracy test and record score.

questions.q: Name three cues for an accurate inside-foot pass.
questions.a: Plant foot beside ball pointing at target; locked ankle with inside of foot; follow through toward target.

weeks.assessment_key: Passing accuracy test: 10 inside-foot passes from 10 m into a 1-m cone goal (5 each foot). Scoring: 9–10 advanced, 7–8 proficient, 5–6 developing, 0–4 beginning. Note form cues observed: plant foot beside ball pointing at target, ankle locked, strike middle of ball, follow through toward target.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball, cones for slalom, a goal or targets (two cones or a wall chart) at 12 m. Small group for 2-v-1 and 3-v-3.
misconceptions: Looking down at the ball the whole time while dribbling. Keep the ball close and glance up to see space and teammates.
Leaning back when shooting, which sends the ball high. Lean over the ball, plant beside it, strike with laces.

days.guide: Dribble a cone slalom using inside, outside and sole touches with both feet. Time it.

questions.q: Why use small touches when dribbling in traffic?
questions.a: They keep the ball close so you can change direction and protect it.

days.guide: Teach the instep (laces) shot: approach at a slight angle, plant beside ball, toe pointed down, strike with laces, land on the kicking foot. Shoot at targets from 12 m.

questions.q: Which part of the foot strikes a powerful shot?
questions.a: The laces (instep), with toe pointed down and ankle locked.

questions.q: What happens if you lean back?
questions.a: The ball rises over the goal.

days.guide: Play 2-v-1: attackers spread wide and move into space; defender tries to win the ball.

questions.a: Spreading players toward the sidelines to stretch the defense and create space.
Players positioned behind and ahead of the ball to provide support and passing options.

days.guide: Play 3-v-3 small-sided games; pause to point out width and support.

questions.q: What should you do right after passing?
questions.a: Move into open space to be available for a return pass (support).

days.guide: Your child self-assesses with the rubric.

questions.q: Name one strength and one goal.
questions.a: Open answer — tied to rubric cues.

weeks.assessment_key: Skill rubric (1–4 each): dribbling (close control, both feet, head up, change of direction), shooting (plant foot, laces contact, toe down, follow-through, accuracy), game play (spreads wide for width, supports ball carrier, moves into open space). Proficient = 3s across; game observation notes at least two times your child created width or support.

weeks.prep: Flying disc (175 g ultimate disc if possible), cones at 5, 10 and 15 m, hula hoop as target.
misconceptions: Throwing with the whole arm and no wrist snap. Power and spin come from stepping, rotating hips and snapping the wrist.
Tilting the disc (letting the outside edge rise) so it curves away. Keep the disc flat or edge slightly down at release.

days.guide: Backhand grip: thumb on top, fingers curled under the rim. Stand sideways, reach back across body, step and snap the wrist, release flat. Throw at 5, 10 and 15 m.

questions.q: Where does the spin come from in a backhand?
questions.a: The wrist snap at release.
It stabilizes the disc so it flies flat and straight.

days.guide: Forehand (flick): two fingers (index and middle) against the inside rim, thumb on top; short arm motion, wrist flick like skipping a stone. 30 throws.

questions.a: Index and middle fingers pressed against the inside rim, thumb on top, disc held flat at your side.

days.guide: Pancake catch: one hand on top, one below, clap together (chest height). Rim catch: thumb down for high catches, thumb up for low.

questions.q: When do you use a pancake catch?
questions.a: For discs coming between the chest and waist — it's the most secure catch.

days.guide: Teach pivot: keep one foot planted and step around a marker to throw. Practice completing passes past a defender.

questions.q: Can you run with the disc in ultimate?
questions.a: No — you must establish a pivot foot and pass it; you may pivot like in basketball.

days.guide: Run the accuracy test.

questions.a: It transfers body weight into the throw for power and aim.

weeks.assessment_key: Throwing accuracy test: 10 throws (5 backhand, 5 forehand) from 10 m into a hoop or to a partner's chest area. Score: 9–10 advanced, 7–8 proficient, 5–6 developing. Observe cues: sideways stance, step toward target, flat release, wrist snap, follow-through pointing at target.

weeks.prep: Disc, cones for endzones (about 20 m apart for small games), a few players. Print or read the 'Spirit of the Game' summary from USA Ultimate.
misconceptions: Running in a straight line to get open. Use a hard cut away, then cut sharply back (change of direction and speed).
Thinking self-officiating means you can make calls in your favor. Spirit of the Game means honest calls and respect even in competition.

days.guide: Teach cutting: jog away, plant and sprint back toward the thrower. Practice 2-v-1 cut-and-catch.

questions.q: What is a cut in ultimate?
questions.a: A sudden sprint and change of direction to get open for a pass.

days.guide: Marker stands an arm's length away, no contact, counts out loud 'Stalling one…' to ten. Thrower must release before ten.

questions.q: What happens if the stall count reaches 10?
questions.a: It's a turnover — the other team gets the disc.

days.guide: Teach rules: score by catching in the endzone; turnovers on dropped, out-of-bounds, intercepted or stalled throws; no contact; self-officiated. Play 3-v-3.

questions.q: Name two ways the disc changes possession.
questions.a: Dropped pass, out of bounds, interception, block or stall.

questions.q: What is the Spirit of the Game?
questions.a: Ultimate's principle that players are responsible for fair play, honest calls and respect, with no referees.

days.guide: Play a full game with self-officiated calls; pause to discuss any calls.

questions.q: What do you do when two players disagree on a foul?
questions.a: Discuss calmly; if unresolved, the disc goes back to the last undisputed thrower.

days.guide: Fill in spirit scorecards for self and teammates.

questions.a: An offensive formation where players line up (usually down the middle) to open space for cuts.

weeks.assessment_key: Spirit scorecard (WFDF style, 0–4 each): rules knowledge, fouls and body contact, fair-mindedness, attitude and self-control, communication. Game play: completes passes, makes cuts to get open, marks with legal stall count (10 seconds, arm's length, no contact). Proficient: average 2–3 spirit scores with examples and correct use of rules.

weeks.prep: Soccer ball, disc, basketball if available, cones. Arrange a homeschool group or family for two mini tournaments. Prepare the skills test stations.
misconceptions: Thinking each sport is totally different. Invasion games share principles: keep possession, create space, move after passing, defend goal-side.
Standing still after losing the ball. Transition immediately to defense.

days.guide: Your child charts offense/defense strategies in soccer, ultimate and basketball.

questions.q: Name one offensive strategy that all three share.
questions.a: Spread out to create space; move to open space after passing; quick passing to advance.
Switching from offense to defense (or vice versa) when possession changes.

days.guide: Run a mini soccer tournament (short games, rotating teams).

questions.a: Staying between the attacker and the goal you're defending.

days.guide: Run a mini ultimate tournament.

questions.q: Why is a quick throw after a turnover helpful?
questions.a: The defense hasn't organized yet, so receivers are open.

days.guide: Run the skills test stations.

questions.q: Name a cue for a secure catch.
questions.a: Watch the object into your hands; for a disc use a pancake catch.

days.guide: Your child writes the strategy-transfer reflection.

questions.q: Give one example of a strategy that transferred between games.
questions.a: Example: give-and-go/moving after passing works in soccer and ultimate.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit skills test (score 1–4 per skill): soccer passing (inside foot to target, 7/10 proficient), dribbling (slalom with control both feet), disc throwing (7/10 to partner), catching (8/10 secure catches). Reflection: proficient names 2 strategies that transfer (e.g., spreading wide, moving into space after passing, man-to-man defense, quick transition) with an example from two games.

weeks.prep: Volleyball (or beach ball for beginners), a wall, a net or rope tied about 7 ft high.
misconceptions: Swinging the arms to bump. Keep the platform still and angled; legs and shoulders provide lift.
Hitting the ball with hands or thumbs separated. Form a flat platform with forearms together and thumbs parallel.

days.guide: Ready position: feet shoulder-width, knees bent, weight forward, arms out. Platform: hands clasped, thumbs parallel, elbows locked, contact on forearms above wrists. 20 bumps to self, then against a wall.

questions.q: Where should the ball contact your arms in a forearm pass?
questions.a: On the flat part of the forearms, just above the wrists.

questions.q: What creates the lift in a bump?
questions.a: Bending and extending the legs, not swinging the arms.

days.guide: Set: hands above forehead forming a triangle window, contact with finger pads, extend arms and legs. Set to self and to a wall target.

questions.q: Which part of the hands contacts the ball in a set?
questions.a: The finger pads (not palms), with hands shaped in a triangle above the forehead.

days.guide: Bump and set with a partner counting consecutive contacts.

questions.q: When do you use a set vs a bump?
questions.a: Set for high balls you can get under, usually the second contact; bump for low or hard-driven balls.

days.guide: Toss to the sides; your child shuffles (no crossing feet) to get behind the ball before passing.

questions.q: Why move your feet before passing?
questions.a: Getting behind the ball lets you face the target and keep the platform angled correctly.

days.guide: Run the consecutive-pass test.

questions.a: The flat surface formed by both forearms held together to pass the ball.

weeks.assessment_key: Consecutive-pass test: count consecutive controlled bumps/sets (to self or with a wall/partner) without the ball dropping or being caught. 15+ proficient, 25+ advanced, 8–14 developing. Note cues: ready position, platform, contact on forearms, legs lift.

weeks.prep: Volleyball, net or rope, cones or tape to mark court zones (6 zones on one side). Explain court rotation with a diagram.
misconceptions: Tossing the ball too high on the serve. Underhand: hold ball low and hit from the hand; overhand: toss slightly in front about arm's length.
Thinking players rotate after every point. Teams rotate clockwise only when they win back the serve (side out).

days.guide: Underhand serve: opposite foot forward, hold ball low in front, swing hitting arm like a pendulum, contact with heel of hand. 20 attempts; track makes.

questions.q: Which foot is forward for a right-handed underhand serve?
questions.a: The left foot.

days.guide: Overhand (float) serve: toss in front of hitting shoulder, elbow high, contact with heel of hand. Compare success rate with underhand.

questions.q: Your underhand made 16/20 and overhand 9/20. What are the percentages?
questions.a: Underhand 80%, overhand 45%.

days.guide: Teach rotation and scoring; play 2-v-2 with three contacts.

questions.q: How many contacts is a team allowed on one side?
questions.a: Three (a block doesn't count in indoor rules).
When it wins the serve back from the other team (side out), rotating clockwise.

days.guide: Play doubles games; encourage bump-set-hit.

questions.q: Why aim to use all three contacts?
questions.a: Passing to a setter then hitting creates a controlled, stronger attack.

days.guide: Run the serving accuracy test.

questions.a: A point is scored on every rally regardless of which team served.

weeks.assessment_key: Serving test: 10 serves into marked zones. Score 1 point for in, 2 for the called zone. Proficient = 7+ serves in; advanced = 4+ zone hits. Game observation: uses three contacts (bump-set-hit), calls 'mine', rotates correctly. Rules key: rally scoring (point every rally), games to 25 win by 2 (15 in a deciding game), rotate clockwise on side out, ball may be played up to 3 times per side, same player cannot hit twice in a row.

weeks.prep: Badminton rackets, shuttlecocks, a net or rope at about 5 ft. Mark a simple court with cones if outdoors (avoid wind).
misconceptions: Gripping the racket like a frying pan with the whole fist. Use a 'handshake' grip and relaxed fingers.
Hitting every shot hard. Mixing deep clears and soft drop shots moves the opponent and creates openings.

days.guide: Teach forehand handshake grip and backhand (thumb on the back of the handle). Practice short serves (low over net to front) and long serves (high and deep).

questions.q: Where must the serve be contacted?
questions.a: Below the waist, hit underhand, diagonally into the opponent's service court.

questions.q: When would you use a long serve?
questions.a: In singles to push the opponent to the back of the court.

days.guide: Teach the overhead clear: side-on, racket back, reach high, contact the shuttle above and in front, hit up and deep.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a clear?
questions.a: To hit the shuttle high and deep to the back of the opponent's court, giving you time and pushing them back.

days.guide: Teach the drop shot: same preparation as a clear, but softly guide the shuttle to just over the net.

questions.q: When should you use a drop shot?
questions.a: When your opponent is deep in the back court, so the shuttle lands far from them.

days.guide: Play singles; coach returning to the center base after each shot.

questions.a: The center gives the shortest distance to reach any next shot.

days.guide: Run the rally-count test.

questions.a: A powerful downward overhead shot used to end a rally when the shuttle is high and short.

weeks.assessment_key: Rally-count test: partners count longest controlled rally in 3 tries (clears and drops). 15+ proficient, 25+ advanced. Strategy observation: uses clears to push opponent back, drops when opponent is deep, returns to base position (center) after each shot. Rules key: serve underhand below the waist diagonally; rally scoring to 21, win by 2; shuttle landing on the line is in.

weeks.prep: Pickleball paddles, perforated plastic balls, a wall or local court (36-inch net at center). Phone for video. Learn the rules from USA Pickleball's summary.
misconceptions: Volleying while standing in the kitchen. You may not volley (hit before the bounce) while touching the non-volley zone, including the line.
Rushing the net after serving. The two-bounce rule means the serving team must let the return bounce, so they stay back first.

days.guide: Forehand and backhand groundstrokes against a wall: ready position, turn shoulders, contact in front, follow through low to high.

questions.q: Where should you contact the ball?
questions.a: Out in front of your body, about waist height.

days.guide: Teach the dink: soft shot from the kitchen line that arcs just over the net into the opponent's kitchen. Volley with a firm, short punch.

questions.a: A soft shot that lands in the opponent's non-volley zone (kitchen).
Hitting the ball before it bounces.

days.guide: Teach serve (underhand, diagonal), the two-bounce rule and kitchen rule; play doubles.

questions.a: The serve must bounce once and the return must bounce once before either team may volley.
The 7-foot non-volley zone on each side of the net; you can't volley while standing in it.

days.guide: Play a round robin at a local court, practicing court etiquette.

questions.q: To how many points is a standard game played?
questions.a: 11, win by 2; only the serving team scores.

days.guide: Film a few strokes, watch in slow motion and analyze follow-through.

questions.a: It keeps the paddle on the path toward the target, improving accuracy and control and reducing strain.

weeks.assessment_key: Video self-analysis rubric: 4 = identifies ready position, paddle face angle, contact point in front of body, weight transfer and full follow-through toward target, and writes one specific correction; 3 = identifies 3 elements; 2 = describes generally; 1 = incomplete. Rules key: underhand serve diagonally, contact below the waist; two-bounce rule; kitchen = 7 ft non-volley zone; games to 11, win by 2; only the serving team scores.

weeks.prep: All net-game equipment. Prepare the net-games skills test: volleyball pass count, badminton rally count, pickleball serves in.
misconceptions: Thinking net games only reward power. Placement (hitting to open space) usually wins more points.
Staying where you last hit. Recover to base position after each shot.

days.guide: Chart strategies shared by volleyball, badminton and pickleball (placement, base position, varying speed/depth, attacking weak side).

questions.q: What strategy do all three net games share?
questions.a: Hit to open space away from opponents and return to a ready base position.

days.guide: Play your child's favorite net game for the session.

questions.a: Aiming shots to specific spots where the opponent can't easily reach.

days.guide: Run the skills test.

questions.q: What is the ready position in net games?
questions.a: Feet shoulder-width, knees bent, weight on the balls of the feet, racket/arms up and in front.

days.guide: Your child teaches one skill to a sibling or parent using 2–3 cues.

questions.a: Short, specific and in order (e.g., 'Turn, contact in front, follow through').

days.guide: Your child writes about base of support and follow-through.

questions.q: Why does a wide base of support help?
questions.a: A wider base lowers and centers your balance, making you more stable when hitting and moving.

weeks.assessment_key: Net games skills test (1–4 each): volleyball forearm pass (15 consecutive = proficient), serve (7/10 in), badminton rally (15 = proficient), pickleball serve (7/10 in) and dink rally (10). Biomechanics reflection: proficient explains how a wide, balanced base of support improves stability and how follow-through toward the target improves accuracy and reduces injury, using their best skill as an example.

weeks.prep: Fitness journal. Write three sample workout plans (one missing intensity, one too much too soon, one balanced). Stopwatch.
misconceptions: Thinking more is always better. Overload must be gradual (about 10% per week); too much too soon causes injury.
Assuming any exercise improves every component. Training is specific — running builds endurance, not upper-body strength.

days.guide: Teach FITT and analyze three sample plans, identifying what each is missing.

questions.a: Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type.

questions.q: Plan: 'Run 5 days a week.' Which FITT parts are missing?
questions.a: Intensity and time (how hard and how long).

days.guide: Do a 25-minute jog/walk interval (e.g., 2 min jog, 1 min walk) and record F, I, T and T.

questions.q: Record the FITT for today's session.
questions.a: Example: F = 3x/week, I = moderate-vigorous (RPE 6–7), T = 25 min, T = jog/walk intervals.

days.guide: Plan a 4-week push-up progression (e.g., 3 sets of 6 → 8 → 10 → 12), then do week 1.

questions.a: Gradually increasing the demands (reps, sets, intensity, time) so the body keeps adapting.

days.guide: Match exercises to fitness components and sports.

questions.q: Which fitness component does a soccer player need most for running the whole game?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance.

questions.q: What is the principle of specificity?
questions.a: You improve the specific component or skill you train.

days.guide: Give the FITT quiz and total the week's MVPA minutes.

questions.q: If you did 45, 60, 30, 70 and 55 minutes this week over 5 days, what is the average?

weeks.assessment_key: FITT quiz key (suggested): 1) F = frequency (how often), I = intensity (how hard), T = time (how long), T = type (what kind) 2) overload = working harder than normal to improve 3) progression = gradually increasing 4) specificity = training matches the goal 5) teens need 60 min MVPA daily 6) aerobic example — running, swimming; strength — push-ups 7) 10% rule. Activity log: daily MVPA minutes totaled.

weeks.prep: Stopwatch or watch with seconds, optional heart-rate monitor, graph paper. Teach pulse-taking with index and middle fingers (not the thumb).
misconceptions: Taking a pulse with the thumb. The thumb has its own pulse; use index and middle fingers.
Pressing hard on both sides of the neck. Press gently on one side only.

days.guide: Teach radial (wrist, thumb side) and carotid (neck, beside windpipe) pulses. Count 15 seconds × 4. Your child measures resting HR on 3 mornings before getting up.

questions.q: You count 18 beats in 15 seconds. What is the heart rate?
questions.a: 18 × 4 = 72 beats per minute.

questions.q: Why measure resting heart rate in the morning before getting up?
questions.a: That is when the body is most at rest, giving a consistent baseline.

days.guide: Calculate max HR and target zone for your child's age.

questions.q: For a 12-year-old, what are max HR and the 60–85% target zone?
questions.a: Max = 220 − 12 = 208 bpm; 60% = about 125 bpm, 85% = about 177 bpm, so the zone is about 125–177 bpm.

days.guide: Do a 20-minute workout (jog, jump rope, dance) checking pulse every 5 minutes and adjusting effort to stay in zone.

questions.q: Your HR is 190 at minute 10. What should you do?
questions.a: Slow down — you're above the target zone.

days.guide: Measure HR immediately after exercise, then at 1 and 3 minutes; graph it.

questions.q: What does a fast drop in heart rate after exercise show?
questions.a: Better cardiorespiratory fitness — the heart recovers quickly.

days.guide: Your child writes how heart rate shows fitness gains (see key).

questions.q: Why does a fit person's resting heart rate go down?
questions.a: The heart muscle is stronger and pumps more blood per beat, so it needs fewer beats.

weeks.assessment_key: Heart-rate data: 3 resting pulse readings averaged; max HR = 220 − age (age 12: 208; age 13: 207); target zone 60–85% (age 12: about 125–177 bpm; age 13: about 124–176). Recovery graph shows HR at 0, 1 and 3 minutes post-exercise. Explanation (proficient): as fitness improves, resting HR decreases, the heart pumps more blood per beat (stroke volume), the same workout feels easier at a lower HR, and HR returns to resting faster after exercise.

weeks.prep: Mat, optional resistance band, form checklist for squat, lunge, push-up, plank, glute bridge. Pull the week-2 curl-up and push-up scores.
misconceptions: Letting knees cave inward on squats or lunges. Knees track over toes.
Holding the breath during strength work. Exhale on the effort (pushing/standing up), inhale on the lowering.

days.guide: Your child matches 10 exercises to muscle groups (see key).

questions.q: Which muscles does a push-up mainly work?
questions.a: Chest (pectorals), triceps and front shoulders, with the core stabilizing.

days.guide: Teach form for squats, lunges, push-ups, planks, glute bridges with the checklist; your child coaches you.

questions.q: Give two cues for a good squat.
questions.a: Feet shoulder-width, sit hips back, chest up, knees track over toes, weight in heels, thighs to about parallel.

questions.q: When should you exhale during a push-up?
questions.a: On the way up (the effort).

days.guide: Design a 6-station circuit covering major muscle groups.

questions.q: Define a rep and a set.
questions.a: A rep is one complete movement; a set is a group of reps done without rest (e.g., 3 sets of 10).

days.guide: Perform the circuit for 2 sets and record reps.

questions.q: Why rest 30–60 seconds between strength sets?
questions.a: To let muscles partly recover so you can keep good form.

days.guide: Re-test push-ups and curl-ups; compare to baseline.

questions.q: Baseline 12 push-ups, now 17. What is the percent increase?
questions.a: 5 ÷ 12 ≈ 42% increase.

weeks.assessment_key: Muscle matching key: squat — quadriceps, glutes, hamstrings; lunge — quads, glutes, hamstrings; push-up — chest (pectorals), triceps, shoulders (deltoids), core; plank — abdominals/core; glute bridge — glutes, hamstrings; superman — lower back (erector spinae); calf raise — calves; tricep dip — triceps; wall sit — quadriceps; bicycle crunch — abdominals/obliques. Circuit design proficient: 6 stations covering legs, chest/arms, back, core, with reps/time and rest. Mid-year re-test: compare with baseline and state change.

weeks.prep: Mat, a 30-minute beginner yoga video (choose one you've previewed), a bag of frozen peas and elastic bandage for RICE demo. Pull SMART goals from week 3.
misconceptions: Bouncing in stretches. Hold static stretches steadily 15–30 seconds; bouncing can strain muscles.
Stretching to the point of pain. Stretch to mild tension only.

days.guide: Teach 8 static stretches (hamstring, quad, calf, hip flexor, chest, triceps, shoulder, butterfly). Discuss static vs dynamic and when to use each.

questions.q: What is the difference between static and dynamic stretching?
questions.a: Static holds a stretch still (best after exercise); dynamic moves through a range of motion (best as a warm-up).

days.guide: Complete a beginner yoga session together; note balance and breathing.

questions.q: Name one fitness component yoga improves.
questions.a: Flexibility (also balance, core strength and stress reduction).

days.guide: Teach common injuries (sprain = ligament; strain = muscle/tendon) and RICE.

questions.a: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.

questions.q: What is the difference between a sprain and a strain?
questions.a: A sprain injures a ligament (bone to bone); a strain injures a muscle or tendon.

days.guide: Your child writes a one-week FITT plan (see rubric).

questions.q: How many days of muscle-strengthening are recommended for teens?
questions.a: At least 3 days per week (as part of the 60 daily minutes).

days.guide: Do day 1 of the plan and review SMART goal progress.

questions.q: Are you on track for your SMART goal? What will you adjust?
questions.a: Open answer — compare current score to target and name a specific change.

weeks.assessment_key: One-week plan rubric: 4 = includes all components (cardio 3–5 days, strength 2–3 days, flexibility daily or most days), FITT details for each day, warm-up and cool-down, a rest/active recovery day, and links to SMART goals; 3 = all components but missing some FITT details; 2 = missing a component; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Basketball, hoop (or a target), cones, a partner. Set up a timed dribble course (e.g., 6 cones, down and back).
misconceptions: Slapping the ball with the palm. Dribble with finger pads, pushing the ball, keeping it waist-high or lower.
Looking at the ball. Keep eyes up to see teammates and defenders.

days.guide: Practice stationary dribbles (high, low, each hand), then moving dribbles and crossovers through cones.

questions.q: What part of the hand controls the dribble?
questions.a: The finger pads.

questions.q: Why dribble with the hand away from the defender?
questions.a: Your body protects the ball.

days.guide: Chest pass (thumbs down follow-through), bounce pass (bounce about two-thirds of the way to the partner), overhead pass. 20 each.

questions.q: Where should a bounce pass hit the floor?
questions.a: About two-thirds of the way to the receiver.

questions.q: When is a bounce pass useful?
questions.a: To get the ball under a defender's arms.

days.guide: Teach triple threat (ready to shoot, pass or dribble) and jab steps.

questions.a: Knees bent, ball held at hip on the shooting side, eyes on the basket, pivot foot set — ready to shoot, pass or dribble.

days.guide: Play 2-v-1 keep-away using dribble and pass.

questions.a: Keeping one foot planted while stepping with the other to turn without traveling.

days.guide: Time the dribble course.

questions.a: Moving the pivot foot or taking steps while holding the ball without dribbling.

weeks.assessment_key: Dribble course: time to weave 6 cones down and back, using right hand on the way down and left on the way back, with crossovers at each cone; add 2 seconds per lost ball. Compare to a baseline trial. Proficient: completes with control, head up, using the correct hand.

weeks.prep: Basketball and hoop. Mark 5 shooting spots about 8–10 ft from the basket (two corners, two wings, top).
misconceptions: Shooting with two hands pushing equally. The shooting hand pushes; the guide hand only steadies the ball.
Jumping off the wrong foot on layups. Right-hand layup: take off from the left foot; left-hand layup: take off from the right foot.

days.guide: Teach BEEF: Balance (feet shoulder-width), Eyes (on the rim), Elbow (under the ball), Follow-through (wrist snap, 'hand in the cookie jar'). 50 close shots.

questions.a: Balance, Eyes, Elbow, Follow-through.

days.guide: Right-hand layup: right-left steps, jump off the left foot, lift right knee, use the backboard square. Then left side.

questions.q: Which foot do you jump off for a right-handed layup?
questions.a: The left foot.

days.guide: Give-and-go: pass, cut to the basket, receive return pass, lay up. Defensive slides: low stance, step-slide, don't cross feet.

questions.a: Pass to a teammate, cut toward the basket and get the ball back for a shot.

questions.q: Why shouldn't defenders cross their feet when sliding?
questions.a: It reduces balance and slows changes of direction.

days.guide: Play 2-v-2 or 3-v-3 half-court; use man-to-man defense.

questions.a: Each defender guards one specific opponent.

days.guide: Run the 5-spot shooting test.

questions.q: You made 3, 2, 4, 1, 3 from the five spots. What is your total and percentage?

weeks.assessment_key: Shooting test: 5 shots from each of 5 spots (25 total). Proficient = 10+, advanced = 15+. Note BEEF cues. Layup check: 3/5 made each side with correct takeoff foot.

weeks.prep: Softball or wiffle ball, bat, gloves, a batting tee, cones at 15 and 25 m. Safety: swing only in a clear zone; no one stands near the batter.
misconceptions: Throwing with the same-side foot forward. Step with the opposite foot toward the target.
Turning away from grounders. Get in front of the ball, glove down, fingers pointing to the ground.

days.guide: Teach overhand throw: side to target, arm back with elbow at shoulder height, step with opposite foot, rotate hips, follow through across body. Crow hop for longer throws.

questions.q: Which foot steps forward for a right-handed thrower?
questions.a: The left foot.
A hop-step that builds momentum toward the target before a long throw.

days.guide: Roll grounders and toss fly balls. Grounders: glove down, fingers point down, body in front. Fly balls: glove up, fingers point up, call 'mine'.

questions.q: How should the glove be for a grounder vs a fly ball?
questions.a: Grounder: open, fingers down on the ground; fly ball: above head, fingers up.

days.guide: Batting stance: feet shoulder-width, knuckles aligned, bat up; level swing, rotate hips, follow through. 40 swings off the tee.

questions.q: Why is a level swing important?
questions.a: It keeps the bat in the ball's path longer, increasing contact.

days.guide: Soft toss from the side; aim at field zones (left, center, right).

questions.q: How do you hit to the opposite field?
questions.a: Let the ball travel deeper and contact it slightly later.

days.guide: Run the throwing and batting test.

questions.q: Name a safety rule for batting.
questions.a: Only swing when no one is close; drop (don't throw) the bat after hitting.

weeks.assessment_key: Throwing accuracy: 10 throws to a partner's chest from 15 m (proficient 7/10). Batting contact: 10 soft-toss swings (proficient 6 contacts, advanced 6 line drives). Observe cues: side-on stance, step with opposite foot, elbow up, follow-through; batting: balanced stance, eyes on ball, level swing, hip rotation.

weeks.prep: Softball equipment, four bases (60 ft apart for full size, shorter for kids), a group for games.
misconceptions: Thinking every runner must be tagged. In a force out, the fielder only needs to touch the base before the runner arrives.
Leaving the base early on a fly ball. If the fly is caught, the runner must tag up (return to the base) before advancing.

days.guide: Practice running through first base (don't slow down) and rounding bases (curve out, touch inside corner).

questions.q: Why run through first base instead of stopping on it?
questions.a: You may overrun first base without being tagged out, so running through is faster.

days.guide: Practice situations: runner on first, ground ball → throw to second for a force out (or first for the sure out).

questions.q: With a runner on first and a ground ball to shortstop, where is the force play?
questions.a: Second base (and first base for the batter).
When a runner must advance because the batter became a runner, the fielder can get them out by touching the base before they arrive.

days.guide: Teach basic rules (3 outs per half-inning, 3 strikes, fair/foul) and play 3-pitch softball (own team pitches, 3 pitches to hit).

questions.q: How many outs end a half-inning?
questions.a: Three.

days.guide: Play a full game.

questions.a: After a fly ball is caught, a runner must touch their original base before advancing.

days.guide: Your child writes about one strategic decision.

questions.q: What is the cutoff player's job?
questions.a: To catch a long throw from the outfield and relay it quickly to the right base.

weeks.assessment_key: Game play: runs through first base, rounds bases correctly, makes correct force-out throw choices, knows when to tag up. Reflection rubric: 4 = describes the situation (outs, runners), the decision made and why, and evaluates the outcome; 3 = situation and decision; 2 = vague; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Mixed equipment for basketball and softball/kickball. Prepare the unit skills test and a leadership checklist.
misconceptions: Leading by only telling others what to do. Good captains demonstrate, include everyone and give specific encouragement.
Running a drill without explaining its purpose. Players engage more when they know why a drill matters.

days.guide: Your child plans and leads a 10-minute drill with a purpose, demo, cues and feedback.

questions.q: What are the parts of a well-run drill?
questions.a: Explain the purpose, demonstrate, give 2–3 cues, practice, give feedback.

days.guide: Play a basketball game.

questions.q: What should a team do on defense after a missed shot?
questions.a: Box out and rebound, then transition quickly.

days.guide: Play softball or kickball.

questions.q: In kickball, how do you get a runner out?
questions.a: Catch a kicked ball in the air, tag/hit them below the shoulders with the ball, or touch the base on a force.

days.guide: Run the unit skills test.

questions.q: Name one cue for each: chest pass and overhand throw.
questions.a: Chest pass: step and push, thumbs down; overhand throw: step with opposite foot and follow through.

days.guide: Your child writes the leadership/sportsmanship reflection.

questions.q: Give one example of good sportsmanship from this unit.
questions.a: Open answer — e.g., helping up an opponent, accepting a call.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit skills test (1–4 each): dribble course (control, both hands), shooting (10/25 proficient), passing (chest/bounce accurate), throwing (7/10), fielding (clean grounders/fly balls), batting contact (6/10). Leadership reflection: proficient gives specific examples of leading, including others and handling a conflict or loss respectfully.

weeks.prep: Music player, three songs of different tempos, videos of the Cupid Shuffle and Electric Slide. Clear space.
misconceptions: Rushing ahead of the music. Count '5, 6, 7, 8' before starting and step on the beat.
Treating dance as not 'real' exercise. Check heart rate — dancing can reach the target zone.

days.guide: Clap and step to the beat of three songs; count in 8-counts and identify the tempo (slow, medium, fast).

questions.a: The speed of the music's beat.
A phrase of 8 beats dancers count to structure movements.

days.guide: Teach grapevine (side, behind, side, touch), step-touch, pivot turn and box step.

questions.q: Describe a grapevine to the right.
questions.a: Step right, cross left behind, step right, touch (or tap) left beside it.

days.guide: Learn the Cupid Shuffle (right 4 steps, left 4, kick 4 counts, 'walk it out' turning a quarter turn left) or the Electric Slide.

questions.q: In the Cupid Shuffle, which way do you turn after 'walk it by yourself'?
questions.a: A quarter turn to the left to face a new wall.

days.guide: Learn a second line dance; take pulse afterward.

questions.q: Your pulse is 32 in 15 seconds after dancing. What is your heart rate, and is it in a 60–85% zone for a 12-year-old?
questions.a: 128 bpm — yes, within about 125–177 bpm.

days.guide: Perform for family without the video.

questions.q: What is a 'wall' in line dancing?
questions.a: The direction dancers face; many line dances rotate to a new wall each sequence.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance rubric (1–4): timing (on the beat), accuracy of steps and sequence, transitions/turns, energy and expression. Proficient = completes the full dance from memory with minor errors and stays with the music.

weeks.prep: Music and videos for La Raspa, the Hora (or Virginia Reel) and a West African dance (e.g., Kuku or Lamban) — preview so you know the formations.
misconceptions: Thinking folk dances are just steps. They carry cultural meaning — celebrations, harvest, community.
Ignoring the formation. Circle, line and longways formations are part of the dance.

days.guide: Teach La Raspa's hop step (hop and switch feet forward like a bleking step) and partner swing.

questions.q: Where does La Raspa come from?
questions.a: Mexico (Veracruz).

days.guide: Learn the Hora (circle, step-cross-step with kicks moving left/right) or the Virginia Reel (two lines, partners do turns and a reel down the middle).

questions.q: What formation is the Hora danced in?
questions.a: A circle with hands joined or on shoulders.

questions.q: What formation is the Virginia Reel?
questions.a: A longways set — two lines facing each other.

days.guide: Follow a West African dance video; discuss how dancers respond to drum rhythms (call and response).

questions.q: How are dance and drumming connected in West African dance?
questions.a: Drummers lead and change rhythms and dancers respond; drum calls signal changes in movement.

days.guide: Compare formations and purposes of the three dances.

questions.q: What is one purpose many folk dances share?
questions.a: Celebrating community events like weddings, harvests or festivals.

days.guide: Perform one folk dance with family.

questions.q: What made the group dance work well?
questions.a: Open answer — e.g., counting together, holding formation, watching partners.

weeks.assessment_key: Folk dance performance rubric (1–4): correct formation, basic steps, timing with music, cooperation with partners. Comparison chart proficient: for each dance names origin (La Raspa — Mexico; Hora — Jewish/Israeli and Eastern European (Romania); Virginia Reel — American, from English country dance; West African dance — e.g., Guinea/Mali), formation (La Raspa — partners/scattered; Hora — circle; Virginia Reel — two facing lines/longways set; West African — often circle or lines facing drummers), and purpose (celebration, social, community).

weeks.prep: Music (clean edit), space, partners if possible, a heart-rate method. Print a choreography rubric.
misconceptions: Making every move at the same level and facing forward. Use levels (high, middle, low), pathways (straight, curved, zigzag) and directions.
Choreographing without counting. Write moves by 8-counts so the routine fits the music.

days.guide: Choose a song; map intro, verse, chorus and count 8-counts in each.

questions.a: So movements change with the music and repeat on the chorus.

days.guide: Choreograph 32 counts (four 8-counts) using levels and pathways; write it down.

questions.q: Give an example of each level.
questions.a: Low: kneeling or floor move; middle: normal standing; high: jumping or on toes with arms up.
Dancers perform the same movement starting at different times, like a round.

days.guide: Rehearse; smooth transitions between 8-counts.

questions.q: How can you smooth a transition?
questions.a: End one move in a position that easily flows into the next, and practice the switch slowly.

days.guide: Perform for family.

questions.a: Four.

days.guide: Use heart-rate data to reflect on dance as exercise.

questions.q: Your HR went from 78 to 150 bpm. What does that show?
questions.a: The routine was moderate-to-vigorous cardio exercise, within the target zone.

weeks.assessment_key: Choreography rubric (1–4 each): structure (32 counts written in 8-count sections that match the music), use of levels and pathways (at least 2 levels and 2 pathways), transitions (smooth), performance (on beat, memorized, energy). Reflection proficient: uses pre/post heart-rate data to show dance raised HR into the target zone and explains it as cardio exercise.

weeks.prep: Jump rope sized correctly (stand on the middle; handles reach the armpits). Smooth surface, supportive shoes.
misconceptions: Jumping too high. Small jumps on the balls of the feet, about 1 inch off the ground.
Swinging the rope with the whole arm. Turn with the wrists, elbows close to the sides.

days.guide: Teach basic bounce, alternate foot step and side swing; 10 minutes of practice.

questions.q: How should you size a jump rope?
questions.a: Stand on the middle; the handles should reach about the armpits.
Close to your sides, turning the rope with your wrists.

days.guide: Teach criss-cross (arms cross in front on the jump) and boxer step (shift weight side to side, tapping the other foot).

questions.q: What's the key to a criss-cross?
questions.a: Cross arms wide in front so the loop opens, then uncross on the next jump.

days.guide: 5 one-minute rounds with 30-second rests; count jumps per round.

questions.q: Which energy system and component does this train?
questions.a: Cardiorespiratory endurance (aerobic) and muscular endurance in calves.

days.guide: Create a 1-minute routine with 5 skills; practice.

questions.q: Why do jump rope skills help other sports?
questions.a: They build footwork, coordination, timing and endurance.

days.guide: Perform the routine and record longest continuous-jump time.

questions.a: The rope passes under the feet twice in one jump.

weeks.assessment_key: Routine rubric (1–4): includes 5 skills (e.g., basic bounce, alternate foot, side swing, criss-cross, boxer step), smooth transitions, 1 minute long, control (few misses). Record continuous-jump time from the endurance test. Proficient: 5 skills with no more than 2 misses.

weeks.prep: Open field or track, stopwatch, cones at 0, 20 and 50 m, a baton (rolled paper or tube), phone for video.
misconceptions: Running on the heels in sprints. Sprint on the balls of the feet.
Swinging arms across the body. Arms swing forward and back ('cheek to pocket'), elbows ~90°.

days.guide: Teach A-skips (high knee with a skip), B-skips (extend lower leg and paw back), high knees.

questions.a: They train correct sprint mechanics: high knees, foot strike under the hips, quick ground contact.

days.guide: Practice standing and three-point starts: low forward lean, push hard, short powerful steps (drive phase), gradually rise.
